explanation: Asked how the recent reports contrast with earlier ones. He supplies the earlier case (Ōpōtiki — town shut down, schools closed) and states the contrast explicitly as a 'marked change in response from police'. Both halves of the comparison are given; the contrast is asserted rather than drawn out, hence not full marks.
question: How did the reports that he’s seen contrast with earlier reports of gang convoys?
statement: The people of the eastern bay do not need long memories to remember the appalling scenes in Ōpōtiki earlier last year. The town of Ōpōtiki was taken over for several days, during which images of patched gang members rolling through the town, flagrantly breaking laws, closing down roads, and preventing law-abiding members of the public going about their daily business were broadcast across the country. At that time, schools were closed and the public felt extremely unsafe. Having visited shortly afterward, that was reflected very clear to me by the locals there, and I’m proud that, already, these people who did feel unsafe have been able to see such a marked change in response from police in terms of an increased gang presence in Whakatāne.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has had from locals about the police approach. He answers that the feedback is positive, though relayed via the local MP and extended to Foxton rather than reported first-hand from locals. The core — what feedback — is delivered, with a talking-point tail that does not change whether the question was addressed.
question: What feedback has he had from locals about police’s approach to the gang convoys?
statement: Well, the outstanding local MP has been very proactive in reflecting to me the positive feedback that she has had from her community when it comes to the recent convoy in Whakatāne. In addition, I’ve continued to receive positive feedback in relation to the change in approach that started with the convoy through to Foxton late last year. I’m proud to be the Minister of Police in a Government that takes public safety seriously and that the public can already see is making a difference—that is, after six years of gang members operating with a sense of impunity.

explanation: Asked what further work is under way to protect freedom of movement over gangs. He lists the work: banning patches and insignia, dispersal notices, consorting prohibition notices. Directly and squarely answered.
question: What further work is under way to ensure that law-abiding citizens have their right to freedom of movement protected over gangs?
statement: As part of the Government’s hundred-day plan, work is under way on banning gang patches and insignia in public, as well as dispersal notices and consorting prohibition notices. These new tools will enhance police’s ability to break up large gang gatherings and convoys, and will go a long way to sending the very clear message that our police are in control, not the gangs. This is a Government that takes public safety seriously, and we’ll work hard to continue to improve that. After six years of chaos, we know this is a big task but we are determined to do it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, complete, nothing avoided.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree with the Prime Minister's quote, and if so, who spoke with him. 'Yes' answers the first part completely and triggers the second, which is then left entirely unanswered. A narrow factual sub-question — who — is squarely avoided, so this is a genuine half-answer.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister: “[And so] there were conversations last night as you’d expect after Mark’s remarks. And we spoke with Mark last night, but that’s our commitment.”; if so, who spoke with him?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether it is correct that a December coalition meeting agreed to stretch the 500 police from two years to three. 'No.' A flat denial is a direct and complete answer to a yes/no question; whether it is true is Veracity, not this.
question: Is it correct that, as reported by Newsroom, a meeting was held between coalition parties in December last year and it was agreed to change the delivery of 500 more police over two years to three years?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether the Deputy Prime Minister is correct about a chiefs-of-staff meeting last night. He says plainly that he has no knowledge and redirects to the Deputy Prime Minister. Stating outright that he cannot speak to it engages the question rather than dodging round it, though it stops short of resolving what was asked.
question: I’ll just say the question again. Is the Deputy Prime Minister correct that a meeting was held last night between the National Party’s chief of staff and New Zealand First’s chief of staff, and at that meeting it was agreed that the Government would return to delivering 500 more police within two years?
statement: I’ve got no knowledge. You’d have to ask the Deputy Prime Minister.

explanation: A loaded two-part question. He explicitly separates and answers both: yes to agreeing with the Prime Minister, no to the 6.5 percent cut premise. Both parts addressed on the record; he does not elaborate on the second, but a 'no' is a complete answer to it.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that “Mark could have expressed himself better”, and, if so, is the reason he’s struggling to express himself because a 6.5 percent cut to the police front line is unexplainable?
statement: Well, I agree with what the Prime Minister said, so yes to the first part; no to the second.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned about how many waterways were too polluted to use over summer. She opens with 'Yes, I am concerned' and cites the Auckland beaches. The long detour into causes and the previous Government is Focus, not evasion — the question itself was answered up front.
question: Is she concerned about how many rivers, lakes, and beaches across the country were too polluted to swim in or gather food from over the summer?
statement: Yes, I am concerned, including with the fact that more than 20 beaches in Auckland in December were unswimmable because of human sewage, which reinforces that polluted rivers, lakes, and beaches are an issue to be addressed by all New Zealanders, both rural and urban. There are, of course, different causes of pollution that range from land use, wild animals, and human waste from infrastructure failures. Pollution occurs in both urban and rural areas, but the evidence does show that urban water bodies are in the poorest state. It is deeply disappointing that six years of the previous Government, Labour-Greens, did not address this, but we are determined to get this right. This Government is committed to improving freshwater quality for the benefit of all, and to do this we need sensible and pragmatic environmental rules. I’m also very pleased to tell you that the beach in Riverton, Southland—the “riviera of the south”—was outstanding all summer.

explanation: Asked whether she has read the open letter from 51 freshwater experts. 'Yes, indeed I have read that letter.' Direct and complete; the following remark about a range of views is surplus, not a substitute for the answer.
question: Has she read the open letter last month from 51 freshwater experts and leaders that states: “New Zealand’s rivers, lakes and aquifers are in a dire state.”, and, “If you proceed with your proposals to undo the country’s freshwater policy, they will only get worse.”?
statement: Yes, indeed I have read that letter from 50-plus freshwater scientists and experts, and I acknowledge the member’s own expertise in this area. There will always be a range of interests and views from academics, from scientists, from commercial and recreation users, and from iwi.

explanation: Asked why the Government pushed the regional council plan deadline out to 2027. She gives a reason — the NPS-FM is being rewritten and Te Mana o te Wai rebalanced — which implies the delay, but never connects it to the deadline or says why the rewrite required pushing it out. It reaches toward the question without landing on the 'why' that was asked.
question: Why, then, did the Government delay freshwater improvements already in progress by pushing out the deadline for regional council plans to 2027?
statement: The Government considers that there needs to be a rebalance of Te Mana o te Wai and a rewriting of the National Policy Statement on Freshwater Management to ensure that it is fit for purpose and that it achieves genuine outcomes.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees that upholding Te Mana o te Wai would help achieve those outcomes. She engages the named concept directly and signals a position (it is 'not in consideration'; the hierarchy of obligations will be rebalanced), which implies disagreement, but she never states agreement or disagreement with the proposition put. Partial engagement, core left implicit.
question: Does the Minister agree that progressing and upholding of Te Mana o te Wai would help achieve those outcomes?
statement: Te Mana o te Wai is not in consideration. It is the hierarchy of the obligations that we consider needs to be relooked at and rebalanced.

explanation: Asked what assurances she can give that local waterways will be swimmable given 45% are not. She offers no assurance about swimmability, instead blaming the past six years and restating a general commitment to replace the NPS and improve water quality. It gestures at the topic but does not reach the assurance asked for. (Vagueness is Specificity; the blame line is Focus — neither is what drops this score, the unaddressed core is.)
question: What assurances, if any, can she provide to Kiwis that their local waterway will be safe to swim in, when 45 percent of the total river length in Aotearoa is currently unswimmable according to the Ministry for the Environment?
statement: We agree that the past six years have not addressed this sufficiently. The Government is committed to replacing the national policy statement for fresh water. We are committed to improving the quality of fresh water.

explanation: Asked for a commitment that changes be informed by scientific evidence. She answers with a commitment to consult widely — scientists among many groups — and a 'balanced approach', which substitutes a broader, weaker undertaking for the one requested. Neither given nor refused; adjacent rather than square.
question: Will she commit to ensuring that any changes to freshwater regulations are informed by scientific evidence on the health of New Zealand’s waterways?
statement: I can assure the member that we will be consulting widely. We will be consulting with academics, with scientists, with iwi, and with commercial and recreational users. So we will consult widely and take a balanced approach to ensure that we come up with workable solutions.

explanation: Asked what steps he is taking to progress the EU FTA. He names the concrete step (first reading of the implementation legislation today) and the intent to move quickly through ratification. Directly and completely answered; the closing swipe at the previous Government is a Focus matter and does not reduce Forthrightness.
question: What steps is he undertaking to progress the New Zealand-European Union Free Trade Agreement?
statement: Today, the coalition Government will have with the House the first reading of the implementation legislation to start the process to quickly implement the New Zealand - EU free-trade agreement (FTA). We will progress quickly with the implementation of this bill so that New Zealand exporters can take advantage of its benefits as soon as possible. You see, the European Union has already completed its part of the ratification process before New Zealand. New Zealand exporters are waiting on the New Zealand Parliament to complete the process so that the agreement can enter into force. This coalition Government is moving quickly so that exporters, particularly in provincial New Zealand, can benefit from tariff reductions of up to $100 million, something that could have been done last year if the last Government had introduced the bill and got it through before the election.

explanation: Asked why the deal matters to exporters. He answers squarely: tariffs and quotas currently lock products out, with the mānuka honey and kiwifruit reductions cited, and levelling the field against competitors. The question is fully engaged.
question: Why is this deal so important to New Zealand exporters?
statement: Well, until now, many New Zealand products have been, effectively, locked out of the EU market due to high tariffs and restrictive quotas. For instance, duties on mānuka honey production will reduce by 17.3 percent to 0; the kiwifruit growers benefit from tariff savings of $37 million on entry into force. The FTA finally levels the playing field for Kiwi businesses exporting to the EU, where many of their key competitors already have competitive access. These savings would’ve benefited New Zealand exporters had the last Government introduced legislation and got it through before the last election.

explanation: Asked what else the FTA delivers. He answers directly with GDP and export effects and duty-free coverage, and volunteers what was not delivered for dairy and red meat. Complete engagement with the question asked.
question: What else does the FTA deliver for New Zealand exporters?
statement: Well, when fully implemented, the FTA is set to provide an annual boost to our GDP of up to $1.4 billion and to our exports to the EU by up to $1.8 billion each year. For the first day of entry into force, 91 percent of New Zealand’s current goods trade into the EU are duty-free, increasing to 97 percent. Unfortunately, the commercially meaningful gains that the dairy and red meat sector expected by our farmers were not delivered in this deal. Access will not be fully liberalised for these products, but quotas do create some additional market access on improvement of status quo. Overall, the FTA creates jobs and grows wealth for all New Zealanders, which is why we want to get it into force as quickly as possible.

explanation: Asked for specific benefits to the agricultural sector; he gives horticulture and seafood tariff outcomes from day one with figures. Squarely on the question. (Whether horticulture and seafood fully cover 'agricultural' is a completeness quibble, not a dodge; the final slogan line is Focus, not this attribute.)
question: What are some of the specific benefits of this deal for the agricultural sector?
statement: Well, a number of key agricultural products will benefit from significant tariff savings from day one of the agreement: 99.9 percent of New Zealand’s current horticultural trade will enter the EU tariff-free at the entry into force—a tariff saving of $46 million for our growers. Tariffs will be eliminated immediately on kiwifruit, onions, apples, and other hort products; 99.5 percent of New Zealand’s current fish and seafood trade will enter the EU tariff-free from day one, which is why the coalition Government wants to so urgently get this agreement into force. This is a Government of action, not talk.

explanation: A standing 'does he stand by all statements and actions' question, answered 'yes, most definitely' with the customary time-and-context qualifier, then an illustration. The yes/no is delivered plainly; the qualifier is conventional rather than an escape.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, yes, most definitely, in the time and in the context that they were given. An example of that I’m sure we’ll always stand for is this Government’s commitment in the Speech from the Throne to establish a Ministry of Regulation and pass the Regulatory Standards Bill. For too long, Governments have neglected the impact of red tape and regulation on the Kiwi can-do attitude and people that want to get on with building a wealthier country. Well, now we’ve got a Government that’s going to do something about it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the quoted answer and, if so, why. He says yes and then supplies the why (an Associate Minister committed to reducing smoking who sought advice). Both halves of the question are answered.
question: Does he stand by his answers to oral questions yesterday, “What I think is fantastic is we have an Associate Minister with delegation for reducing smoking. She’s incredibly focused on that goal, and she’s asked her officials for a range of advice to actually lower smoking in New Zealand.”; if so, why?
statement: Yes, we do, because, actually, it is fantastic to have an Associate Minister committed to reducing smoking rates. It’s fantastic to have a Minister who asked for a range of advice. I can’t imagine the psychology of someone who doesn’t want a Minister who is (a) committed to reducing smoking and (b) interested in listening to advice.

explanation: Asked whether anyone affiliated with the tobacco industry helped develop or write the documents Costello passed to officials. He answers a different question — that coalition partners took no tobacco funding and that he is confident of no undue influence. Authorship of the documents is never addressed, and the substitution is the dodge.
question: Can he assure this House that no person affiliated with the tobacco industry was involved in developing or writing the documents Casey Costello passed on to her officials?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I’ve had assurances from all coalition partners in this Government that they have had no funding from the tobacco industry, and I am confident that there has been no undue influence on the policies of this Government by the tobacco industry.

explanation: The identical question, re-put; the response narrows further to a confidence assertion about 'undue influence on policy formation'. Who wrote or contributed to the documents is again untouched, with even the funding assurance now dropped. A narrow factual question squarely avoided.
question: Can he assure this House that no person affiliated with the tobacco industry was involved in developing or writing the documents Casey Costello passed on to her officials?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I am confident that there has been no undue influence on the policy formation of this Government.

explanation: Asked whether the Prime Minister had put the question to Minister Costello. The reply is a plain, explicit declination to answer about that conversation — not a pivot, not an attack, no filibuster. Per the refusal rule a stated 'I won't answer' engages the question rather than dodging it, though 'can't ... at this time' is softer and less complete than a flat refusal, so it sits below the blunt-no benchmark.
question: Has the Prime Minister asked Minister Costello whether or not the tobacco industry informed the policy document or wrote the policy document she gave to health officials?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I can’t answer in respect to that conversation, at this time.

explanation: Asked whether he is confident all Ministers have declared conflicts of interest. Answered with a flat "Yes" before a gratuitous jab — the jab is a Civility matter, not a dodge. The question was engaged directly and completely.
question: Is he confident that all of his Ministers have declared all conflicts, or potential conflicts, of interest?
statement: Yes. And that question was about as effective as a Marama Davidson etymology lesson.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a specific quoted Seymour statement about secret donation foundations, and if not, why not. Never says agree or disagree with the statement; offers generic admiration for Seymour and pivots to coalition unity talking points. The core of the question is left untouched.
question: Does he agree with David Seymour, “We can’t sit around the table everyday with somebody that, in the past, at least, has had secret foundations where all of the donations go, doesn’t declare them like any other political party would, and, of course, we don’t know why that money was paid, by whom, for what purpose”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Prime Minister, I’m a great admirer of the wisdom that David Seymour brings to many matters. The other thing I would note is that, in spite of his prognostication, this coalition Government is far more united and effective than the Opposition’s worst nightmare—in fact, we’re your nightmare dressed up as a daydream.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by being responsible for all Ministers, and when will he dismiss Casey Costello. Confirms the first part and effectively answers the second — full confidence in her, i.e. no dismissal. The "when" is answered only by implication rather than stated outright, so short of complete.
question: Does he stand by his comment that “Well, I’m responsible for all Ministers, irrespective of which party they come from”, and, if so, when will he dismiss Casey Costello?
statement: Well, you know, the member has been in Cabinet, so she’ll be aware that the Prime Minister is responsible for all Ministers. In respect of Casey Costello, I have full confidence in her, and I’m sure that, in time, that member will too.

explanation: Asked whether she had seen any recent reports on income growth. Says she has and states what the report showed. Directly and completely answered.
question: Has she seen any recent reports on income growth in New Zealand?
statement: I’ve seen a report showing that the median wage in 2010 was $40,000, and that now it has risen to $65,000. This means that someone earning the median wage back in 2010 was firmly in the 17.5 percent personal income tax bracket, and now they are firmly in the 30 percent tax bracket. Through neglect, the personal income tax scale has failed to keep up with growth in incomes.

explanation: Asked what tax bracket minimum wage earners are in. States the dependency on hours and then gives the bracket — 30 percent for a 40-hour worker. The question is squarely answered.
question: What tax bracket are minimum wage earners in?
statement: That depends on how many hours they work, of course, but let me give you an example. A person working 40 hours a week on the minimum wage in 2010 was earning $27,000. After the increase in the minimum wage, a person working 40 hours a week on the minimum wage will now be earning more than $48,000, and therefore—like median income earners—will be in the 30 percent tax bracket. Again, through neglect, the personal income tax scale has failed to keep up with the growth in incomes.

explanation: Asked when New Zealanders last saw a reduction in personal income taxes. Gives a precise date, 1 October 2010, with context. Complete answer to the question asked.
question: When was the last time New Zealanders saw any reduction in the personal income taxes they pay?
statement: Well, sadly, you have to go all the way back to 1 October 2010, when the National Government reduced personal income taxes after Budget 2010. That is 14 years ago. To be fair, personal income tax reductions were legislated for in 2017. However, the incoming Labour Government cancelled them, and then introduced a new top tax rate of 39 percent. So, apart from the new top rate, personal income tax rates and thresholds have remained exactly as they are since October 2010.

explanation: Asked whether she had seen any reports relating to personal income tax reductions. Answers yes and identifies the report. Direct and complete.
question: Has she seen any reports relating to personal income tax reductions?
statement: Yes, I have seen a report on reductions in personal income tax. This came from Australia, where the Labor Government has just announced the third in a series of personal income tax reductions. I thought this was highly relevant for New Zealand as it shows that such reductions are commonplace and can be adopted by Governments of all political stripes.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the quoted coalition agreement wording. Confirms the wording is as quoted and that the Government is delivering on it — an affirmative answer to the stand-by question, though it confirms the text slightly more squarely than the endorsement.
question: Does she stand by the statement in the National Party and ACT Party coalition agreement, “The concepts of ACT’s income tax policy are considered as a pathway to delivering National’s promised tax relief, subject to no earner being worse off than they would be under National’s plan”?
statement: I can confirm to the member that that is indeed the wording in the coalition agreement, and the Government is delivering on that commitment.

explanation: Asked to rule out cutting the top rate from 39c to 33c this term. "I've already done so" — a one-line, unambiguous, complete answer.
question: Will the Minister rule out cutting the top income tax rate from 39c to 33c in this term of Government?
statement: I’ve already done so.

explanation: Asked how ACT's tax system can still be under consideration when a core plank has been ruled out. Offers only that "there are many aspects" under discussion, then turns to attacking the questioner's record. It brushes the question without resolving the contradiction put to her.
question: How, then, can the ACT Party system of taxation be being considered by the Minister when a core plank of it she has just ruled out?
statement: Well, there are many aspects to the proposals that Mr Seymour and I are discussing along with other Ministers in the Cabinet. I have to say that I am delighted to see the new-found interest from the Opposition member in the necessity to reduce taxation. If only he’d taken one of the six opportunities he had to do so.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he had made on health workforce safety and security. Names the announcement — 200 extra security staff across 32 EDs. The question is answered directly.
question: What recent announcements has he made about improving the safety and security of our health workforce?
statement: Our health workforce is the backbone of our health system and we will support them. That is why we increased the number of security staff in emergency departments (EDs) by an additional 200 staff across 32 EDs over the Christmas and new year period.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has received about the security uplift. He reports the feedback directly — from staff and patients at hospitals he visited, and a noticeable reduction in abuse. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What feedback has he received about this important uplift in security?
statement: I have visited a number of hospitals across the country and have heard firsthand from staff and patients how beneficial this programme has been. I am told that there has been a noticeable reduction in the number of people who have been abusive towards staff. This has improved due to the increased presence of security in our EDs and has ensured people feel safer when they access care in their times of need.

explanation: Asked why this was a priority for the Government. He gives a reason (a gang fight remedied by ED guards) and explicitly ties it back: "That is why this programme was such a priority." Direct.
question: Why was this such a priority for the Government?
statement: Just last week, guards that were provided through our ED security boost helped to swiftly remedy a fight in Christchurch Hospital’s emergency department between gang members. That is why this programme was such a priority for the Government. The safety of our health workforce and patients is and always will be a top priority. We must say no to violence in our EDs.

explanation: Asked what the next steps are. He names them — assess the impact of the programme, look for long-term safety improvements. The steps are thin on detail, but detail is Specificity; the question was engaged, not dodged.
question: What are the next steps for security in emergency departments?
statement: This programme addressed an urgent, immediate need over the busy summer period. We’ll be assessing the impact that this has had and will look for ways to improve safety long term. Ideally, we would not and should not require security in our EDs. This Government is committed to law and order and making our streets safer for everyone, including our EDs.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statements and policies. "Yes." One word, complete.
question: Does she stand by all of her statements and policies?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how she justifies removing section 7AA given rising abuse rates. She supplies a justification (best interests must lead every decision) and engages the abuse figures by attributing harm to placements back into family care. Answers the "how do you justify" core, though it slides toward wraparound services at the end.
question: How can she justify removing section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act when rates of abuse for tamariki Māori in the Crown’s care have almost doubled in the last five years?
statement: Repealing section 7AA is something that I have campaigned on for the last three years. We need to make sure that the best interests are first and foremost in every decision we are making around our children, and those reports are showing that a lot of that harm is when children are being placed back into family care. We need to make sure that we are creating the best wraparound services possible so that these young people have a chance in life to not just survive but thrive.

explanation: A yes/no question: will she accept responsibility for further increases in abuse resulting from her policies? She never says yes or no — she pivots to taking the role seriously and her focus on child safety. The core is left untouched.
question: Will the Minister accept responsibility for any further increases in rates of abuse of tamariki Māori in State care as a result of her policies, including removing section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act?
statement: I take this role very seriously, and every report of harm of a child is disappointing. My focus is to make sure that every child—Māori or non-Māori—is safe, loved, and cared for.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statements and actions. "Yes", followed by elaboration on which statement in particular. Answered.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in particular what I said in answering the member’s question in the House yesterday, when I said, “When I received this delegation, I provided a range of information to officials, including things like Hansard … and previous policy proposals around smoke-free and vaping to help guide conversations. The health paper came back setting out a number of areas … [to provide] advice [on] … and I marked that I wanted advice on [each] of them”. That health briefing refers to proposals and notes. I want to be clear they were not my proposals or notes. They were not things I had written. This was general information I had provided officials, and I’m sure they can verify this.

explanation: Asked why her RNZ statement conflicts with the notes she gave officials. She does offer an explanation of the discrepancy — that the question she was answering was about seeking specific advice, which she had not done. It engages the contradiction, though it opens by blaming media distortion and reframes the premise rather than confronting the notes' content.
question: Why did she tell Radio New Zealand, “I haven’t looked at a freeze on the excise duty at all” when the notes she gave to officials said, “Freeze the excise rates on smoked tobacco for three years starting 31 December 2023”?
statement: It is unfortunate the actions have been distorted by a media article. The fact is I was asked a question about whether I had sought specific advice. I had not sought specific advice, which is the question I answered, and I referred to a range of advice I had sought from officials.

explanation: Asked to explain the same apparent contradiction. She restates her earlier position ("I stated I had not sought specific advice on the excise tax") rather than explaining it. It stays on the topic asked and is not a pivot to talking points, but a restatement only half-reaches an "explain" question.
question: How does she explain her statement to RNZ that “I had not sought that advice at all.” when she had requested it through the documents she provided to the Ministry of Health?
statement: As I said, I stated I had not sought specific advice on the excise tax.

explanation: A narrow factual question: who wrote or collated the notes? She describes what the document is (historical NZ First policy positions, five pages) but never names or characterises the author or collator. Partial — provenance is gestured at, authorship is not given.
question: Who wrote or collated the notes that said, “Freeze the excise rate on smoked tobacco” that she gave to health officials?
statement: The documentation is a range of historical policy positions and notes that were held in New Zealand First policy positions. Some of it relates to things that were passed in the legislation when New Zealand First was in Government. This is a range of points and positions and it’s about five pages long.

explanation: Asked how a historical document could contain a proposal dated December 2023. She does not address the date contradiction at all; she answers the previous question instead, about authorship, and re-asserts that they were historical positions.
question: The question cannot have been credibly answered, because how could a historical document contain a policy proposal for December 2023?
statement: The pages of notes that were provided to the officials were a compilation of information that was extracted; the authors, I’m not sure of. They were historical policy positions.

explanation: Asked who wrote the note. "I couldn't tell you the author of that document." An unhelpful answer, but a direct and complete one — a plain "I don't know" answers the question rather than dodging it.
question: Who wrote the note that said, “Freeze the excise tax on smoked tobacco in 2023” that she gave to officials?
statement: I couldn’t tell you the author of that document. It’s in the document archives.

explanation: Asked how the public can trust her given notes saying nicotine isn't harmful. She never touches the notes or the trust question — she restates that she is 'seeking a broad range of advice' on vaping and quitting. The core of the question is left untouched; this is a pivot to a general policy position.
question: How can the public trust her to take action on youth vaping when she is sending notes to officials saying that nicotine isn’t harmful?
statement: As I’ve stated in the policy positions that we have taken, I’m seeking a broad range of advice, including how we deter youth from vaping and taking up, and also how we give the tools to those who are addicted to nicotine to quit smoking.

explanation: A closed yes/no question about whether she denied seeking advice on an excise freeze. Answer: 'No.' Complete and unambiguous. Whether the denial is true is Veracity, not Forthrightness; as an answer it is maximally direct.
question: Did she deny seeking advice on a tobacco excise tax freeze when asked by Radio New Zealand, despite having actually sought that advice, because she did not want to be questioned on her plans to give tax breaks to the tobacco industry?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether the 500-police commitment is Government policy. Answer: 'Yes; the Government will deliver 500 net more police on the beat in two years.' Direct affirmative with the commitment restated. Slight rewording ('net more on the beat' vs 'trained') but the question is squarely engaged.
question: Is it the Government’s policy to train “no fewer than 500 new frontline police within the first two years”, as per the National and New Zealand First coalition agreement?
statement: Yes; the Government will deliver 500 net more police on the beat in two years.

explanation: Asked when he first became aware recruitment practices wouldn't deliver growth. He gives a timing answer — 'as the incoming Minister' — then elaborates on the causes. That is an answer to 'when', just an imprecise one; the imprecision is a Specificity issue, not a dodge. Marked down only because the bulk of the response drifts to the reasons rather than the timing.
question: Given the Minister’s renewed commitment to the National and New Zealand First coalition agreement of 500 new police within two years, when did he first become aware that Police’s current recruitment practices would not enable police to achieve any desired growth without other interventions?
statement: Well, as I’ve said many times in this House, I became aware as the incoming Minister that Police faced major challenges around recruiting due to the fact that the Australians are here recruiting our police officers, they were finding it difficult to fill recruit wings, and we’ve got many police officers that are fast approaching retirement age.

explanation: A narrow factual question: when did he inform the Prime Minister's office. He answers a different question — that he had 'several conversations ... with several of my colleagues' — giving neither a date nor confirmation that the PM's office was among them. A tightly-specified question with its core avoided.
question: When did he first inform the Prime Minister’s office that Police’s current recruitment practices would not enable Police to achieve any desired growth without other interventions?
statement: I had several conversations when I became aware of the situation around recruiting, with several of my colleagues.

explanation: Two-part question: which specific interventions, and will he rule out lowering standards. He offers one anecdote (a Gisborne constable mentoring recruits) which glances at part one, concludes with 'look at many different options', and never addresses the rule-out at all. Half the question is unanswered and the other half only gestured at.
question: What specific interventions is he considering in order to meet his renewed commitment to the 500 new police in two years, and will he rule out lowering current recruitment standards as one of them?
statement: I was recently at the Gisborne Police Station and there was a young constable there that had been put in charge of mentoring and identifying young people in the community that may be interested in a career in Police. He has been very successful. In the latest recruit wing, I think there were four that had been recruited through that process and were proudly graduating. So I think we’re just going to have to look at many different options in terms of how we meet our target of 500 over two years.

explanation: Asked whether the 500 are all constabulary or include authorised officers. He answers it: '500 sworn police officers' — i.e. all constabulary — and volunteers the standards answer he withheld earlier. The swipe at the previous Government is a Civility/Focus matter and does not lower this; the question itself is answered squarely.
question: Will the 500 new police all be constabulary or does it include authorised officers?
statement: No. Unlike the previous Government, who deceived New Zealand by saying they had recruited 1,800 front-line police officers when in fact they hadn’t—it was 1,500—we will be recruiting, training, and deploying 500 sworn police officers. In relation to standards, no we will not be dropping standards.

explanation: Asked whether he considers the EV road user charges fair, and if so why. Answer: 'Yes', followed by the reason — EVs will pay the same RUC as other light vehicles. Both limbs of the question are engaged directly.
question: Does he consider the proposed road user charges for electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids fair, compared with road user charges and fuel excise duty for similarly sized vehicles; if so, why?
statement: Yes. The Government has announced that electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids will contribute towards the maintenance of our roads, as other vehicles do. The changes proposed for electric vehicles will ensure that they pay the same amount as a road-user charge as those other light vehicles which pay a road-user charge. There are variances throughout the system, and that is why the coalition agreement with ACT commits this Government to progress a fleet-wide transition to road-user charges that will result in a much fairer charging system based on how much people travel the roads and the weight of their vehicle.

explanation: Asked how it is fair that an EV owner pays more than double on a specific trip. He concedes 'there are variances throughout the system' — which touches the premise — but then answers about a future fleet-wide transition and the last Government instead of defending the fairness of the case put. Partial engagement, core not reached.
question: How is it fair that the average electric vehicle or plug-in hybrid owner would pay more than double the tax of a similarly sized petrol vehicle for a return trip from Wellington to Auckland?
statement: There are variances throughout the system, as I acknowledged. That is why the coalition Government has agreed to progress a fleet-wide transition to road-user charges that will result in a much fairer charging system. This was an issue that was not addressed under the last Government, and this is the first step towards ensuring that all vehicles who use the road pay towards contributing towards maintaining it.

explanation: Asked to confirm a specific factual proposition (EV pays more than twice on Wellington–Auckland). He neither confirms nor denies: 'a range of variables' is followed by a restatement of the reform rationale. A confirm/deny question left unresolved.
question: Therefore, I can confirm that the Minister acknowledges that an electric vehicle or plug-in hybrid, as shown here, would pay more than twice as much in road tax under his proposal on a trip from Wellington to Auckland?
statement: There’s a range of variables around how much based on the fuel usage. The problem with the current system is that it charges people based on how many litres of fuel they put into their car rather than how much they use the road. We want to move to a system which charges based on how many kilometres and the weight of that vehicle, rather than what type of fuel motors that vehicle. That is the reform that we are progressing.

explanation: Asked whether the Government is happy to disincentivise EVs in the interim. Answer: 'No', with the reason (the exemption was always time-limited and the 2 percent threshold is reached). Direct denial that engages what was asked.
question: So his Government is happy to financially disincentivise electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles relative to polluting fossil fuel vehicles in the interim while we wait for his alternative road-user charges proposal?
statement: No. This Government has confirmed that the exemption, which would run out on 1 April this year—which was, actually, by the way, put in place by the last National Government to help incentivise electric vehicle uptake—will end now that 2 percent of the fleet is electric. What we’re saying is all users of our road should pay and contribute towards maintaining it.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about the combined disincentive effect. Answer: 'No' — a direct response to the yes/no put to him. He then disputes the questioner's framing rather than engaging the Ministry of Transport advice about the third emissions budget, which was part of the question's grounds, so it falls short of complete.
question: Is he concerned about the combined disincentive effect of charging electric vehicles more tax, given the Ministry of Transport’s advice that scrapping the Clean Car Discount means transport may fail to meet its third emissions budget?
statement: No. The issue that the member continues to raise is she’s just simply looking at how much tax is paid based on the number of litres or the type of fuel used. We want to move it to being a distance and weight change, and that member’s graph that she continues to raise doesn’t take into account the full running costs of those vehicles. As everyone knows, electric vehicles are far cheaper to use and drive, as many members of this House know, but that graph that she uses misinforms the House.

explanation: Asked for the logical connection between a vehicle having lower running costs and contributing less per kilometre. Brown does not touch the question at all — he mocks the questioner's co-leadership bid and invites her to table it. Attacking the questioner in place of any engagement is the clearest form of dodge.
question: Is the Minister aware that the running charges for efficient petrol vehicles would also be lower, therefore their contribution to tax is lower than less efficient vehicles, and, therefore, what is the logical connection between cars having lower running costs and contributing less to the roads on a per-kilometre basis?
statement: Well, I really enjoyed the co-leadership bid from the member opposite, and if she would like to table a copy of that document, I’d be very happy to have a read.

explanation: Asked on what basis EVs are said to have lower running costs and so should pay more, when the same is not applied to efficient petrol vehicles. Brown engages the inconsistency directly — he concedes 'there are variances throughout the system' and answers that the resolution is moving all vehicles to RUC charged on distance and weight rather than fuel type. He reaches the core of the question but never justifies the current asymmetry he was asked to defend, so this is a partial answer rather than a complete one.
question: Is the Minister aware that vehicles that run on petrol that have lower running costs would also contribute less to the roads on a per-kilometre basis, and, therefore, on what basis is he saying that electric vehicles have lower running costs and therefore should pay more to run on the roads, when that’s not the case for petrol vehicles?
statement: As I’ve said to the House a number of times, there are variances throughout the system and that is why we have started work to move all vehicles to the road-user charges system so people pay based on distance travelled and vehicle weight rather than the type of fuel that is used. We think that is a far fairer way to charge, and that is where we are heading.

explanation: Asked what proposals he has made to streamline conduct requirements for financial institutions. Bayly answers directly and enumerates the three elements announced: three regulators to two, six licences to one, and reform of the CoFI requirements for smaller institutions. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What proposals has he made to streamline and simplify the conduct requirements for financial institutions in New Zealand?
statement: Yesterday, I announced at the Financial Services Council meeting my intention to simplify regulations, cut red tape, and reduce costs to financial institutions. There were three elements: first of all, the proposal to move from three to two regulators; secondly, to reduce from a maximum of six licences to a single licence; and thirdly, to reform the Conduct of Financial Institutions requirements to make it easier for smaller financial institutions to meet their obligations. We are committed to reducing compliance and regulation, where appropriate, and getting the economy back on track.

explanation: Asked how clearly defining the two regulators' roles will assist financial institutions. Bayly answers the 'how': institutions currently answer to up to three regulators, the change gives a prudential regulator and a single conduct regulator, producing clearer lines of responsibility so firms can focus on running their businesses. Direct and complete.
question: How will clearly defining the roles of the two regulators assist financial institutions?
statement: Currently, some institutions are accountable to up to three regulators. What I announced yesterday is a move to just two regulators—the first being a prudential regulator, who is, of course, the Reserve Bank, but, more importantly, moving to a single conduct regulator, being the Financial Markets Authority (FMA). By making this change, financial institutions will have clearer lines of responsibility, which means they can focus on running their businesses more effectively.

explanation: Asked what the benefits of a single licensing regime are. Bayly names them — replacing up to five FMA licences plus an additional CoFI licence with one, giving less duplication and reduced operational burden without compromising conduct requirements. The benefits asked for are actually stated.
question: What are the benefits of moving to a single licensed regime of conduct?
statement: Currently, some institutions have to apply up to or hold five licences with the FMA. With the new Conduct of Financial Institutions—or CoFI—bill, that requires an additional licence. What we’re proposing to do is to move to a single licence issued by the FMA—or Financial Markets Authority—which means less duplication, reduces the operational burden for institutions without compromising conduct requirements.

explanation: Asked how the Government will make it easier for smaller institutions to meet CoFI obligations. Bayly gives the mechanism: he is requesting the FMA issue clear guidance on the minimum requirements for smaller institutions, letting them take a proportionate, tailored approach. Answers the 'how' directly.
question: How will this Government make it easier for smaller financial institutions to meet their CoFI obligations?
statement: As I announced yesterday, I’m requesting that the FMA issue clear guidance on the minimum requirements necessary for smaller institutions to meet their obligations under CoFI regulations and legislation. This will allow the smaller institutions to develop a more tailored approach, ensuring obligations are both proportionate and fit for purpose, while balancing the importance of fair treatment for customers.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on New Zealand's fiscal position. Willis names the report — Treasury's briefing to the incoming Minister, publicly released a week and a half ago — and states what it told her. The question was for a report; a report is identified.
question: What recent reports has she seen on New Zealand’s fiscal position?
statement: I received Treasury’s briefing to the incoming Minister (BIM), which was publicly released a week and a half ago. The BIM told me that between 2019 and 2023, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has calculated, according to their own cross-country measure, that net debt in New Zealand increased by 18 percent of GDP—18 percent of GDP.

explanation: Asked whether the debt increase was greater or less than in comparable countries. Willis does not utter 'greater', but she answers by putting New Zealand's 18 percent against Australia's 2 percent, reductions in Denmark and Ireland, and a 4 percent average across 32 advanced economies. The comparison asked for is supplied and the direction is unambiguous.
question: Is that increase in debt greater or less than in other comparable countries?
statement: As I said, the increase in New Zealand’s net debt over the period 2019-23 was 18 percent of GDP on the IMF’s measure. Treasury’s BIM tells me that Australia’s net debt over this period rose by only 2 percent, Denmark’s and Ireland’s net debt reduced, and the average increase across 32 advanced economies was only 4 percent.

explanation: Asked whether the 18 percent increase in net debt was due to COVID. Willis answers first — 'In part, it will have been' — and only then argues that COVID is no excuse because all countries suffered it. The yes/no core is given before the argument, which is the mark of a forthright answer.
question: Was that 18 percent increase in net debt due to COVID?
statement: In part, it will have been. But I am reliably informed that all countries in the world suffered from COVID, so COVID is no excuse for New Zealand to have such a large increase in its debt.

explanation: Asked how New Zealand's net debt compares with previous years. Willis flags that the 2022 change of definition complicates the comparison, then gives it on the old measure: 44 percent of GDP forecast this year against 22 percent in 2017, and the highest in 30 years. The caveat precedes rather than replaces the answer.
question: How high is New Zealand’s net debt compared to previous years?
statement: Historical comparisons are made a little difficult by the fact that, in 2022, the previous finance Minister changed the definition of net debt in a way that instantly lowered it by about 20 percentage points of GDP. However, if you use the old, established measure of net debt, it is evident that New Zealand’s net debt this year is forecast to be 44 percent of GDP, compared to 22 percent when National left office in 2017. Furthermore, net debt of 44 percent is the highest it has been in New Zealand in 30 years.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the Government's statements and actions. Answered "Yes" outright; the law-and-order material that follows is volunteered elaboration, not a substitute for the answer. Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and in particular I stand by this Government’s recent actions to begin restoring law and order and cracking down on crime by removing taxpayer funding for section 27 reports to further discount sentences and by chucking out Labour’s prison reduction target. New Zealanders voted for a Government that’s going to restore law and order, deal with victims over criminals, and that’s what we’re going to get on and do.

explanation: Asked to adjudicate between two positions — his own ("no intention beyond first reading") and Seymour's prediction that he will change his mind. The reply restates his own position, which implicitly picks himself, but never engages Seymour's claim about changing his mind. Reaches the substance sideways without answering the "who's correct" that was put.
question: Who’s correct when it comes to the proposed Government legislation on Treaty principles: the Prime Minister, when he said, “Well, we’ve never been open-minded, we’ve always said there’s no intention, no commitment, no support for it beyond first reading”, or David Seymour, who said, “But ultimately the bit I don’t believe is he won’t change his mind”?
statement: Well, we have a coalition agreement that says we’re going to support a bill through to first reading, and that’s no commitment beyond that.

explanation: Asked yes/no whether Seymour is correct that he has lost his nerve. "I reject the member's assertion" is a direct denial and does answer the question; everything after it pivots to attacking Labour. Answered, then abandoned — the denial stands, so this is not a dodge, but the bulk of the response goes elsewhere.
question: Is David Seymour correct that he’s lost his nerve on the Treaty principles bill?
statement: I reject the member’s assertion, but what I’d say is that member should be the one that is nervous, because when Kieran McAnulty starts shaving off that beard, he needs to be ready to go, and, as I would have said, as we observed over summer, who was the de facto leader of the Labour Party? Michael Wood.

explanation: Asked whether it is acceptable for a Minister to say publicly that the PM has lost his nerve and is not being truthful. Rejects the premise, then offers "we have different views and that's fine", which implies acceptability without ever saying so. Gestures at the question without landing on it.
question: Is it acceptable for one of his Ministers to tell the media that the Prime Minister has lost his nerve and he doesn’t believe the Prime Minister is being truthful with the public?
statement: Well, I reject that member’s assertion in that question. What I’d say to you is that we are a coalition Government. We are a coalition Government, we have different views and different perspectives, and we are aligned on the things that matter, which is getting things done, cleaning up after your Government’s mess. So that’s what we’re going to get on and do.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question: was the Newshub quote incorrect? The reply says nothing about the quote at all and pivots to praising Seymour's schools delegation and attacking the questioner's record as education Minister. Complete dodge of a question that had a one-word answer available.
question: Was Newshub incorrect when they quoted David Seymour as saying, “ultimately the bit I don’t believe is he won’t change his mind if the public really wants it,”?
statement: Well, I can tell you David Seymour is doing a great job. He’s going to make sure that we get our kids back in school. He’s got special delegation getting kids back into school, which is something that this Government and you as education Minister didn’t care about.

explanation: Asked a hypothetical: would a Minister other than Seymour survive saying that? "I support all of my Ministers" does not address the counterfactual, and the rest turns the "nervous" line back on the questioner. The core — is Seymour being treated differently — is untouched.
question: If any Minister other than David Seymour was to claim publicly that the Prime Minister had lost his nerve and wasn’t being truthful with the public, would they still be a Minister?
statement: I support all of my Ministers. They’re doing a fantastic job—they’re doing a fantastic job. The only member in this whole House who should be nervous is the person answering the questions.

explanation: Asked why the public should trust the PM's word if his own Minister does not. The reply changes the subject to the coalition agreement's clarity on first reading, which is an answer to the earlier Treaty-bill question, not this one. Trust is never addressed.
question: If David Seymour doesn’t believe the public should be able to trust the word of the Prime Minister, why should the public?
statement: We have a coalition agreement; it’s crystal clear. We’re going to support a bill to first reading, and there is no commitment beyond that.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Peters' quoted criticism of Seymour. Never says agree or disagree; offers a general "three parties, different views, that's healthy" and then attacks the questioner for not asking about the economy. The specific agree/disagree put to him is avoided.
question: Does he agree with the Rt Hon Winston Peters about David Seymour: “Well, it’s disgraceful that somebody is so desperate.”; “This petty, childish schoolboy behaviour just won’t do”?
statement: What I’m going to say to you is that this is a coalition Government of three parties. We have different views from time to time, and that’s actually quite OK. It’s quite healthy and it’s quite constructive, and, unlike that previous Government that was all about control and spin and management, I have not heard—in the whole time since he’s become Leader of the Opposition, we haven’t had one question on the economy, not one on health, not one on education, not one on housing, not one on infrastructure.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the Government's policies and actions. Answered "Yes" directly, with a qualifier about context that does not retract it. Complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s policies and actions?
statement: Yes, and particularly in the context they’re made, and particularly about our efforts to try and improve Māori health and education outcomes for young Māori.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with three legal bodies about the impact of scrapping section 27 funding, and if not, why not. Answers "No, I don't" plainly and supplies a reason. The reason speaks to Māori victimisation rather than rebutting the disproportionate-sentencing claim, so the "why not" is only partly met — but the question was engaged, not deflected.
question: Does he agree with Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa, the New Zealand Law Society, and the New Zealand Bar Association that scrapping funding for section 27 reports will disproportionately impact Māori, undermine rehabilitation, and lead to higher rates of offending, and, if not, why not?
statement: No, I don’t. The reality is that Māori are higher victims of crime than anybody in this country, and we’re making sure that Māori feel safe in their own businesses, their homes, and their communities.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts the policy creates a double standard between those who can and cannot privately fund reports. Answers "No, I don't", then addresses the mechanism directly — the option to bring a family member still exists for anyone. Squarely on the question asked.
question: Does he accept that his policy will create a double standard in sentencing: for the wealthy, who can afford to privately fund their own section 27 reports, and for those who cannot?
statement: No, I don’t. The intention of section 27 reports was that someone could bring a friend or a family member to speak to their past. That was what was intended to happen. Instead, what’s happened is that there has been a cottage industry of reports, often prepared by people who don’t even know the offender. So the reality is that we’re putting it back to its original purpose. That option still exists and will continue to exist.

explanation: Asked what work the Government is doing — a request for specific measures. The reply names no work at all, only the assertion that the system will be fair and victim-focused. A narrow "what are you doing" question answered with a slogan.
question: What work is this Government doing to ensure that Māori and those on lower incomes will not be unfairly sentenced as a result of this policy?
statement: Well, we are making sure that we actually have a fair system. That is fair and stands up for the victims of crime; it doesn’t stand up for the offenders.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements were made to increase NZ-trained doctors. Names the announcement directly (MOU signed two hours ago for a third medical school). Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has the Minister made to increase the number of New Zealand - trained doctors?
statement: Just two hours ago, the Government completed another key commitment from our 100-day plan, the signing of a memorandum of understanding (MOU) for a third medical school. This is the first step in a process to help increase the number of New Zealand - trained doctors.

explanation: Asked what the next steps after the MOU signing are. States them: Ministry of Health and University of Waikato progress a business case and cost-benefit analysis. Answers squarely; the trailing justification doesn't displace the answer.
question: What are the next steps following today’s signing of the MOU?
statement: The signing of the MOU enables the Ministry of Health and the University of Waikato to progress with establishing a business case and carrying out a cost-benefit analysis, as described in the National-ACT coalition agreement. This is an important step as our country faces a dire shortage of Kiwi doctors, with many planning to retire over the next 10 years.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement that repeal will be cheaper. He restates and affirms the claim ('I am confident that Local Water Done Well will be implemented cheaper'), which engages the yes/no core, though he never uses the words 'I stand by it' and drifts into policy framing.
question: Does he stand by his statement that he is confident repealing the Affordable Water Reforms will be “cheaper”?
statement: I am confident that the Local Water Done Well will be implemented cheaper than the previous Government’s three waters reform that cost the taxpayers over $1.2 billion with very little to show for it. My focus is on ensuring this Government delivers what the vast majority of councils have consistently asked for, which is local water done well. It means local assets in local council control, with the flexibility to structure their delivery of services in a way that works best for them and their communities.

explanation: Narrow question: does 'cheaper' mean cheaper for ratepayers? He talks about councils setting rates and funding tools, and compares cost to the previous Government's programme, never specifying who 'cheaper' is cheaper for. The specific core is avoided.
question: When the Minister uses the term “cheaper”, does he mean cheaper for ratepayers?
statement: Ultimately, councils set rates for their local communities, and this is about ensuring that councils can access the long-term funding and financing tools that they need so they can deliver the infrastructure. This will be far cheaper than what that Government was proposing—over a billion dollars spent with nothing getting delivered.

explanation: Asked why he won't guarantee it will be cheaper for ratepayers. He asserts it will be cheaper for ratepayers — which addresses the substance behind the question — but never engages the actual question of why no guarantee is given, and the rest is an attack on the previous Government.
question: Why won’t the Minister guarantee that his repeal and replacement will be cheaper for ratepayers?
statement: Well, it will be cheaper for ratepayers, because we won’t be spending a billion dollars—like the last Government did—with nothing to show for it. The last Government thought there was a magic money tree, where they could throw it around and apparently solve problems, but, actually, they didn’t, after six years, even solve this problem for local councils.

explanation: Yes/no question about awareness of specific DIA advice on the department's website. He glances at it ('there's a range of advice out there in terms of what the member may be pointing to') without confirming or denying awareness, then pivots to what councils and mayors wanted. Minimal engagement with the question asked.
question: Is he aware of advice from the Department of Internal Affairs (DIA), currently still available on the DIA website, that states what he is proposing as a replacement to the affordable water reforms won’t work and will lead to higher rates for ratepayers?
statement: Well, there’s a range of advice out there in terms of what the member may be pointing to. But what I would say is that this is going to give councils what they asked for, which is ensuring they can deliver and have the long-term funding and financing tools that they need. Mayors across this country opposed that Government’s plan. They opposed the mega entities and the forced mandated bureaucracies on local communities. We believe in local councils choosing and delivering for their local communities.

explanation: Asked whether he is arranging things to shift blame to councils for rate rises. He neither confirms nor denies; he argues rates were rising anyway and that 'councils are ultimately responsible', which touches the premise obliquely but leaves the accusation unaddressed.
question: Isn’t it actually the case that the Minister is setting things up so that when rates inevitably rise—unaffordably, for some—he can blame councils instead of taking responsibility himself?
statement: Well, the last Government said that most of these entities weren’t going to come into force until 2026, so the rates that were being proposed over the next couple of years were actually going to be proposed, regardless of that Government’s reforms. Now, councils are ultimately responsible. We’re giving the long-term funding and financing tools that councils need so they can invest sustainably, in a fiscally responsible manner, in water infrastructure for their local communities.

explanation: Asked whether CPI rather than wage indexation will produce lower benefit increases. 'That will depend on the actual increase in inflation and increase in wages' is a genuine, on-point response to the question, but it hedges around the core rather than resolving it, and then moves to defending the policy.
question: Will indexing benefit levels to inflation rather than wages result in lower increases to benefits?
statement: That will depend on the actual increase in inflation and increase in wages in the given year, and, of course, how you measure inflation and wages. For the last 31 of 35 years, main benefits have been indexed to the Consumers Price Index (CPI) as a measure of inflation to ensure they increase with the cost of living. We think it is fair to protect the real purchasing power of those on main benefits, and this is the approach our Government is taking.

explanation: Asked why written-answer projections show lower increases. She concedes the point in part by quantifying it ('approximately $2'), which engages the fact, but never explains the why, moving instead to jobseeker numbers and cost of living.
question: Why is it the case, then, that projections given to me via parliamentary written answers show that people will see lower increases to benefits?
statement: The difference this year will be approximately $2, and our Government is absolutely focused on, first of all, reducing the number of people on jobseeker benefit, because we’ve seen a blowout in dependency under the last Government, and also we are focused on reducing the cost of living and the pressures that households—those receiving benefits and on low incomes—are facing.

explanation: Asked what recent water-infrastructure announcements he has made. He identifies the announced course of action — repealing three waters and replacing it with Local Water Done Well — so the question is reached, though much of the answer is justification aimed at the previous Government rather than the announcement.
question: What recent announcements has he made about water infrastructure?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker, and thank you to the member for that question. The coalition Government is restoring council ownership and control of water assets by replacing Labour’s three waters legislation. Three waters was divisive and hugely unpopular, and all it would have delivered was a mega - co-governed bureaucracy. We heard the concerns that many New Zealanders had with the proposals, which is why we’re committed to repealing three waters and replacing it with Local Water Done Well.

explanation: Asked why the Government is repealing the Water Services Entities Act. Gives a reason directly: the previous proposals would have created mega co-governed bureaucracies and failed to address infrastructure challenges. Squarely answered.
question: Why is the Government repealing the Water Services Entities Act 2022?
statement: Well, as I said, the last Government’s proposals would simply have created mega - co-governed bureaucracies and failed to actually address the infrastructure challenges that New Zealand councils are facing. Later today, I will be starting the process to repeal three waters. This was part of the Government’s 100-day plan, and I want to acknowledge our partners, ACT and New Zealand First, for their support in this.

explanation: Asked what the next steps are. Lists them: two further bills, what each does, and when the second is introduced. Direct and complete.
question: What are the next steps in making sure that local water is done well?
statement: Well, good question. There will be two further bills progressing through Parliament to transition to Local Water Done Well. The first bill will provide streamlined requirements for establishing council-controlled organisations, enabling councils to start shifting the delivery of water services, and a second bill, to provide for a long-term replacement regime, will be introduced in December this year. This will set out the long-term requirements for financial sustainability and provide for a complete economic regulation regime and a new range of structural and financial tools.

explanation: Asked how Local Water Done Well helps councils prepare for future water infrastructure. Answered: it gives councils tools to access long-term funding and financing, and preserves local decision-making over delivery. A mechanism is actually named, so the question is engaged; the closing swipe at the former Government is padding but does not displace the answer.
question: How will Local Water Done Well help councils prepare for future water infrastructure?
statement: New Zealand’s water infrastructure is facing significant challenges, and Local Water Done Well will enable councils to have the tools that they need to access long-term funding and financing. Local Water Done Well recognises the importance of local decision-making and flexibility for communities and councils to determine how their water services should be delivered in the future, rather than the Government coming over top, like the former Government.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. Answered with an unqualified "Yes" and then an example. Complete and direct; the length of the follow-on is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes—in particular, the actions that I took earlier this year to support the roll-out of NCEA level 1. On becoming the Minister of Education, it was very concerning to find that the implementation of NCEA level 1 standards had been rushed without providing key components to teachers, like subject learning outcomes or external assessment exemplars. After being contacted by subject associations and teachers who raised their serious concerns, this Government took immediate actions to produce subject learning outcomes for all level 1 subjects, and we managed to get this work done with the help of those subject associations so they were delivered to teachers at the start of term 1. The New Zealand Qualifications Authority (NZQA) exemplars were not going to be released until May this year, when much of the teaching would have already taken place. On becoming the Minister, I instructed NZQA to urgently expedite the availability of all level 1 exemplars, and exemplars for science standards were available before the start of term 1, while other subjects will become available through February and March—much earlier than the May deadline. This Government wants students to succeed, and we have stepped in to ensure teachers have the tools they need for NCEA level 1, which the previous Government failed to do in their rush to implement.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question: how many schools are facing cuts to building projects. No number is given; the response pivots to the inherited pipeline, cost escalation and a quote from the questioner, and only in the final clause concedes she is "still coming to grips with the total number." That buried concession is the sole engagement with the question, so this is close to a full dodge of a specific factual ask.
question: How many schools are currently facing cuts to building projects?
statement: I’m pleased the Minister—oh, the ex-Minister asked that question. On becoming the Minister, it was very concerning to find that there was an enormous pipeline of school build projects that were not able to be delivered on. Schools had had their expectations raised, buildings costs had skyrocketed, there were properties that were being designed with bespoke arrangements and architecturally designed buildings, schools had had their expectations raised, and there was poor communication. I’d like to just point out that the Minister herself said in a recent article: “You’ve got schools that have been really suffering, and suffering for quite some time”—that is the point. This has been ongoing and left to us by the previous Government, and now we’re having to come to a point where this Government are having to tidy up a list of schools that I am still coming to grips with the total number.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her bespoke-classroom statement and whether she is aware of the ministry's existing modular/standard-design programme. She never says "yes, I stand by it" in terms, but she directly engages the second half — the modular programme is only now being rolled out, the existing pipeline is architecturally designed, and she has directed the ministry toward repeatable designs. The core is addressed, the first limb only implicitly.
question: Does she stand by her statement: “You know, it is, and it’s part of, that is, the increasing costs of building, but part of it is because we are building these extremely bespoke classrooms, rather than just going ‘Look, here is option A, option B, and option C.’ ”, and, if so, is she aware that the Ministry of Education currently has a modular-building programme and off-site classroom construction options with a suite of standard designs introduced in 2018, helpfully available on the ministry’s website for her reference?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’m pleased that the member asked that question. The point is that the ministry are only just at this point in time starting to roll that out. The pipeline that we are dealing with—that runs into the billions of dollars—includes architecturally designed classrooms that teachers have spent many hours outside the classroom dealing with, and many, many classrooms in that pipeline are in exactly that position. I have now directed the ministry to make sure that we have repeatable modular designs that we can save on these costs, rather than these architecturally designed classrooms that blow out budgets.

explanation: Asked what she says to a principal who reported that no one knows her priorities or has been able to sit down with her. She replies about meetings with the ministry's property team and being "across the detail" — responsive to the competence implication, but she neither addresses the access complaint (meetings with principals) nor states any priorities. Partial engagement, core of the criticism sidestepped.
question: What does she say to James Hargest College principal and Secondary Principals’ Association of New Zealand executive member Mike Newell, who, when asked about the property cuts, said that “no one seemed to know what the priorities were or [had] been able to sit down with the new minister. ‘So that’s really frustrating that we have a new education minister in there, and we’re unsure of what [her] priorities are.’ ”?
statement: I have sat down and had multiple meetings with the property team to try and get to the bottom of how it can be that we have such an enormous pipeline of raised expectations that this previous Government was unable to deliver on. I can assure that Minister that I am across the detail and getting to the bottom of this enormous, enormous mess that they have left that we are about to clean up.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made about the COVID-19 royal commission. Answered directly: on 2 February she announced public input into expanding the inquiry's scope, with the surrounding rationale. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcements has she made regarding the royal commission of inquiry into COVID19 lessons?
