Named the specific report (the Commerce Commission's final competition report into personal banking services, released that day) and summarised its findings. Direct and complete; the fact that it is a friendly question and the answer is spun does not bear on whether it was engaged.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the banking sector?
statement: Today, the Commerce Commission released its final competition report into personal banking services. The report provides substantial evidence that New Zealand’s banking sector is uncompetitive and that Kiwis are not well served by a two-tier oligopoly. The report makes it clear that our banks are highly profitable compared with international peers, they lack innovation, and do not aggressively compete for market share. Instead, competition resembles a cozy pillow fight, with greater focus given to maintaining profit margins than serving New Zealanders well. We are concerned that New Zealand customers are missing out and that as a result of this imperfect competition, they are facing higher prices, limited choices, and poorer service, even when compared to customers of the same parent banks in Australia.

explanation: Asked what recommendations the Commerce Commission made. Gave the count (14) and their three aims, plus the short-term (Kiwibank capital) and medium/long-term (open banking) priorities. Squarely on the question.
question: What recommendations did the Commerce Commission make?
statement: The commission has made 14 recommendations aimed at encouraging more disruptive players into the market, increasing the level of competition between existing players, and empowering consumers to get a better deal from their banking services. In the short term, the commission found that providing Kiwibank with access to more capital has the greatest potential to disrupt and deliver more competitive services to New Zealanders. In the medium to long term, the commission finds that open banking has the greatest potential to promote ongoing disruptive competition by allowing innovative new players such as fintech firms to enter the market and offer banking services to Kiwi consumers that compete with the traditional banks.

explanation: Asked what the report recommends about Kiwibank. Answered immediately — that the Government support Kiwibank to become a real competitor, which requires significantly more capital. The subsequent material on Treasury advice and Cabinet timing goes beyond the question but the core was answered first.
question: What recommendations does the report make about Kiwibank?
statement: Well, one of the key recommendations is for the Government to support Kiwibank to become a real competitor to the major banks. At the moment, Kiwibank is only just nipping at the heels of the big Australian-owned banks, with just 5 percent of the market. To compete more aggressively with the Aussie banks, Kiwibank needs significantly more capital. I have asked the Treasury to engage with Kiwibank’s owner, Kiwi Group Capital, to understand the best options for providing Kiwibank with the capital it needs. The Government will explore all the options for where that additional capital might come from. Possibilities include KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment funds, and everyday New Zealanders themselves looking for home-grown places in which to put their money and invest in New Zealand’s future. I will take proposals to Cabinet no later than December this year.

explanation: Asked what other actions the Government is taking in response. Began answering on-point — recommendations map to work already under way — and named a concrete example (the consumer data right, led by another Minister) before the response was cut off. Engaged with the question; incomplete only because the transcript breaks off.
question: What other actions is the Government taking in response?
statement: A number of the Commerce Commission’s recommendations relate to existing work that is already being progressed by this Government. For example, the Government, led by Minister Bayly, is progressing work to create a consumer data right—

explanation: Asked (a) whether they had read the 2019 WEAG passage and (b) what specific evidence they had seen that sanctions support people into employment. Answered (a) with a plain 'Yes', then produced the evidence they rely on for (b): the 2017-2023 rise in jobseeker numbers alongside a 58% fall in sanctions. Whether that evidence actually supports the conclusion is a Rigor question, not a dodge — the question asked what evidence they had seen and they said.
question: Has she read the analysis in the Welfare Expert Advisory Group’s 2019 report that “There is little evidence in support of using obligations and sanctions (as in the current system) to change behaviour; rather, there is research indicating that they compound social harm and disconnectedness”; if so, what specific evidence, if any, has she seen that benefit sanctions support people into employment?
statement: Yes, I did read that in 2019, and I’ve also looked into the empirical evidence in New Zealand between 2017 and 2023. During this time, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent, which included periods of prolonged labour shortages. During the same time, the use of sanctions nosedived from 60,588 to 25,329, or a decrease of 58 percent. Our Government believes this demonstrates that sanctions are a necessary part of the tools needed, including more proactive support, to motivate people to take the steps needed to shift into work. Sanctions are also about enforcing the basic responsibility to fulfil obligations if you are being supported by taxpayers.

explanation: Asked why they are ignoring the research and conflating correlation with causation. The reply restates the mutual-obligations position and that job seekers who fail their end should face consequences. Neither the choice to set the research aside nor the causal-inference charge is touched — a pivot to standing talking points.
question: Why is she choosing to ignore the research that shows sanctions do not support people into employment and, instead, conflating correlation with causation when it comes to the so-called empirical evidence she quoted?
statement: This side of the House is clear that there must be mutual obligations, rights, and responsibilities. Just as the Ministry of Social Development will provide support and assistance, job seekers who fail to hold up their end of the bargain should face some consequences.

explanation: A narrow binary question: is it easier or harder to find work after losing half a benefit and falling behind on rent, food and bills. The answer describes the traffic light system and says people will not lose entitlement. It never says easier or harder, and does not engage the hardship premise; a specific question left unanswered.
question: Is it easier or harder for someone to find suitable employment when they have lost half of their benefit and fall behind on rent, food, debts, and bills?
statement: That’s why we’ve introduced a traffic light system. We want people to be really clear about where they are, whether they’re at green, orange, or red, so they don’t lose any entitlement.

explanation: Asked why they have been unable to substantiate that sanctions support employment. Mostly a return to the rights-and-responsibilities framing, but it does reach the question's edge by offering a data point — an increase in work exits in July — as the substantiation being demanded. Partial engagement; the 'unable to substantiate' charge itself is never met.
question: Why has she been unable to substantiate and produce evidence that sanctions support people into employment, and instead continues referring to contributions on talkback radio and conflating correlation with causation?
statement: It’s really simple, and that’s why I was pleased to support another colleague’s common-sense approach to this. This side of the House believes that there should be rights and responsibilities, obligations—and those obligations are pretty simple work obligations to be available for work and to look for work—and consequences when they don’t. I would add that we have seen in July an increase in the number of work exits from a year ago, so I’m confident that what we’re doing is working.

explanation: Two parts: do they stand by 'caregiving is work', and will they guarantee caregivers are exempt from work obligations and sanctions. The 'caregiving is work' half is ignored entirely. The guarantee half is effectively refused rather than dodged — work obligations will apply to jobseekers, with assessment only for health conditions and disability — which is a real, if implicit, no. Half the question answered.
question: Does she stand by her answers to supplementary questions last sitting week when she said that caregiving is work, and, if so, will she guarantee that caregivers will not be subject to work obligations and sanctions under the traffic light system?
statement: There will be work obligations for those on the jobseeker benefit. There may be some conditions or capacity that is assessed for those with health conditions and disabilities. But where there are work obligations, our expectation is that they are fulfilled.

explanation: Asked whether they stand by all statements made at the 19 June Estimates hearing. Opened with 'Yes', then qualified with what has changed since (the independent review's findings). The qualification is responsive to the question rather than a substitute for answering it.
question: Mālō e lelei, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by all her statements made during the Disability Issues Estimates hearing at the Social Services and Community Committee on 19 June 2024?
statement: Yes, but since then the independent review has found that the disability support system was in a much worse state than we first understood. Access to disability support services is a postcode lottery based on where someone lives, not their level of need, and Whaikaha - Ministry of Disabled People lacks the capabilities necessary to deliver disability support services effectively, partly due to their rushed establishment under the last Government. The independent review recommended that the initially planned phase two not proceed, as stabilising the disability support system was urgent. That’s why last week our Government announced a series of measures to ensure that the increased budget of $2.6 billion is distributed in a fairer, more consistent way, based on need.

explanation: Two parts: do they stand by the commitment to Enabling Good Lives, and how is that reconciled with pausing it. The first is answered (committed to the vision and principles, with 'mainstream first' singled out). The second gets only 'the review highlighted dire issues; we are taking urgent action' — the pause is never mentioned, let alone reconciled. Half answered.
question: Does the Minister stand by her statement that “Our Government remains committed to the Enabling Good Lives approach”, and, if so, how does she reconcile this with her decision to pause Enabling Good Lives?
statement: Our Government of course is committed to the vision and principles of Enabling Good Lives, particularly the principle that talks about mainstream first and ensuring that disabled people are supported to access mainstream services before specialist disability services. The independent review highlighted dire issues with a disability support service that required urgent action. Our Government is taking that urgent action.

explanation: Asked whether they stand by the stabilise-and-give-certainty statement and, if so, how the transfer of services from Whaikaha to MSD is justified when its cost and timeframe are unknown. No answer on standing by the statement, and nothing on cost or timeframe. It offers a general justification for urgent action from the review findings and stocktake, which brushes the 'how can she justify' part without addressing the transfer itself.
question: Does the Minister stand by her statement that “The most critical thing we do is for people who are already accessing and in need of disability support services, that we stabilise the system and give them certainty”; if so, how can she justify uprooting and transferring disability support services from Whaikaha to the Ministry of Social Development, a process for which the cost and time frame is unknown?
statement: The report that came from the independent review panel, unfortunately, was bleak. That was on top of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet stocktake that was undertaken for the previous Government and released before the election, as well as an independent assurance report that also showed poor financial controls. That is why, in order to stabilise and ensure services that are delivered to disabled people are stabilised, we’ve taken urgent action. That is why we are prioritising disabled people, their families, and carers by making these changes.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her claim that the review engaged widely, and how that squares with the Disability Support Network CEO saying the Government didn't talk to affected people. She engages the core factual dispute head-on — she lists whom she met with during the review and explicitly includes the very organisation the questioner cited, which is a direct rebuttal of the engagement claim. Marked down slightly because she never states plainly that she stands by the statement and leaves the 'reconcile' half implicit rather than addressed.
question: Does the Minister stand by her statement that the review into disability support services engaged “with a number of organisations and groups and individuals—disabled and non-disabled.”; if so, how does she reconcile this with the comments made by New Zealand Disability Support Network chief executive, Peter Reynolds, who said, “The Government’s bombshell decision to cut disability support funding in real terms, while gutting the Ministry designed by and for disabled people without even deigning to talk with the people affected first is heart-breaking”?
statement: The state of the books and the rapid decline of the ministry’s ability to maintain within its appropriation meant that changes were required. That’s why an independent review panel was set up at pace. And over that time that the independent review panel was doing its work, I met with disabled people, with families, with carers, with organisations, with the Disabled People’s Organisations Coalition, with providers—including the organisation that that member referred to—to understand exactly how they saw the disability support service and what their experience was. It’s fair to say it was bleak; that’s why urgent action has been taken.

explanation: Asked how the disabled community can trust a Minister given three alleged reversals (Enabling Good Lives paused, services uprooted, engagement promised but not delivered). The answer reconfirms 'what this review was about', asserts the current system is unfair and a postcode lottery, and cites a $1.1 billion budget. Trust is never addressed and none of the three reversals is engaged — it is a pivot to prepared framing.
question: How can the disabled community trust a Minister who said her Government was committed to Enabling Good Lives, then paused it; said they would stabilise disability support services, then uprooted it; and said they would engage with the disabled community when she didn’t?
statement: I just want to reconfirm what this review was about and the actions that were taken. Over many, many weeks and the discussions with disabled people, families, carers, and providers, it is very clear. It is very clear that the system we have today is unfair, it is inconsistent, and it is a postcode lottery that delivers to disabled people depending on where they live. That is not sustainable, and that is why, with an increased budget of $1.1 billion, we want to ensure that those with the highest needs get their needs met.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes.' One word, but a complete and direct answer to a yes/no question.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees his Government's policies are worsening race relations. Answered 'No.' Blunt and unelaborated, but it squarely answers the question that was put; elaboration would be Specificity, not Forthrightness.
question: Does he agree with the mounting evidence that his Government’s policies and actions are worsening race relations in Aotearoa?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether he believes his Government's actions are changing the country's constitution. Answered 'No.' Direct and complete for a yes/no question.
question: Does he believe that his Government’s actions and policies are changing the constitution of this country?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether the constitution allows for three Prime Ministers at the same time. Answered 'No.' A direct answer to the question as framed.
question: Does our constitution allow for three Prime Ministers at the same time?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether Parliament's constitution grants a coalition agreement supremacy over Te Tiriti o Waitangi — a yes/no about constitutional precedence. The reply says the coalition agreement is clear and that they honour their coalition agreements, which asserts commitment to the agreement without ever addressing whether it takes precedence over the Treaty. The core of the question is stepped around.
question: Does Parliament’s constitution grant supremacy to a coalition agreement over Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: We have a very clear coalition agreement. We honour our coalition agreements.

explanation: Asked to describe the distribution of constitutional power created by iwi Māori agreeing to Te Tiriti. The answer offers one characterisation — the Treaty is a foundational document that 'protects both Crown and Māori interests' — which gestures at the question but never describes any distribution of power. It reaches the topic without reaching the question.
question: Can the Prime Minister describe the distribution of constitutional power created by the agreement of te iwi Māori to Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: As I’ve said before, the Treaty of Waitangi is a foundational document of New Zealand. It protects both Crown and Māori interests.

explanation: Asked how many Oranga Tamariki community providers had funding increased and by how much. Both figures are given directly: 34 services across 25 providers, at least $18.7 million. The subsequent attack on the previous Government is surplus but does not displace the answer, which was delivered first and in full.
question: How many Oranga Tamariki community service providers, if any, have had their funding increased, and by how much, if anything, as a result of the Budget 2024 Reduction in Contracting Service Costs?
statement: I’m advised that 34 services across 25 providers will have their funding increased, with a total increase of at least $18.7 million. On top of that, Oranga Tamariki (OT) will be procuring at least 50 new services, and this will include additional services for high and complex needs, and the expansion of the Fast Track programme by $7.6 million. I’ve asked OT to make sure that there’s a more rigorous approach to contracting to ensure the $500 million worth of services it funds each year gets to where it will have the greatest impact. Under the last Government, OT was allowing providers who were under-delivering on their contracts to keep unused funding, they were funding services that weren’t core business, and they were duplicating services in various parts of New Zealand. If the last Government had taken this same approach to contracting now, at least $132 million more could have gone to the children, rather than letting some bank accounts build up.

explanation: Asked to confirm that the Independent Children's Monitor and Chief Children's Commissioner had written raising continued concerns, and what she is doing to reassure them. Neither half is answered: the letter is never confirmed or denied, and no reassurance action is named. The reply switches to a different question — whether funding was cut — and asserts reprioritisation instead.
question: Can she confirm that the Independent Children’s Monitor and the Chief Children’s Commissioner have written to Oranga Tamariki stating that they had continued concerns on a range of aspects of the current change process, given its potential detrimental impact for tamariki and whānau, and, if so, what is she doing to reassure them?
statement: It is the same amount of funding—no cuts have been made to funding. What we are doing is reprioritising that funding to where it will make the biggest impact. Oranga Tamariki needs to go back to its core purpose. We can’t keep the status quo, and those organisations you’re speaking to have said that over and over, over the years, Oranga Tamariki is not performing and needs to get back to what they should be doing: looking after our children’s safety.

explanation: Asked for an assurance that funding changes are like-for-like with no service gaps, and if not, why not. She refuses the assurance plainly — 'nobody has ever said it would be like-to-like' — and gives the reason, realigning money to Oranga Tamariki's core purpose. A direct refusal that answers the question rather than dodging it; short of full marks only because the 'no gaps in service provision' limb is left untouched.
question: Sure. Can she provide an assurance that any funding changes to community service providers are, in fact, like for like and that there will be no gaps in service provision for all communities across the country, and, if not, why not?
statement: Nobody has ever said it would be like-to-like services; what we’ve said is we are going to realign the money where it’s going to make the greatest impact and where it is focusing on the core purpose of Oranga Tamariki, which is the care and protection of children in their care.

explanation: Asked whether she shares the Commissioner's and Monitor's concern that transitional arrangements could not be guaranteed, and if not, why not. She never says whether she shares the concern, but she answers its substance directly — provisions exist to wind down services and safely transition tamariki, with three- or six-month wind-downs — which functionally addresses the guarantee at issue. Partial because the question as asked was about her position, and that is left unstated.
question: Does she share the concerns of the Chief Children’s Commissioner and Independent Children’s Monitor, who have said, “Oranga Tamariki could not guarantee that transitional arrangements were in place, but hoped they would be”, and, if not, why not?
statement: I have been advised that for services that will be discontinued, provisions have been made to support partners and providers to wind down the services and to safely transition tamariki, rangatahi, and whānau receiving the services to another service. These provisions also allow for either a three-month or a six-month wind-down, depending on the terms of their contract.

explanation: Asked how the cuts, poor provider communication and lack of transition assurance square with the stated child-safety priority. The response never touches any of the three, and instead refuses to "be lectured", attacks the questioner's former government and describes the state of Oranga Tamariki on taking over. A complete pivot to attack — none of the question's core is reached.
question: How do shambolic cuts to service providers, poor communication with providers about their contracts, and having no assurance about transitioning children and family to alternative services fit with her stated commitment that child safety is her priority?
statement: I actually refuse to stand here and be lectured by a member of that previous Government, which made absolutely no progress when it came to the safety of the wellbeing of our young people. The state of Oranga Tamariki when I took over was absolutely disgusting, and I’m not going to allow that to continue.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements had been made about supporting jobseekers into work. The response names the announcement directly — last week's welfare reform package, tougher consequences, and the new traffic light system. Squarely answered; the closing talking-point sentences are surplus, not evasion.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about supporting people on the jobseeker benefit into work?
statement: Last week, I announced a comprehensive package of reforms to the welfare system to support more people off jobseeker support into work and to introduce tougher consequences for those who repeatedly do not meet their benefit obligations. This includes a new traffic light system to inform people what is required of them to continue receiving a benefit and warn them when they are not meeting those expectations. Our Government believes that work is the best pathway to independence and further opportunities. We continue to take action to support New Zealanders into work, and the traffic light system is an important tool to achieve this.

explanation: Asked why the traffic light system was introduced. The response gives the purpose directly: to communicate expectations clearly, ensure compliance, and signal risk of breach and its consequences. Direct and complete.
question: Why was the traffic light system introduced?
statement: The traffic light system was introduced to clearly communicate to job seekers what is expected of them and to ensure they comply with their obligations. It spells out if they are at risk of breaching their work obligations and what the consequences are of failing to comply. Our Government expects those receiving taxpayers’ support to meet their basic obligations to become work-ready and to find work, because we believe in rights and responsibilities.

explanation: Asked how the traffic light system will work. The response describes the mechanism — green on track, orange failed with five days to re-comply, red breached with sanctions. Exactly the question asked, fully answered.
question: How will the traffic light system work?
statement: The traffic light system categorises job seekers based on their compliance level, providing crystal clear steps on how to comply with their obligations. Green means a beneficiary is on track and complying with all their work obligations. Orange means a job seeker has failed an obligation and must re-comply within five days. Red means a job seeker has breached their obligations, which will result in sanctions being imposed.

explanation: Asked what other effects the system has on jobseekers. The response lists further effects: six-monthly reapplication, a mandatory jobseeker profile, new non-financial sanctions, and a two-year rather than one-year failure record. Directly on the question.
question: How else does the traffic light system affect job seekers?
statement: Job seekers will be required to reapply for their benefit every six months, and they must also complete a mandatory job seeker profile. This will enable the Ministry of Social Development to match people with job vacancies. There will also be new, non-financial sanctions that will be available next year, and past failures will be counted against a job seeker’s record for two years, instead of one. Our Government is making our welfare system more proactive to help job seekers into work and experience the benefit of greater financial independence and further opportunities that come from work.

explanation: A two-part "does she stand by the statement; if so, why" question. The response answers "yes" outright and then supplies the why — avoiding rushed lawmaking, and four consultation opportunities through the reform programme. Both limbs engaged.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “Good legislation involves everybody, and bad legislation is usually when somebody goes off and does something by themselves … I’m never going to be arrogant enough to think that I have the answers to everything”; if so, why?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. In answer to the question, yes. That means that, for example, we need to avoid the type of rushed lawmaking that led to a three-day select committee and a 10-day—total—process for the last reform of the Arms Act by the previous Government. I also stand by another statement I made in the article that the member references: “I’ve got to make sure it’s not my personal views that go forward but rather collected views.” As part of my four-phase firearms reform work programme, New Zealanders will have four opportunities to submit their views to the select committee. Furthermore, stakeholders from both sides of the debate have had the chance to participate in focused consultation on both clubs and ranges reforms and the review of the firearms registry. This Government cares about the voices of New Zealanders, and we are doing the due diligence that should have been done back in 2019.

explanation: Asked why an attempt was made to remove the Police comment from the Cabinet paper. The response gets partway to a reason — unfamiliarity with Cabinet process, and wondering why the comments were there "seeing as it was my paper" — but frames it around what was learned afterwards rather than the motive, then moves on to the Police Association's absence from the consultation list. Partial answer, hedging around the core.
question: Why did she attempt to remove Police’s comment “The stakeholder consultation is heavily weighted towards firearm licence holders and should include broader perspectives, including from groups like the Police Association.” from the Cabinet paper on firearms reforms?
statement: As I have actually publicly said, learning about the Cabinet process and how we go about utilising the papers, I was informed that I could not remove some of the comments, and I wondered why they were there in the first place, seeing as it was my paper. I’m very pleased with the advice that I got that I should keep it there and actually respond to those comments. I’d also point out that the Police Association were never on the original list of those that should have been spoken to that was given to me, and the list that the Labour Government used beforehand. I’m quite happy with the very fulsome response I’m getting from New Zealand Police and the fact that they are being so fulsome with their responses. They represent their entire workforce; not just their union.

explanation: Two limbs: does she agree with Cahill's quote, and is she concerned that A-category firearms will reach criminals without a registry. The first is answered flatly and directly ("I do not agree with Mr Cahill", with a reason). The second — the concern about criminal access — is never addressed at all. Half the question squarely answered, half dropped.
question: Does she agree with Police Association president, Chris Cahill, that “Without a registry, you buy as many firearms as you like. There’s no controls, whether you still have them or you pass them on to someone else.”, and is she concerned that without a firearms registry, A-category firearms like Alfa Carbine rifles will get into the hands of criminals who directly threaten front-line police officers’ safety; if not, why not?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, I do not agree with Mr Cahill, because legislation actually has restrictions around the legal transfer of firearms—part of the reason why we need to have people involved in the consultation that actually understand the legislation.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Police advice that the programme should report to at least two Ministers, and if not, why not. The response never says agree or disagree, nor addresses the two-Minister point; it recites being given the opportunity to lead the reform, Government agreement on process, and a jab at the other side. A pivot to talking points.
question: Does she agree with Police advice—not Police Association advice; Police advice—on the Government’s firearms reform programme that “This should report back to at least two Ministers, as National Party supports the registry.”; if not, why not?
statement: I have been given the opportunity, on behalf of the Government, to lead this reform in the firearms space. What is really important is that we as a Government, as a whole, agree with the process as we move through the transparent process of four firearms reform phases. I’m really happy with the opportunity that I have been given to make New Zealand a safer place, because that side failed to do that post-2019.

explanation: Asked to justify attempting to remove Police's ability to comment given the Government's stance on police powers. The response claims the point was already answered and expresses gratitude for Police advice and satisfaction with the process; the alleged inconsistency is never justified or engaged. The mention of liking the chance to rebut brushes the topic but offers no justification.
question: How does she justify attempting to remove the power of Police to comment in a Cabinet paper when she is part of a Government that has spoken so strongly about increasing the powers of police?
statement: I think I answered that where I had already said that I am very grateful for New Zealand Police giving me their thoughtful and fulsome advice, and I also like the opportunity that I have to be able to rebut or even comment back. I’m happy with the process. I’m happy with New Zealand Police being involved.

explanation: Asked what recent announcement had been made on gene technology. The response states the announcement directly — overturning the ~30-year effective ban, new legislation and a dedicated regulator on the Australian model. Directly and completely answered.
question: What recent announcement has the Government made about gene technology?
statement: Last week, the Prime Minister and I announced that we are overturning the nearly 30-year effective ban on gene technology, for the benefit of New Zealand. We will establish new legislation and a dedicated regulator based on the Australian regime. The science has matured, other countries have embraced gene technology, and it has potential to treat cancers, increase agricultural production, lower emissions, adapt to a changing climate, and, ultimately, grow the economy. Gene tech is already being used safely in 29 other countries, including many of our trading partners such as Australia, China, Japan, the US, Canada, and many European countries. New Zealand needs to keep up, and we will be able to do so with this new regime. I’d also point out that I’ve had some good conversations with colleagues across the House on this move and I’m happy to provide briefings for MPs who are interested, and if they just get in touch with my office, we’ll arrange that for them.

explanation: Asked how gene technology can support higher productivity and growth. The response answers the mechanism — crop productivity gains, year-round fruit and faster breeding, better returns for growers and cheaper produce — and notes the current constraint keeping it in the lab. Engages the question asked.
question: How can gene technology support higher productivity and growth?
statement: We’re committed to building a productive and growing economy, and I’m confident that gene technologies will contribute to that goal. In the primary sector, New Zealand scientists, including those at Plant and Food—where we launched the policy—have used gene technology to increase the productivity of crops, but only in laboratories. For example, researchers are looking at how to make fruit like apples and blueberries produce year-round, meaning faster breeding and, potentially, no off-season. Ultimately, this means better returns for growers and cheaper produce for consumers. However, under existing rules, virtually none of this research ever leaves the lab in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked how gene technology supports health outcomes and lowers emissions. Both halves are engaged: a named health application (CAR T-cell therapy access) and an emissions rationale (agriculture as half of NZ emissions, competitiveness). The emissions limb is answered more thinly — 'can also help' plus a competitiveness argument rather than a mechanism — so it addresses the question squarely on one half and reaches it only loosely on the other.
question: How will gene technology support better health outcomes and lower greenhouse gas emissions?
statement: This policy will allow many more New Zealanders to access highly effective cancer treatments, including CAR T-cell therapy developed at Wellington’s Malaghan Institute, and this treatment has already successfully treated patients with cancer for the handful of those who were able to participate in its trial. This change in the gene technology regime means more New Zealanders will be able to access this advanced treatment and others like it. Gene technologies can also help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. New Zealand is an agricultural nation, which is why around half of our emissions come from agriculture. Our world-class farmers are at risk of being left behind their competitors if they don’t access advanced gene technologies just as our competitors are.

explanation: Asked how the new regime will manage risk. Answers directly: risk-based tiering with stricter rules for higher-risk technologies, a regulator focused on human health and environment, public consultation, MPI enforcement, technical and Māori advisory groups. The trailing material on timelines and select committee is surplus, not evasion — the core was engaged and answered.
question: How will this new regime adequately manage risk?
statement: Gene technologies have moved significantly since the current legislation passed nearly 30 years ago, and I want to assure New Zealanders and this House that risk management will be at the forefront of the new regime. The regulator will focus on risks to human health and to the environment. The regime will be risk-based, which means technologies with greater unknowns or higher risks will be subject to the most stringent rules. The regime includes public consultation, and the Ministry for Primary Industries will be responsible for enforcement. A technical advisory group will support the regulator, and a Māori advisory group will consider implications for Māori. I expect this new legislation will be in the House by the end of this year. It will have a full select committee process, and I encourage members of this House and the public to engage. I intend the new regulator to be in place by the end of 2025. I’m very confident that this regime will get New Zealand up to speed with the rest of the world.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' outright before pivoting to volunteered material on road safety. The yes/no core is given plainly; the added talking points follow the answer rather than replace it.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially this Government’s action to improve road safety by going after drugged and drunk drivers. Our Government is absolutely committed to building great roads and Kiwis deserve to be safe when they drive on them, and alcohol and drugs are the number one cause of fatal crashes on New Zealand roads; in fact, around 30 percent of deaths on our roads involve drug-drivers. So our Government is taking action, with more funding for roadside tests as part of a package of $1.3 billion for road policing in the next three years. But we know funding isn’t enough, which is why we’re setting targets for alcohol and drug tests so we see better results for where the money is spent.

explanation: A two-part question: does he stand by the quoted statement, and if so, does he believe Māori ceded sovereignty. He answers only the first part, and explicitly flags that he is answering only the first part, leaving the substantive core untouched. Narrow question, core squarely avoided — partial engagement at best.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “Part of the history of modern New Zealand has been our struggle to understand the intentions and expectations of those who signed the Treaty. … That work is still happening and will keep going.”, and, if so, can he set out his understanding of Te Tiriti o Waitangi by telling the House whether he believes that Māori ceded sovereignty?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

explanation: Asked a direct yes/no belief question: does he believe Māori ceded sovereignty. The reply substitutes an adjacent proposition — that the Crown is sovereign — which is a claim about present status, not about whether sovereignty was ceded. It stays on topic without ever reaching the question asked.
question: Does the Prime Minister believe that Māori ceded sovereignty?
statement: Our position is that the Crown is sovereign.

explanation: Asked whether his prior answer should be read as believing Māori ceded sovereignty — an invitation to confirm or deny. He neither confirms nor denies, instead asserting that his earlier answer was already clear. That is a deflection back to a reply that had not in fact answered it; the yes/no is still withheld.
question: Are we to take it from that answer that the Prime Minister believes that Māori ceded sovereignty?
statement: I don’t know how I can be clearer in answer to the first question.

explanation: Asked 'when' — a request for a time or event. He names the Treaty of Waitangi as the founding document and restates that Māori ceded sovereignty to the Crown, which implies the Treaty as the occasion but never states a date or moment. It gestures at the question and answers a neighbouring one (whether, not when).
question: When did Māori cede sovereignty?
statement: I’d just say to the member that we have the Treaty of Waitangi as the founding document of New Zealand; in there is protection for both Crown and Māori interests. But, as I’ve said to you, the position is very clear: Māori ceded sovereignty to the Crown.

explanation: Asked whether the Treaty principles bill takes account of the Tribunal's 2014 finding. 'We haven't seen a Treaty principles bill yet' is blunt but genuinely responsive — it gives a reason the first limb cannot be answered as posed rather than pivoting away. The second limb about sidelining the Tribunal goes unaddressed, so the engagement is real but incomplete.
question: Does his Government’s Treaty principles bill consider the Waitangi Tribunal’s finding from 10 years ago that “The rangatira who signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi in February 1840 did not cede [their] sovereignty to Britain,” or does he intend to continue to sideline the Waitangi Tribunal?
statement: We haven’t seen a Treaty principles bill yet.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes' is given immediately and unambiguously; the subsequent material on inflation and the OCR is volunteered addition, not a substitute for the answer.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to rein in inflation and to reduce the cost of living as part of our plan to rebuild the economy. We had a plan to fight inflation and we started work on day one: stopping the wasteful spending, removing costs on businesses, and returning the Reserve Bank to a single focus on inflation. Now, we see inflation is tracking down to 3.3 percent and heading lower, and last week brought more good news for every Kiwi with a mortgage, with the first cut to the official cash rate in 4½ years. We know life is tough out there, but there are encouraging early signs that our plan is working to get New Zealand back on track.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the economy. She identifies a specific recent report — the Reserve Bank monetary policy committee's OCR decision and its forecast track. The opening framing about the cost of living crisis is preamble, but the question is reached and answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Over the past few years, New Zealand has endured a cost of living crisis, with rampant inflation eating away at New Zealanders’ incomes and savings. In response, interest rates were lifted very sharply, imposing additional costs on Kiwi households and businesses. I was delighted to see that last week marked a significant turning point, with the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee deciding to cut the official cash rate (OCR) by 25 basis points, to 5.25 percent. What’s more, the bank has set out a forecast track for the official cash rate which shows a steady decline over the next few years, back down to 3 percent in 2027.

explanation: Asked what an OCR cut means for families and businesses. The answer maps directly onto both groups: lower mortgage and personal loan interest for households, cheaper borrowing to expand and hire for businesses. The question's core is engaged head-on.
question: What does an OCR cut mean for New Zealand families and businesses?
statement: Lowering the official cash rate will lead to lower interest rates across the economy; in fact, this process has already started. It means Kiwis will pay less interest on their mortgages and on their personal loans, easing the cost of living for families. It also improves the conditions for businesses, making it easier for them to borrow to expand, hire people, and grow. Lower interest rates will be a breath of fresh air for the economy. Coupled with the tax relief package we introduced on 31 July, this is an important milestone in beating the cost of living crisis.

explanation: Asked for the Reserve Bank's inflation forecast. The figure is supplied — 2.3 percent for the September 2024 quarter, within the target band. Direct and complete; the historical comparison around it does not displace the answer.
question: What is the Reserve Bank’s forecast for inflation?
statement: During the cost of living crisis, annual Consumers Price Index inflation got to 7.3 percent and was over 7 percent for most of 2022. The Reserve Bank’s latest forecast is for inflation in this quarter—that is, the September quarter of 2024—to be well within the target band, at 2.3 percent. That is a very considerable drop. The Reserve Bank clearly has confidence that inflation is under control and that the age of extreme price increases is over, after four years where the only way for interest rates was up.

explanation: Asked what fiscal policy's contribution has been. She states it directly — fiscal policy has been helpful rather than obstructive, tax relief was fiscally neutral, spending as a share of the economy is forecast to fall — and cites Treasury on the point. Partisan framing, but the question is squarely engaged.
question: What has been the contribution of fiscal policy?
statement: Fiscal policy can either get in the way of monetary policy, as we saw with big spending over the last few years, or it can be helpful. This Government has been helpful, as the Budget demonstrates. New Zealanders benefited from long-overdue tax relief, and this tax relief was delivered in a way that was fiscally neutral and did not add to inflationary pressure, with every single dollar accounted for. More importantly, Government spending as a proportion of the economy is forecast to fall over the next few years, as the Monetary Policy Statement shows. As the Treasury said in the Budget update, “The decisions taken through Budget 2024 will on balance reduce the contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure.”

explanation: A two-part question (does she stand by the statement; is she confident on the gains-vs-savings comparison) answered "Yes, and yes." Both parts answered, nothing dodged. Zero detail, but detail is Specificity, not this.
question: Mālō ‘aupito, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by her statement, “We’ve acted swiftly to root-out waste, reduce bureaucracy and move resources from the back-office to the front line”; if so, is she confident New Zealanders have gained more from the tax cuts than they lost from the Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise?
statement: Yes, and yes.

explanation: Asked why 190 contracts were ended and whether they were wasteful spending. She openly declines the detail by referring it to the relevant Minister — a stated refusal, which is not itself a dodge — but then never engages the wasteful-spending limb, instead offering overall funding figures and attacking the questioner. Partial engagement at best.
question: Why has Oranga Tamariki ended contracts with 190 front-line social service providers and a further 142 providers have had their funding reduced, or are these contracts wasteful spending, as described by the Prime Minister?
statement: Well, if the member wants detailed answers on specific contract decisions by Oranga Tamariki, I would encourage her to put those questions to the relevant Minister. I will make two points: first, overall funding for Oranga Tamariki in the Budget increased; and, second, if that member thinks that the position of a Government should be that every single contract signed up to needs to be stuck in stone and never changed, then she’s delusional. In fact, what our Government has committed to do is drive better services. We want New Zealand children to be safe, we want there to be good and effective service delivery, and Oranga Tamariki is expected to deliver on that.

explanation: Two narrow questions — is 100% delivery on 70% funding reasonable, and is that consistent with the commissioning model. Neither is touched. The reply is a general statement of expectations plus a passage about Wellington headcount growth. The core of a specific question is entirely avoided.
question: Is it reasonable, as part of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise, for front-line social service providers to provide 100 percent of their contracted Government services with only 70 percent of the Government funding, and is this consistent with the social services commissioning model?
statement: Our expectation is that we will drive better results for the taxpayers’ money we invest in social service provision. We are particularly conscious that in recent years, social service providers have watched while Wellington grew, the dollars that went into Government agencies expanded, and the number of policy analysts and managers hired grew, and yet those front-line service providers often only saw in return more contracting requirements, more compliance, and, actually, weren’t able to deliver better results. Our Government is focused on ensuring the dollars actually make it to the front line.

explanation: The question asked what she would say to the named providers, and she says something to them directly — the Government values them and wants to work with them. It answers the question as framed, though it hedges around the funding reductions the question attached to it.
question: What does she say to providers like Taeaomanino Trust, Wesley Community Action, Porirua Whānau Centre, Barnardos Aotearoa, Wairere Care Services, North Shore Women’s Centre, WELLfed New Zealand Trust, E Tipu E Rea, and the Salvation Army, who have all had reductions in funding and lost front-line staff as a result of her Budget 2024 baseline savings exercise?
statement: Well, I’d say to each of those social service providers that the Government values what you do. You play a significant role in helping New Zealanders in need, and our Government wants to work with you to ensure we can make the maximum impact for the people you serve.

explanation: Asked whether the cuts were worth it to pay for tax cuts. She rejects the premise explicitly and gives the counter-claim — savings were reinvested in Oranga Tamariki, whose funding rose overall. Denying the premise head-on is engagement, not evasion; whether the denial is true is Veracity.
question: Was making funding cuts for Oranga Tamariki providers, who serve our most vulnerable children, worth it to pay for her tax cuts?
statement: Well, I completely reject the accusation in the member’s question. We invested every single dollar gained from savings at Oranga Tamariki back into Oranga Tamariki, which, overall, had increased funding in the Budget.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on banking. She names the Commerce Commission's final competition report into personal banking services and summarises its findings. Direct and complete.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the banking sector?
statement: Today, the Commerce Commission released its final competition report into personal banking services. The report provides substantial evidence that New Zealand’s banking sector is uncompetitive and that Kiwis are not well served by a two-tier oligopoly. The report makes it clear that our banks are highly profitable compared with international peers, they lack innovation, and do not aggressively compete for market share. Instead, competition resembles a cozy pillow fight, with greater focus given to maintaining profit margins than serving New Zealanders well. We are concerned that New Zealand customers are missing out and that as a result of this imperfect competition, they are facing higher prices, limited choices, and poorer service, even when compared to customers of the same parent banks in Australia.

explanation: Asked what recommendations the Commission made. She gives the count (14), their thrust, and the short- and medium-term priorities. The question is answered on its own terms.
question: What recommendations did the Commerce Commission make?
statement: The commission has made 14 recommendations aimed at encouraging more disruptive players into the market, increasing the level of competition between existing players, and empowering consumers to get a better deal from their banking services. In the short term, the commission found that providing Kiwibank with access to more capital has the greatest potential to disrupt and deliver more competitive services to New Zealanders. In the medium to long term, the commission finds that open banking has the greatest potential to promote ongoing disruptive competition by allowing innovative new players such as fintech firms to enter the market and offer banking services to Kiwi consumers that compete with the traditional banks.

explanation: Asked what the report recommends about Kiwibank. She answers directly — support it to become a real competitor, more capital — and adds what she has done about it, including a Cabinet timeline. Fully responsive.
question: What recommendations does the report make about Kiwibank?
statement: Well, one of the key recommendations is for the Government to support Kiwibank to become a real competitor to the major banks. At the moment, Kiwibank is only just nipping at the heels of the big Australian-owned banks, with just 5 percent of the market. To compete more aggressively with the Aussie banks, Kiwibank needs significantly more capital. I have asked the Treasury to engage with Kiwibank’s owner, Kiwi Group Capital, to understand the best options for providing Kiwibank with the capital it needs. The Government will explore all the options for where that additional capital might come from. Possibilities include KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment funds, and everyday New Zealanders themselves looking for home-grown places in which to put their money and invest in New Zealand’s future. I will take proposals to Cabinet no later than December this year.

explanation: Asked what other actions the Government is taking. She begins listing them (consumer data right work led by Minister Bayly) and is cut off mid-sentence. On-point for as far as the record runs; the truncation is not a dodge.
question: What other actions is the Government taking in response?
statement: A number of the Commerce Commission’s recommendations relate to existing work that is already being progressed by this Government. For example, the Government, led by Minister Bayly, is progressing work to create a consumer data right—

explanation: Two parts: has she read the WEAG passage, and what evidence has she seen that sanctions support employment. She answers yes to the first and then supplies the evidence she relies on — jobseeker numbers up 57%, sanctions down 58% over 2017–2023. Whether that evidence actually supports the conclusion is Rigor; the question itself was engaged.
question: Has she read the analysis in the Welfare Expert Advisory Group’s 2019 report that “There is little evidence in support of using obligations and sanctions (as in the current system) to change behaviour; rather, there is research indicating that they compound social harm and disconnectedness”; if so, what specific evidence, if any, has she seen that benefit sanctions support people into employment?
statement: Yes, I did read that in 2019, and I’ve also looked into the empirical evidence in New Zealand between 2017 and 2023. During this time, the number of people on the jobseeker benefit increased by 70,000, or 57 percent, which included periods of prolonged labour shortages. During the same time, the use of sanctions nosedived from 60,588 to 25,329, or a decrease of 58 percent. Our Government believes this demonstrates that sanctions are a necessary part of the tools needed, including more proactive support, to motivate people to take the steps needed to shift into work. Sanctions are also about enforcing the basic responsibility to fulfil obligations if you are being supported by taxpayers.

explanation: Asked why she is ignoring the research and conflating correlation with causation. Neither limb is addressed — no defence of the inference, no engagement with the research. The reply is a statement of position on mutual obligations, i.e. talking points in place of an answer.
question: Why is she choosing to ignore the research that shows sanctions do not support people into employment and, instead, conflating correlation with causation when it comes to the so-called empirical evidence she quoted?
statement: This side of the House is clear that there must be mutual obligations, rights, and responsibilities. Just as the Ministry of Social Development will provide support and assistance, job seekers who fail to hold up their end of the bargain should face some consequences.

explanation: Asked a binary comparative question — is it easier or harder to find work after losing half a benefit. The answer never says easier or harder; it pivots to describing the traffic light system and entitlement clarity, which is a different question. Near-total dodge of a narrow question.
question: Is it easier or harder for someone to find suitable employment when they have lost half of their benefit and fall behind on rent, food, debts, and bills?
statement: That’s why we’ve introduced a traffic light system. We want people to be really clear about where they are, whether they’re at green, orange, or red, so they don’t lose any entitlement.

explanation: Asked why she has been unable to produce evidence that sanctions move people into work, and about conflating correlation with causation. Most of the reply is a rights-and-responsibilities philosophy statement, but she does finally offer a piece of evidence (a July increase in work exits) and asserts the policy is working. That reaches the edge of the question — evidence was requested and something was offered — without addressing why the evidence was previously unsubstantiated or the causation point. Partial engagement.
question: Why has she been unable to substantiate and produce evidence that sanctions support people into employment, and instead continues referring to contributions on talkback radio and conflating correlation with causation?
statement: It’s really simple, and that’s why I was pleased to support another colleague’s common-sense approach to this. This side of the House believes that there should be rights and responsibilities, obligations—and those obligations are pretty simple work obligations to be available for work and to look for work—and consequences when they don’t. I would add that we have seen in July an increase in the number of work exits from a year ago, so I’m confident that what we’re doing is working.

explanation: A two-part question: does she stand by 'caregiving is work', and will she guarantee caregivers face no work obligations or sanctions. She ignores the first part entirely, and answers the second only implicitly — work obligations apply to jobseekers, exemptions are assessed for health conditions and disability, expectations must be fulfilled. That amounts to declining the guarantee without ever saying so, and carers are never named. Half the question engaged, hedged around its core.
question: Does she stand by her answers to supplementary questions last sitting week when she said that caregiving is work, and, if so, will she guarantee that caregivers will not be subject to work obligations and sanctions under the traffic light system?
statement: There will be work obligations for those on the jobseeker benefit. There may be some conditions or capacity that is assessed for those with health conditions and disabilities. But where there are work obligations, our expectation is that they are fulfilled.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all statements at the Estimates hearing. Answer opens with a flat 'Yes' — the question is answered completely in the first word. The following material qualifies the position rather than substituting for an answer, so the direct response stands. Marked slightly below 1.0 only because the lengthy 'but' begins walking back the yes without stating which statements are affected.
question: Mālō e lelei, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by all her statements made during the Disability Issues Estimates hearing at the Social Services and Community Committee on 19 June 2024?
statement: Yes, but since then the independent review has found that the disability support system was in a much worse state than we first understood. Access to disability support services is a postcode lottery based on where someone lives, not their level of need, and Whaikaha - Ministry of Disabled People lacks the capabilities necessary to deliver disability support services effectively, partly due to their rushed establishment under the last Government. The independent review recommended that the initially planned phase two not proceed, as stabilising the disability support system was urgent. That’s why last week our Government announced a series of measures to ensure that the increased budget of $2.6 billion is distributed in a fairer, more consistent way, based on need.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the commitment to Enabling Good Lives and, if so, how she reconciles that with pausing it. The commitment half is answered (yes, to the vision and principles, with a narrowing to 'mainstream first'). The reconciliation half gets only an implicit answer — the review found dire issues requiring urgent action — and the pause itself is never mentioned. Half answered, half gestured at.
question: Does the Minister stand by her statement that “Our Government remains committed to the Enabling Good Lives approach”, and, if so, how does she reconcile this with her decision to pause Enabling Good Lives?
statement: Our Government of course is committed to the vision and principles of Enabling Good Lives, particularly the principle that talks about mainstream first and ensuring that disabled people are supported to access mainstream services before specialist disability services. The independent review highlighted dire issues with a disability support service that required urgent action. Our Government is taking that urgent action.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her 'stabilise and give certainty' statement and how she justifies moving services to MSD when cost and time frame are unknown. She never says whether she stands by it, and never touches the unknown cost or time frame; the reply recites the bleak reports that motivated action generally. It restates why change was needed rather than justifying this change, so the specific core is avoided.
question: Does the Minister stand by her statement that “The most critical thing we do is for people who are already accessing and in need of disability support services, that we stabilise the system and give them certainty”; if so, how can she justify uprooting and transferring disability support services from Whaikaha to the Ministry of Social Development, a process for which the cost and time frame is unknown?
statement: The report that came from the independent review panel, unfortunately, was bleak. That was on top of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet stocktake that was undertaken for the previous Government and released before the election, as well as an independent assurance report that also showed poor financial controls. That is why, in order to stabilise and ensure services that are delivered to disabled people are stabilised, we’ve taken urgent action. That is why we are prioritising disabled people, their families, and carers by making these changes.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the claim that the review engaged widely, and how that squares with Peter Reynolds saying affected people were not consulted. She answers the reconciliation squarely: she lists who she met with during the review and explicitly includes the organisation the member cited. That directly contradicts the quoted claim rather than sidestepping it. Held below 0.9 because she never confirms she stands by the original statement about the review panel's own engagement, substituting her own meetings for it.
question: Does the Minister stand by her statement that the review into disability support services engaged “with a number of organisations and groups and individuals—disabled and non-disabled.”; if so, how does she reconcile this with the comments made by New Zealand Disability Support Network chief executive, Peter Reynolds, who said, “The Government’s bombshell decision to cut disability support funding in real terms, while gutting the Ministry designed by and for disabled people without even deigning to talk with the people affected first is heart-breaking”?
statement: The state of the books and the rapid decline of the ministry’s ability to maintain within its appropriation meant that changes were required. That’s why an independent review panel was set up at pace. And over that time that the independent review panel was doing its work, I met with disabled people, with families, with carers, with organisations, with the Disabled People’s Organisations Coalition, with providers—including the organisation that that member referred to—to understand exactly how they saw the disability support service and what their experience was. It’s fair to say it was bleak; that’s why urgent action has been taken.

explanation: Asked how the disabled community can trust a Minister given three alleged reversals. The reply addresses none of the three and never engages the question of trust; it re-describes the review's findings and the funding increase. This is a hostile but genuine question, and the answer relocates to safer ground rather than contesting the premise or answering it.
question: How can the disabled community trust a Minister who said her Government was committed to Enabling Good Lives, then paused it; said they would stabilise disability support services, then uprooted it; and said they would engage with the disabled community when she didn’t?
statement: I just want to reconfirm what this review was about and the actions that were taken. Over many, many weeks and the discussions with disabled people, families, carers, and providers, it is very clear. It is very clear that the system we have today is unfair, it is inconsistent, and it is a postcode lottery that delivers to disabled people depending on where they live. That is not sustainable, and that is why, with an increased budget of $1.1 billion, we want to ensure that those with the highest needs get their needs met.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, complete, no evasion.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees that his Government's policies are worsening race relations. 'No.' A flat denial with no elaboration is still a complete answer to a yes/no question — brevity and unhelpfulness are not evasion.
question: Does he agree with the mounting evidence that his Government’s policies and actions are worsening race relations in Aotearoa?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether he believes his Government's actions are changing the constitution. 'No.' Direct and complete; the question admitted a one-word answer and got one.
question: Does he believe that his Government’s actions and policies are changing the constitution of this country?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether the constitution allows for three Prime Ministers at once. 'No.' Answers the question as put, squarely.
question: Does our constitution allow for three Prime Ministers at the same time?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether the constitution grants a coalition agreement supremacy over Te Tiriti — a yes/no constitutional question. The reply only asserts that the coalition agreement is clear and honoured, which is a talking point about a different subject; the supremacy question is never engaged.
question: Does Parliament’s constitution grant supremacy to a coalition agreement over Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: We have a very clear coalition agreement. We honour our coalition agreements.

explanation: Asked to describe the distribution of constitutional power created by iwi Māori agreeing to Te Tiriti. The reply gestures at the territory ('protects both Crown and Māori interests') but offers a stock characterisation of the Treaty rather than any description of how power is distributed. It brushes the question without reaching it.
question: Can the Prime Minister describe the distribution of constitutional power created by the agreement of te iwi Māori to Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: As I’ve said before, the Treaty of Waitangi is a foundational document of New Zealand. It protects both Crown and Māori interests.

explanation: Asked how many providers had funding increased and by how much. The answer gives both numbers directly up front (34 services across 25 providers, at least $18.7m). The later attack on the previous Government is padding, not evasion — Focus/Civility, not Forthrightness — and the core was squarely answered.
question: How many Oranga Tamariki community service providers, if any, have had their funding increased, and by how much, if anything, as a result of the Budget 2024 Reduction in Contracting Service Costs?
statement: I’m advised that 34 services across 25 providers will have their funding increased, with a total increase of at least $18.7 million. On top of that, Oranga Tamariki (OT) will be procuring at least 50 new services, and this will include additional services for high and complex needs, and the expansion of the Fast Track programme by $7.6 million. I’ve asked OT to make sure that there’s a more rigorous approach to contracting to ensure the $500 million worth of services it funds each year gets to where it will have the greatest impact. Under the last Government, OT was allowing providers who were under-delivering on their contracts to keep unused funding, they were funding services that weren’t core business, and they were duplicating services in various parts of New Zealand. If the last Government had taken this same approach to contracting now, at least $132 million more could have gone to the children, rather than letting some bank accounts build up.

explanation: A two-part question: confirm the Monitor and Children's Commissioner wrote raising continued concerns, and say what she is doing to reassure them. Neither part is answered — no confirmation of the correspondence, no reassurance measures — instead the reply pivots to a funding-cuts point that was not asked about.
question: Can she confirm that the Independent Children’s Monitor and the Chief Children’s Commissioner have written to Oranga Tamariki stating that they had continued concerns on a range of aspects of the current change process, given its potential detrimental impact for tamariki and whānau, and, if so, what is she doing to reassure them?
statement: It is the same amount of funding—no cuts have been made to funding. What we are doing is reprioritising that funding to where it will make the biggest impact. Oranga Tamariki needs to go back to its core purpose. We can’t keep the status quo, and those organisations you’re speaking to have said that over and over, over the years, Oranga Tamariki is not performing and needs to get back to what they should be doing: looking after our children’s safety.

explanation: Asked for an assurance that changes are like-for-like with no service gaps, and if not, why not. The like-for-like half is answered directly and in the negative ('nobody has ever said it would be like-to-like') with the reason given — a refusal that answers. The 'no gaps in service provision' half is left untouched, so it is a partial answer.
question: Sure. Can she provide an assurance that any funding changes to community service providers are, in fact, like for like and that there will be no gaps in service provision for all communities across the country, and, if not, why not?
statement: Nobody has ever said it would be like-to-like services; what we’ve said is we are going to realign the money where it’s going to make the greatest impact and where it is focusing on the core purpose of Oranga Tamariki, which is the care and protection of children in their care.

explanation: Asked whether she shares the watchdogs' concern that transitional arrangements could not be guaranteed, and if not, why not. She never says whether she shares the concern, but does respond to its substance with concrete transition and wind-down provisions, which implicitly rebuts it. Engaged on the merits, evasive on the direct yes/no.
question: Does she share the concerns of the Chief Children’s Commissioner and Independent Children’s Monitor, who have said, “Oranga Tamariki could not guarantee that transitional arrangements were in place, but hoped they would be”, and, if not, why not?
statement: I have been advised that for services that will be discontinued, provisions have been made to support partners and providers to wind down the services and to safely transition tamariki, rangatahi, and whānau receiving the services to another service. These provisions also allow for either a three-month or a six-month wind-down, depending on the terms of their contract.

explanation: Asked how the cuts and lack of transition assurance square with her stated child-safety priority. The reply refuses to be 'lectured' and attacks the questioner's former Government; the tension the question put to her is never addressed. Textbook attack-the-questioner dodge.
question: How do shambolic cuts to service providers, poor communication with providers about their contracts, and having no assurance about transitioning children and family to alternative services fit with her stated commitment that child safety is her priority?
statement: I actually refuse to stand here and be lectured by a member of that previous Government, which made absolutely no progress when it came to the safety of the wellbeing of our young people. The state of Oranga Tamariki when I took over was absolutely disgusting, and I’m not going to allow that to continue.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements the Government has made on moving jobseekers into work. The answer names the announcement and its content directly. A soft patsy question, but the pair is judged on engagement, not on how easy the question was.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about supporting people on the jobseeker benefit into work?
statement: Last week, I announced a comprehensive package of reforms to the welfare system to support more people off jobseeker support into work and to introduce tougher consequences for those who repeatedly do not meet their benefit obligations. This includes a new traffic light system to inform people what is required of them to continue receiving a benefit and warn them when they are not meeting those expectations. Our Government believes that work is the best pathway to independence and further opportunities. We continue to take action to support New Zealanders into work, and the traffic light system is an important tool to achieve this.

explanation: Asked why the traffic light system was introduced. The answer states the purpose directly — to communicate expectations and enforce compliance — and gives the underlying rationale. Directly responsive.
question: Why was the traffic light system introduced?
statement: The traffic light system was introduced to clearly communicate to job seekers what is expected of them and to ensure they comply with their obligations. It spells out if they are at risk of breaching their work obligations and what the consequences are of failing to comply. Our Government expects those receiving taxpayers’ support to meet their basic obligations to become work-ready and to find work, because we believe in rights and responsibilities.

explanation: Asked how the traffic light system will work. The answer sets out exactly that: what green, orange and red each mean and what follows from each. Complete and squarely on the question.
question: How will the traffic light system work?
statement: The traffic light system categorises job seekers based on their compliance level, providing crystal clear steps on how to comply with their obligations. Green means a beneficiary is on track and complying with all their work obligations. Orange means a job seeker has failed an obligation and must re-comply within five days. Red means a job seeker has breached their obligations, which will result in sanctions being imposed.

explanation: Asked how else the system affects jobseekers. The answer lists further effects — six-monthly reapplication, mandatory profile, non-financial sanctions, two-year failure record. Directly responsive.
question: How else does the traffic light system affect job seekers?
statement: Job seekers will be required to reapply for their benefit every six months, and they must also complete a mandatory job seeker profile. This will enable the Ministry of Social Development to match people with job vacancies. There will also be new, non-financial sanctions that will be available next year, and past failures will be counted against a job seeker’s record for two years, instead of one. Our Government is making our welfare system more proactive to help job seekers into work and experience the benefit of greater financial independence and further opportunities that come from work.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a quoted statement and why. The answer opens with an unambiguous 'yes' and then supplies the 'why' with specific consultation and select committee processes. Both halves engaged.
