question: Who is correct in relation to high-powered semi-automatic rifles: the police Minister when he said, in response to written questions, “As [of] 1 March 2024 there are 328 persons authorised to possess and use (including firing live ammunition) a prohibited firearm for the purposes of pest control”, or the Minister when she said, “we have 6,600 people who have endorsements to be in possession of those firearms”?
statement: Both those statements are correct. But the way that the member has asked the question, I think he needs to go and have a look at the difference between the endorsements and prohibited licences, because, yes, there are 328 pest controllers out there, but there’s also a large number of members of the licensed firearms community that can still use those prohibited firearms. Now, there is a difference between what Brenton Tarrant used and what is a centre-fire semi-automatic, and I suggest, if the member would like, I can give him some education in differing and understanding what they both are.

explanation: Asked: why did she cite the 6,600 figure in reply to a question about prohibited high-powered semi-automatics? She contests the premise (denying the category "high-powered semi-automatic" exists), which is genuine engagement, but never explains why she gave that figure, and closes by offering to sit down and explain endorsements. The premise is challenged; the actual "why" is left unanswered.
question: Why did she say that “currently, over 6,600 New Zealanders are licensed to possess semi-automatic firearms” when asked by Mark Cameron in this House on 27 February 2024 “Will her Government allow competitive shooters to use semi-automatics for sporting purposes?” when the question was clearly referring to high-powered semi-automatic rifles which are prohibited for such events?
statement: I’m very confused by that question. For one, there’s no such thing as a high-powered semi-automatic—we have rim-fire; we’ve got centre-fire. And if I may, Mr Speaker, all firearms that are in the wrong hands of the wrong people can actually make damaging and catastrophic effects. But I just kind of wonder—I’m more than happy to sit with the member and work through so that he understands the differences between our different endorsements: prohibited, restricted, and endorsements.

explanation: Asked: does she agree with the quoted Tom Mauser statement, and if so why is she overstating availability? She offers sympathies and pivots to "we are not America" and New Zealand's own laws, never saying whether she agrees or addressing the follow-on. Talking points in place of an answer.
question: Does she agree with Tom Mauser, whose son was killed in the Columbine school shooting, when speaking of semi-automatics being used for sport shooting: “I understand that there are people who have fun firing these weapons … But, we have to get beyond fun and we really have to consider the danger.”; if so, why is she distracting from the debate on the danger of semi-automatics by suggesting they’re more widely available than they really are?
statement: My sympathies go out to all of the families that have been affected by the Columbine shooting, but it is of an important note that we are not America, we do not have their laws, and our laws and legislation will be relative to what we have here in New Zealand and the use of those firearms.

explanation: Asked: what recent announcements has the Government made about emergency housing? He gives the announcement — a target of a 75 percent reduction in households in emergency housing by 2030 — plus the framing. The question is answered.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about emergency housing?
statement: It is calamitous to see so many whānau in emergency housing, and we’ve recently announced a target of 75 percent reduction of the number of households in emergency housing by 2030. We want emergency housing, motels, and other accommodation to be a last resort, for a short period of time, for those in genuine need.

explanation: Asked: how realistic is the 75 percent reduction? "The target is deliberately ambitious" and "not a quick fix" do concede something about realism, but the rest is aspiration and process (safe warm homes, sustained effort, targets focus attention) with no account of what makes it achievable. Half-answers by conceding stretch, then hedges around the core.
question: How realistic is the 75 percent reduction in emergency housing?
statement: The target is deliberately ambitious. We want whānau and tamariki to have safe, warm, and nice homes. Emergency housing should be a last resort, for a short period of time, for those who genuinely need it. The mahi is not a quick fix—it’s hard mahi. It requires sustained and coordinated effort, something that, in our role as the Kāwanatanga, as the Government, we are committed to do, and setting a target, rather than talk, focuses attention.

explanation: Asked what the Minister will do to meet the emergency-housing target. He names an actual measure — a priority one category on the social housing register for whānau with tamariki in emergency housing 12+ weeks — which engages the question, then trails into a generic 'many tools to increase supply' quote. The core was reached, if only once before the pivot.
question: What are the kinds of things the Minister will be doing to meet this target?
statement: Tamariki are a big focus. No one wants to see tamariki, our children, growing up in these motels. And the Kāwanatanga has announced a priority one category for whānau with tamariki who have been in emergency housing for 12 weeks or more, prioritising them on the social housing register. As my learned sentinel the Hon Chris Bishop has most recently said, to end New Zealand’s cataclysmic housing crisis, we need to use many tools to increase housing supply and to enable more homes and houses for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked why emergency housing was chosen for a target rather than another part of the system. The first sentence answers it squarely — that is where they think they can have the most impact on vulnerable New Zealanders — with the catastrophe framing as supporting reason. The long anecdote that follows is padding, not evasion; the question was already answered.
question: Why is there a target for emergency housing and not another part of the housing system?
statement: Emergency housing is the basis of a target because that’s where we think we can have a significant impact on vulnerable New Zealanders. Long-term, large-scale use of emergency housing is a social, moral, and cultural catastrophe. We can make an impact right now by prioritising tamariki in emergency housing—like a mother and her three tamariki who moved into a home in Tūranganui-a-Kiwa recently, who said, “At one stage, we were all living in a tent in a friend’s backyard. That’s where we were when Cyclone Gabrielle struck, and that backyard got flooded. I’ve been grateful to have a roof over our heads, even though it has been very cramped and restrictive. Four of us living in a small bedroom in a studio has been challenging.” Kia kaha tātou. Mauri ora. [Let us all be strong. Power and wellbeing (to all).]

explanation: Asked whether he has confidence in all his Ministers. 'I have confidence in all of my Ministers.' Complete and direct.
question: Does he have confidence in the statements and actions of all his Ministers?
statement: I have confidence in all of my Ministers.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree with the Auditor-General's comment, and if so has he sought advice on managing ministerial conflicts of interest. He never says whether he agrees and never says whether he sought any advice; 'that is why we'll manage conflicts of interest and we have an independent panel' brushes the topic while answering neither leg.
question: Does he agree with comments from the Auditor-General on the Fast-track Approvals Bill that, “conflicts of interest, whether real or perceived, can create public concern around the integrity of decision making.”, and, if so, has he sought any advice on how to manage conflicts of interest for ministerial decision-makers?
statement: That is why we’ll manage conflicts of interest and that’s why we have an independent panel to make assessments around the economic and environmental impacts.

explanation: Asked how many of the 280 companies written to are subject to declared ministerial conflicts of interest. No number, no engagement with the conflicts question at all — he praises the Minister's outreach, redirects to the member, and closes on 'we are going to get things built'. Pure talking points against a narrow factual question.
question: How many of the companies that Minister Bishop wrote to on 3 April about the fast-track bill are the subject of conflicts of interest that any of his Ministers have declared?
statement: Well, the Minister did a great job reaching out to 280 organisations, many of them iwi-led organisations that actually want to participate in getting things built in this country. What I’d just say to that member is we are going to get things built in this country and we are very, very proud of that fast-track legislation.

explanation: Same count question. He does not give the number, but he engages the question directly by contesting it — no projects have been selected, so the question is moot. That is a stated position on why he won't answer rather than a pivot, which is more forthright than the surrounding attempts, though it still leaves the factual core unaddressed.
question: How many of the companies that Minister Bishop wrote to on 3 April about the fast-track bill are the subject of conflicts of interest that any of his Ministers have declared?
statement: No projects have been selected yet for the fast-track process. So the question is moot.

explanation: The count question a third time. Same 'no projects selected yet' argument, but now diluted with an aside that the member doesn't understand and is 'well ahead of herself', plus a general assurance that conflicts will be managed. The engagement with the question is thinner and the number is again never given.
question: How many of the companies that Minister Bishop wrote to on 3 April about the fast-track bill are the subject of conflicts of interest that any of his Ministers have declared?
statement: Well, the member is not understanding where we are. The bottom line is that there have been no projects that have been selected yet, right? What we’re saying very clearly is—[Interruption] Would you like the answer? We will make sure that conflicts of any interest are managed well, and we’ll make sure that we’ve got an independent expert panel considering all things related to the project. But the member is well ahead of herself, because there have been no projects selected at this stage.

explanation: Asked on what date he became aware that a company in contact with Ministers had donated to a coalition party. 'I'm not aware of that' is a direct and complete answer to a question about his own knowledge — the date is none, because the awareness is denied. Only the trailing conflicts-of-interest assurance is off-question.
question: On what date did he become aware that at least one company in contact with his Ministers about applying for fast-track approval had donated to a coalition political party?
statement: I’m not aware of that, but I know that we will manage conflicts of interest incredibly well with this process.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: did Minister Jones disclose the $50,000 donations before Bishop wrote to Kings Quarry. He answers about project approvals and form letters instead — a different question entirely. The disclosure is never confirmed or denied.
question: Thank you. Did Minister Jones disclose donations of $50,000 to New Zealand First from entities with a connection to Kings Quarry before Minister Bishop wrote to Kings Quarry inviting them to apply for the fast-track process?
statement: I don’t know how to be any more clear with the member, but there are no projects that have been approved under the fast-track provisions at this stage. All that has happened is a form letter has gone out to a series of organisations making them aware of the process and the application process.

explanation: Asked whether Jones disclosed the donations to Cabinet before the Kings Quarry letter. He announces he will 'answer that leg' and then answers a leg that was not asked — no projects confirmed, form letters sent — before moving to why the Government backs fast-track. Explicitly substituting a different question is the clearest form of the dodge.
question: Thank you. Did Minister Jones disclose to Cabinet donations of $50,000 to New Zealand First from entities with a connection to Kings Quarry before Minister Bishop wrote to Kings Quarry inviting them to apply for the fast-track process?
statement: Well, in response to the later part of that question—I’ll answer that leg—I’ve said very clearly, no projects have been confirmed. All that has happened is a form letter has been sent out to a series of organisations—many of them iwi-led organisations—a range of corporates that actually want to participate in fast-track legislation. But the bigger point is very simple here: we are going to get things built in this country and we are not apologising for that. We believe in fast-track legislation because we want modern, reliable infrastructure in this country so we can become more productive; we can get a higher standard of living.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to public scrutiny of projects before the third reading. He neither commits nor refuses; he restates that projects aren't determined and describes the panel process, closing with 'won't that be great?'. A yes-or-no commitment question left with no answer either way.
question: Will he commit to providing an opportunity for public scrutiny of projects before the bill is set down for third reading, to ensure transparency in light of the real risk of conflicts of interest?
statement: Again, projects haven’t been determined yet. We have a clear process that involves an expert panel that will weigh up the economic considerations, the environmental considerations, and Ministers will make decisions. And won’t that be great? Because we’ll finally get some stuff built in this country.

explanation: Asked whether she had seen recent reports on tax. Answered "Yes" and identified the report (OECD on fiscal drag and indexation) plus its content. Direct and complete.
question: Has she seen any recent reports on tax?
statement: Yes. I have seen a report from the OECD on fiscal drag and indexation of personal taxes. It explains how, in a progressive tax system, nominal wage growth leads to larger tax burdens. This includes wage growth that simply reflects inflation. If personal income tax thresholds are not adjusted over time, workers end up paying more and more of their income in tax.

explanation: Asked for an example of fiscal drag in New Zealand. Gave one immediately — the median full-time earner, 2011 vs today, with tax share. Squarely engaged; the transcript cuts off mid-figure but the answer is on target.
question: Can the Minister give an example of fiscal drag in New Zealand?
statement: The example I like to use in New Zealand is the median full-time wage and salary earner. In 2011, that person earned $48,000 a year and paid 15.5 percent of their income in tax. Today, they earn $73,400—

explanation: Asked how other countries deal with fiscal drag. Answered that more than half of the OECD index thresholds, gave the count (17 of 38) and named examples. Directly responsive.
question: How do other countries deal with fiscal drag?
statement: More than half of OECD countries index their personal income tax thresholds. The report I referred to in my primary answer shows that of the 38 OECD countries, around 17 automatically adjust thresholds for inflation or some other index. Those countries include Canada, the United States, Denmark, France, Norway, and Sweden.

explanation: Asked what other OECD countries do about fiscal drag. Answered the question — indexation for most, discretionary relief for the rest, named countries. The closing jab at New Zealand's record is a Focus/Civility matter, not a dodge; the question was answered first.
question: What do other OECD countries do about fiscal drag?
statement: As I said, most OECD countries index tax thresholds. Of the rest, most have decided on a discretionary basis to adjust thresholds and/or rates over the last decade or so to provide tax relief, including Australia, the United Kingdom, and Germany. Only a very small minority of OECD countries have decided not to provide personal income tax relief since 2010, and, in fact, have raised taxes. Those countries include Portugal, Greece, and New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. Answered "Yes" outright. The following advertisement for the phone ban is surplus, not evasion — the yes/no was given.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes. In particular, I stand by this Government’s action to ban mobile phones in schools. Officially kicking in yesterday, the ban is already helping young Kiwis focus on learning the skills they need to succeed, and schools across the country are reporting more engaged kids, louder playgrounds and sports fields at lunchtime, more positive interaction, and less cyber-bullying. We’re committed to delivering better public services for Kiwis. This is just one part of our plan to do exactly that.

explanation: Asked what additional factors he was made aware of between expressing confidence in Melissa Lee and dismissing her. Offered one general factor (the portfolio became more complex) but never says what he learned or when, which was the core of the question. Partial engagement.
question: What additional factors was he made aware of between 4 March, when he expressed full confidence in Melissa Lee, and last week, when he dismissed her from the broadcasting portfolio?
statement: As I discussed last week, Melissa Lee, and Penny Simmonds, for that matter, are hard-working, good Ministers doing an excellent job, but those portfolios became more complex and more complicated, and I want them managed by senior Ministers.

explanation: Same question about Penny Simmonds. Repeats the generic "more complicated" reason without naming any factor he was made aware of, then pivots to attacking the questioner's own record. Less of the question reached than in the Lee answer.
question: What additional factors was he made aware of between 26 March, when he expressed full confidence in Penny Simmonds, and last week, when he dismissed her from the disability portfolio?
statement: Again, as I said, the agenda in disability issues became more complicated and complex, and I want that managed by more senior Ministers. But what I’d just say is that that’s the same leader who was a Prime Minister, along with Grant Robertson, his former Minister of Finance, who actually got advice about the problems in that department, agency, and their management of their money and their budget and did nothing about it. It was typical of his Government to not face up to issues, to not deal with them. We’re doing that.

explanation: Asked a direct yes/no — does he agree with Seymour's and Jones' criticism of the Waitangi Tribunal, and if not why not. Answered with praise for his Ministers and never says whether he agrees. Neither limb of the question is touched.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does he agree with David Seymour and Shane Jones’ criticism of the Waitangi Tribunal; if not, why not?
statement: Again, what I’d say to you: I have strong Ministers doing an excellent job, and both those Ministers are doing exactly that.

explanation: Asked whether he believes the criticism breaches the Cabinet Manual. "I wouldn't characterise it that way" is a clear no, and the question was yes/no. Mildly indirect phrasing and the deflection to prior statements keep it short of a flat answer, but the core is engaged.
question: Does he believe that David Seymour’s and Shane Jones’ criticism of the Waitangi Tribunal breaches the Cabinet Manual?
statement: I wouldn’t characterise it that way, and you’ve seen my statements on the issue.

explanation: Asked why it does not breach the Cabinet Manual — a request for a reason. "Because I don't believe it does" restates the position and supplies no reason at all. Not a pivot or an attack, but the core of the question is never reached; this is a tautology standing in for an answer, not a terse-but-complete one.
question: Why does it not breach the Cabinet Manual?
statement: Because I don’t believe it does.

explanation: Asked whether he will take disciplinary action, and if not why not. Responds entirely with an attack on the questioner over Michael Wood; no action, no reason, no engagement with either limb.
question: Will the Prime Minister take disciplinary action against ministerial colleagues like David Seymour and Shane Jones attacking the legitimacy of the Waitangi Tribunal, in breach of the Cabinet Manual; if not, why not?
statement: Look, I have to say the sanctimony from that member is quite outrageous, because it took him longer to sack Michael Wood than it will take for the backbench to sack him.

explanation: Asked which of two people is right. "The Prime Minister." Two words, and a complete answer to exactly what was asked.
question: Who is right: the Prime Minister, who said that ultimately he determines the performance of Cabinet Ministers, or David Seymour, who said that the Prime Minister sacking an ACT Minister would be a breach of the faith of the coalition agreement and would be a major problem?
statement: The Prime Minister.

explanation: Closed yes/no question ('Does he stand by all his Government's policies and actions?') answered with 'Yes.' One word, but complete and unambiguous.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s policies and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked what opportunity the PUBLIC will be given to weigh in. The answer describes the fast-track process and an independent expert panel that informs Ministers — it never says whether or how the public gets a say. Pivots to a defence of the process instead of reaching the question.
question: What opportunity will the public be given to weigh in on projects that will be approved in their community as a result of the Fast-track Approvals Bill?
statement: Again, what I’d say is that we have a great fast-track process. It’s designed to get things built in this country, but a key component of it is an independent expert panel that will weigh up considerations economically, environmentally, and socially, and inform Ministers.

explanation: Asked how the public can have confidence given undisclosed ministerial conflicts. The reply ('there are no projects that have been approved') engages by rejecting the premise's urgency, which is a real if minimal response, but it never addresses confidence or disclosure. Partial engagement.
question: How can the public have confidence in this Government’s Cabinet overseeing the decisions of the hundred projects in the Fast-track Approvals Bill when Ministers are not disclosing their conflicts of interest?
statement: Well, there are no projects that have been approved.

explanation: Asked what actions he will take to ensure Cabinet Manual adherence. 'We have well-established processes on managing perceived or real conflicts of interest' does answer — the action is the existing process — but the rest is talking points about getting things built. Answers around the core rather than through it.
question: What actions will the Prime Minister take to ensure that his Cabinet Ministers will adhere to the Cabinet Manual around the conflict of interests, if given, for the Fast-track Approvals Bill?
statement: We have well-established processes on managing perceived or real conflicts of interest, but, again, we make no apologies about introducing fast-track legislation. It is important that we get things done in this country. We are over the talk and discussion; we need to get things built.

explanation: A narrow yes/no factual question: does a register of current conflicts exist, before or after select committee? The answer never says yes or no, restating 'well-established processes' and diverting to the absence of approved projects. A specific question squarely avoided.
question: Has the Prime Minister got any register of current conflicts of interest before the beginning of the Fast-track Approvals Bill as it hits the select committee, or after the select committee process?
statement: Again, we have well-established processes for managing ministerial conflicts of interest, the Cabinet Office, and Ministers, but, again, we have not yet got a full set of projects. We haven’t got any projects that are approved yet. That’s the point of introducing this legislation: so we can get some projects approved and done and building.

explanation: Asked for the Government's response to the Tribunal's 'actual harm' finding. He declines explicitly and with a stated reason — the matter is before the courts, so it is inappropriate to comment. A plain refusal is a direct response, not a dodge; marked down slightly for the wellbeing-of-children preamble that stands in place of the answer.
question: What is the response to the Waitangi Tribunal’s urgency on his Government’s plan to repeal section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, released yesterday, which stated it would cause “actual harm” to vulnerable children?
statement: Our Government is going to make sure that the wellbeing of children comes first, but that issue is before the courts and it’s inappropriate for me to comment.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a quoted Potaka statement. He does not give a view but says outright that the matter is before the courts and he will not comment further. An unambiguous refusal to answer, stated as such — forthright even though unhelpful.
question: Does he agree with Tama Potaka on 26 July 2023, regarding the repeal of section 7AA, that “It would be contradictory of us to dismiss this provision entirely, which is intended to be a genuine option to address and meet the best interests of the child in State care.”?
statement: Again, this Government is focusing on making sure the wellbeing of a child comes first and foremost as the important thing that we have to do, but this matter is before the courts and I won’t be commenting any further on it.

explanation: Two-part question (does he agree with Hipango, and what has changed?). Again a plain, reasoned refusal — under appeal this week, no further comment — which counts as engaging rather than dodging, but the 'what has changed' half is left untouched even by the refusal's framing.
question: Does he agree with Harete Hipango on July 2023, regarding section 7AA, that “If the National Party gets into Government, we would not be repealing it,”, and, if so, what has changed since then?
statement: We are going to make sure that we prioritise the welfare of our most vulnerable children so they end up in loving homes. That is job number one. But I will not be making any further comments, given that this is under appeal through the courts this week.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen; she names one (the Secondary Principals' Association of New Zealand's report of less distraction and more playground interaction). Squarely on the question, with a policy-boosting tail that does not detract from the answer given.
question: What reports has she seen about the “away for the day” cellphone policy?
statement: There have been overwhelmingly positive responses to our “off and away all day” policy to ban the use of cellphones in schools. The Secondary Principals’ Association of New Zealand said that schools who started the year with a ban are reporting less distraction and more interaction in the playground, with a lot of children out playing sport or heading to the library. I am proud of this Government that we are prepared to take decisive action, and that’s why, from the first day of term 2, all schools were required to implement the cellphone use ban to ensure every student has the same opportunity to succeed at school.

explanation: Asked what evidence she has seen; she cites a specific Norwegian Institute of Public Health study and its findings. Directly and completely responsive to what was asked.
question: What evidence has she seen to support New Zealand’s cellphone policy?
statement: A recent study published by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health wrote that banning smart phones significantly reduced bullying, improved the grades of students, and significantly decreased the number of visits students made to see mental health specialists. The study also found that schools that implemented a policy removing phones for the whole day—not just class time—experienced a larger increase in student educational performance. That is why it is our expectation that cellphones are off and away all day, so we can get back to basics and ensure our kids are literate, numerate, and aspirational about their futures.

explanation: Asked for principals' feedback; she relays principals' feedback, including a Dunedin secondary principal and a named quote from the Hornby High School principal. Exactly the thing requested.
question: What feedback has she seen from school principals about the “away for the day” cellphone policy?
statement: Principals from across the country continue to write to me to tell me how wonderful it is to hear the noise in the playground, with more students talking to each other, playing games, and connecting. One Dunedin secondary school principal reported that restricting pupils’ cellphones had resulted in a massive drop in harmful social media incidents. The Hornby High School principal said he wished they’d done it five years ago. He said, “We’re seeing kids … outside … playing games, throwing balls, reading books and generally interacting more positively rather than having heads down on a phone.” This policy is part of our wider plan to lift student achievement and wellbeing.

explanation: Asked what feedback she received abroad; she reports what counterparts in Singapore asked her about and cites the UK. The 'feedback' is thin (they asked her to share the approach) but the question is engaged head-on rather than deflected.
question: What feedback has she received while recently abroad about the cellphone policy?
statement: Last week, in Singapore, I had the opportunity to meet with many of my international counterparts. The number one thing I was asked about was cellphones. Education Ministers from around the world asked me to share our approach and why it had been so successful. Other countries are also making changes. The UK Government has also taken steps to prohibit cellphones in their schools. The UK Secretary for Education explained that “By prohibiting mobile phones, schools can create safe and calm environments free from distraction so all pupils can receive the education they deserve.” This Government is committed to getting the basics right, supporting Kiwi kids to succeed. Getting cellphones out of schools was just the start and there’s a lot more to come.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a quoted statement. She says "Yes" and restates the statement — a direct, complete answer. The "in the context in which it was given" qualifier is a mild hedge, not a dodge.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “We will … both [be] sustaining front-line services and, in the cases of the areas … I outlined in my opening remarks, increasing funding for those services.”?
statement: Yes, I stand by my full statement in the context in which it was given. In my opening remarks to the Finance and Expenditure Committee about the Budget Policy Statement, I said, “front-line services like health, education and law and order will get more funding.”, and I’m proud to say that in Budget 2024 they certainly will.

explanation: Asked what directions she gives Ministers/chief executives to avoid front-line cuts. She states the direction given (apply good judgment, don't put front-line services at risk). Vague in content, but it squarely answers the question asked — vagueness is Specificity, not Forthrightness.
question: What directions does she give to Ministers or chief executives in avoiding cuts to front-line services?
statement: I said that when agencies were putting forward savings proposals, they should apply good judgment and be careful that proposals should not put front-line services at risk.

explanation: Asked whether specific named cuts (child exploitation team, Whaikaha, Customs) constitute good judgment. She opens by attacking the questioner's framing, then says the proposals are under consultation with no final decisions. That is a procedural deflection touching the topic; the good-judgment question is never answered.
question: Is it good judgment for the Department of Internal Affairs to make cuts to the child exploitation team, cuts to care or support funded through Whaikaha—Ministry of Disabled People, and Customs cutting its border services?
statement: In what has become a habit from that member, she tends to paraphrase and summarise a series of loosely connected facts and make assertions about them. In the case of what I think are restructuring proposals that the member is in this question referring to, I would note that they are under consultation and, therefore, no final decisions have been taken.

explanation: Asked whether she can hold to her no-front-line-cuts commitment given she is doing nothing to enforce her expectations. "We enforce our expectations" directly rebuts the premise of the question, so the core is engaged, but the commitment half is left unaddressed. Partial.
question: Does she believe she can commit to her commitment of no front-line service cuts when she is doing nothing to enforce her expectations as part of Budget 2024?
statement: Mr Speaker, I’ll tell you how we roll over here: we enforce our expectations.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet has signed off the Budget and on what date. She explicitly declines to divulge Cabinet processes — a stated refusal, which is a direct response rather than a dodge. Marked down slightly because the refusal is wrapped in Budget-day banter rather than delivered plainly.
question: Has Cabinet signed off this year’s Budget, and, if so, on what date was it agreed to?
statement: Cabinet processes are not something that I think is in the public interest to divulge at this time. But I am pleased that the member opposite is obviously as excited as I am about the 2024 Budget. You’ll have to wait until 30 May when I deliver it, and, I’m sorry, you’re not going to get first dibs on the content.

explanation: Asked whether her commitment to tax cuts is about protecting her own job over front-line workers' jobs. She does answer the "why tax relief matters to me" half on its own terms, but never engages the imputation about her job, and drifts into attacking the previous government. Partial engagement.
question: Is the reason she is so committed to delivering her tax cuts as part of Budget 2023 because protecting her own job is more important than the jobs of front-line workers?
statement: Why it’s important to me to provide tax relief to working people is that, unlike the members opposite, I don’t think it’s the man in high-vis or the woman in the nurse’s uniform that should always be the last to get relief. Unlike the members opposite, I’m not going to continue on a path of low-value spending, of wasteful programmes—like merging TVNZ and RNZ, and three waters reform—when there are working people paying more and more of their income in tax, who’ve had to endure a cost of living crisis that her party fuelled. We are delivering them tax relief. They’ve worked hard and they earned it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. "Yes" — direct and complete; the added three-strikes material is elaboration, not evasion.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially this Government’s action to bring back three strikes. Communities across New Zealand are sick and tired of seeing what happens when a Government spends years embedding a “soft on crime” approach that prioritises offenders over victims, and that’s why we’re making the changes, because New Zealanders expect this Government to restore law and order.

explanation: Asked for two concrete figures (today's two-zone teen bus fare and tomorrow's). He redirects the member to lodge a specific question. This defers rather than refuses on stated grounds, and the narrow factual core is left entirely untouched.
question: What is the cost of a two-zone fare on the bus for a teenager in Auckland today, and what will it be tomorrow when the Government cancels half-price public transport fares?
statement: If you’d like to put that in a specific question, I’m sure we can get an answer for you.

explanation: Asked how doubling teen public transport costs helps families with the cost of living. He notes remaining concessions (community services card, student rates), which glances at the question, then pivots to tax relief talking points. The "how does this help" core is never reached.
question: How exactly does doubling the cost of public transport for teenagers help families with the cost of living?
statement: Well, there’ll still be support for those that are on community services cards and mobility services; obviously, student discount rates. But what’s important, and what this Government’s working incredibly hard to do, is making sure that we support low and middle income working New Zealanders by giving them tax relief. It’s been 14 long years. It’s been a 40 percent increase in the cost of goods through inflation. They deserve tax relief. They work incredibly hard. We’re going to deliver it to them, and that will help them navigate the cost of living crisis.

explanation: Asked for Trade Me's national median rent now and at the election. Again redirects to a written question; the two requested figures are not addressed at all. A narrow factual question left wholly unanswered.
question: What is Trade Me’s national median rent price today, and what was it when his Government was elected last year?
statement: Again, if you’d like to put that as a specific question, I’m sure we can get you an answer.

explanation: Asked when, if ever, the landlord tax cut reaches renters. The answer discusses supply challenges and working hard on downward pressure; no timeframe is given and the link between the tax cut and renters is never addressed.
question: When, if ever, will the $2.9 billion landlord tax cut trickle down to the 1.5 million renters in this country?
statement: Well, as I’ve said to this member before, we have a problem with housing in this country, and it has not been solved by the previous administration over the last six years, but we are determined to work hard at solving it. The problem is a supply challenge. It’s a supply challenge—you can’t buy a house; you can’t afford one. Supply challenge on the rental market; supply challenge on the State housing market. We are working incredibly hard to make sure we get the settings right to put downward pressure on rents, because we’re not having a $170 per week increase in average rents. We are working hard to make sure we put downward pressure.

explanation: Asked for a commitment that rents will come down, or an admission it is hot air. He substitutes "downward pressure on rents" and lists policies, which is adjacent but declines the binary commitment without ever saying he won't give it.
question: Will the Prime Minister, then, commit to rent prices coming down under his Government, or is that all hot air?
statement: We’re putting downward pressure on rents, and we’re doing that by restoring interest deductibility—a legitimate business expense, we’re making sure we bring back the brightline test, and we’re balancing the laws between tenants and landlords.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a quoted statement. Opens with "Yes, I stand by my statement" — a direct, complete answer to a yes/no question. The following commitment sentence is padding but does not displace the answer.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “We stand by our commitments, that we won’t be reducing the front line, that we will continue to deliver services as effectively as we can, and that the cuts that we’re talking about are mostly back-office cuts”?
statement: Yes, I stand by my statement. This Government is absolutely committed to delivering services as effectively as we can to ensure that New Zealanders can access the healthcare they deserve.

explanation: Asked how front-line services can be undiminished when hospitals are told to cut casual nurse cover. He engages the mechanism directly: 2,500 nurses entered the workforce, so less penal time and overtime is needed. That is an on-point account of why casual cover is falling without a front-line cut. Whether it is true or sufficiently detailed is not this attribute's business.
question: How can it be true that front-line services aren’t being reduced when hospitals are under instruction from Health New Zealand leadership to reduce the use of casual nurses who cover roster gaps across a range of services?
statement: This is a reflection that in the calendar year 2023, I am informed that 2,500 nurses entered the workforce. As a consequence of that, we are needing to acquire less penal time and less overtime.

explanation: Asked why doctors are being told they cannot fill vacant specialist roles. He never addresses the instruction not to fill them — he concedes the market is tight, cites 200 FTE specialists joining, and pivots to reassurance about safety and a procurement saving. It circles the topic without reaching the question.
question: Why are doctors being told that they cannot fill vacant specialist roles in hospitals, even when they have identified appropriately qualified doctors in what is still a globally tight market for specialists?
statement: It is a globally tight market for specialists, and I am informed that 200 fulltime-equivalent specialists joined the health workforce in the calendar year 2023. Having said that, I am reassured by Health New Zealand that health services are safe and they are simply looking for efficiencies, such as the $2.75 million that they found in one hospital in the past three months for more efficient procurement of consumables.

explanation: Same question, re-put. Slightly more engagement than the first attempt: "sometimes this is simply a matter of timing" is at least a proffered reason why roles sit vacant. Still mostly a restatement of the recruitment number rather than an account of why hiring is being blocked.
question: Why are doctors being told that they cannot fill vacant specialist roles in hospitals, even when they have identified appropriately qualified doctors in what is still a globally tight market for specialists?
statement: As I said, I am informed by Health New Zealand that 200 fulltime-equivalent specialists were entered into the health system in calendar year 2023, and sometimes this is simply a matter of timing. We look forward to employing more senior medical officers as we are able to.

explanation: Asked why he denied a hiring freeze given HNZ's 17 April letter. "People are currently being hired today" is a terse contest of the question's premise — it addresses whether a freeze exists, which is the core of the challenge, but not the "why did you deny it" framing or the letter itself. Brevity is not the deduction here; the unaddressed half is.
question: Why did he deny in a statement to Radio New Zealand that there is a hiring freeze in public hospitals when Health New Zealand wrote to health unions on 17 April to say that all unfilled roles were being reviewed and considered for removal?
statement: People are currently being hired today.

explanation: Asked whether he can understand why health workers are angry. He substitutes his own "what I do understand" and turns it into a campaign-priorities comparison with the questioner. The question asked is never engaged.
question: Can he understand why health workers are angry that after he campaigned on a workforce crisis, the Minister is now blocking hospitals from filling gaps through a hiring freeze in public hospitals?
statement: What I do understand is that during the campaign, I said the health workforce was a number one priority; that member did not.

explanation: Asked why he won't admit the promise on front-line health jobs is broken. He answers by attacking the questioner's own wait-list record. There is a faint implicit refusal to admit it, but no engagement with the question — a refusal only scores high when it is stated as one, and this is a counter-attack instead.
question: Why won’t he admit that six months in, his Government has already broken its promise not to cut front-line health jobs and it’s taking the country backwards?
statement: I won’t take advice on broken promises from a member who said that non-orthopaedic wait-lists of more than 365 days would be met by the end of last year, which was a terrible failure.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made. She names one immediately — the independent review of Disability Support Services — and elaborates. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements, if any, has the Minister made?
statement: This morning, I announced an independent review of Disability Support Services. Our Government is committed to improving the lives of disabled New Zealanders. This review aims to ensure that support services enhance the lives of disabled people in the long term. We’ve already committed additional funding this financial year to ensure disabled people get the services they need.

explanation: Asked why the review is needed. Answers on point: substantial delivery challenges, the current track is unsustainable. Squarely responsive to the question asked.
question: Why is the independent review of Disability Support Services needed?
statement: Substantial challenges have been encountered delivering support services. Despite the hard work of many, the current track is unsustainable. Something has to be done. The review aims to ensure that support services enhance the lives of disabled people and gives them certainty about access to support. Whaikaha - the Ministry of Disabled People welcomes this review and I look forward to working with them.

explanation: Asked how long the review will take. Gives the timeframe — recommendations within four months — then adds consultation plans. The core is answered; the phrasing is slightly loose about whether four months is the review or her consideration of it.
question: How long will the review take?
statement: I should review recommendations within four months. Once the review is complete, I will consult the disability community, seeking their feedback. I’m committed to listening to the views of disabled people, their families, and their carers before making changes.

explanation: Asked whether this is the first review of Disability Support Services in recent years. "No", followed by context. A complete answer to a yes/no question.
question: Is this the first time in recent years Disability Support Services have been reviewed?
statement: No. The ministry was created to improve Disability Support Services and it was established quickly, which meant longstanding challenges weren’t addressed.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on access to medicines. After an aside about a visitor in the gallery, he answers directly: a budget of nearly $1.6 billion a year for medicines over four years. The digression delays but does not replace the answer.
question: I’ve spared the House by singing my question! What recent announcements has he made about improving Kiwis’ access to medicines?
statement: I’d like to acknowledge the presence of the Rt Hon John Key, who’s clearly at a loose end! In respect of pharmaceuticals and medicines for New Zealanders, I announced yesterday that we will have a budget of nearly $1.6 billion a year for medicines for Kiwis for the next four years. For many New Zealanders, funding medicine means life or death, or the difference between a life of pain and suffering or living freely. This Government has managed to make the sacrifices in other areas by cutting waste to fund these vital medicines, so they don’t get cut.

explanation: Asked why the package needed announcing. The response opens by attacking the previous Government's record on funding medicines — it gestures at a reason (the previous funding shortfall) but is cut off before reaching it and spends what it has on the other side rather than on the need.
question: Why was there a need to announce this package?
statement: The previous Government talked a big game about care and kindness, but when it came to funding medicines—

explanation: Asked how the announcement supports healthcare. Answered squarely: medicines at risk of delisting continue, 30 newly funded, 31 with widened access, plus named upcoming decisions. The core of the question is reached directly.
question: How will this announcement help to support New Zealanders’ healthcare?
statement: We are, at the moment, in a time of extraordinary technical revolution when it comes to medicines. The question is whether New Zealanders can keep up with the First World expectations that they have for themselves and their families. This funding means that many medicines that would have been at risk of delisting will continue. That includes 30 new medicines funded since 2022; 31 with widened access to more patients; and decisions that have been recently made or are in progress, such as funding continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps, and myeloma treatments. Those would have been at risk under the Budget this Government inherited. They are now viable because we’ve found the savings of waste elsewhere to put the money into medicines Kiwis need.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. "Yes." One word, complete, no evasion.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a specific statement about no front-line cuts. "Yes." Direct and complete.
question: Does she stand by her statement that there will be no front-line cuts to services providing care and protection to children?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked for an assurance the International Child Protection Unit will not be disestablished, and if not, why not. The response declines on the ground that she lacks ministerial responsibility — that engages both limbs (no assurance, and the reason), but "some of those" leaves it unclear which part of the question she is disclaiming, so it stops short of a complete answer.
question: Can she assure the House that the International Child Protection Unit, that focuses on cross-border issues like child labour exploitation, sexual exploitation, and child trafficking will not be disestablished, and, if not, why not?
statement: I don’t have ministerial responsibility for some of those.

explanation: Asked directly whether she supports the proposal to disestablish the unit. The response describes a restructure, consultation and her general expectations, never saying supported or not. A narrow yes/no question left unanswered.
question: Does the Minister support the ministry’s proposal to disestablish the unit that plays a crucial role in preventing and addressing child labour exploitation, child sexual exploitation, and child trafficking and smuggling?
statement: Oranga Tamariki is currently going through a restructure. All this is still under proposal, and consultation is still happening. Oranga Tamariki has my expectation that the best interests of our young people are at the forefront of all their decision making. That is my expectation.

explanation: Asked why she is standing by cuts to child-protection agencies. A reason is given — returning Oranga Tamariki to a core care-and-protection focus by streamlining — which addresses the "why". It reframes cuts as streamlining rather than defending them as cuts, so the core is engaged but not fully met.
question: As the Minister for Children, why is the Minister standing by cuts to agencies and services that are dedicated to the protection of children?
statement: Oranga Tamariki needs to get back to its core focus, which is care and protection of our young people. We are streamlining the organisation to focus on the care and protection of our young people. We need to get back to the basics and do it better than we have been.

explanation: Asked what recent CCCFA announcements he had made. Both announcements are named and described. Directly and completely answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding regulations in the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003?
statement: The coalition Government recently announced two important but related announcements relating to the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act (CCCFA), which has plagued personal and mortgage lending over recent years. Firstly, we are removing 11 pages of overly prescriptive affordability regulations to consumer and mortgage lending so people can more easily borrow money when and if they need it. And, secondly, we’re streamlining and enhancing dispute resolution services so Kiwis are properly protected if they are subject to poor lending practices.

explanation: Asked why the reforms were a priority. Two reasons given: the coalition agreement, and harm from the previous regulations. Squarely responsive to the question asked.
question: Why were these reforms a priority for the coalition Government?
statement: First of all, these changes were part of the National-ACT coalition agreement, but, secondly, they were a priority, because the regulations introduced by the previous Government were so bad that they harmed the very people they were meant to protect. This coalition Government is committed to cutting red tape, and these regulations were a handbrake and did more harm than good.

explanation: Asked how removing the regulations helps people get a mortgage or personal loan. The response supplies the mechanism — rebalancing affordability assessment, lenders re-entering small personal loans, fewer hoops for mortgage applicants. Engages the question directly.
question: How will removing 11 pages of regulations from the CCCFA help people get a mortgage or personal loan?
statement: By removing these regulations, it will bring back more balance to the need to properly assess affordability with the need for Kiwis to access finance when they need it. At the moment, many reputable lenders simply do not offer small personal loans, because of the overbearing compliance cost. It is families who have worked hard to buy a house who can’t actually get a mortgage, because they have to jump through unnecessary hoops.

explanation: Asked whether he has further CCCFA plans. Answered yes in substance: consultation on legislative changes in coming weeks, with more reform to follow.
question: Does the Minister have any further plans regarding the CCCFA?
statement: In the coming weeks, we’ll begin consulting on the legislative changes to the CCCFA reforms. But I’ll just say this is just the beginning of reforms that will help improve Kiwis’ access to finance, cut red tape, and help rebuild the economy.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. "Yes" is given up front; the subsequent unrelated boasting about the phone policy does not retract or hedge the answer, and off-topic padding is a Focus matter, not evasion.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes. In particular, I stand by the Government’s “phone away for the day” policy, which is so popular with parents and students and schools—and with great feedback from people like the Hornby High School head boy, Khush Patel, who said the ban “has helped students focus more academically”. Cameron Stone, the principal of Stratford High School in the mighty Whanganui electorate, said, “It’s an awesome, overwhelming success for us.” I have to say, I am proud to lead a Government that makes the changes that we need to ensure our kids are well set up for a great future, because we’re getting our country back on track. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what reaction she had seen. She names a reaction she saw (a commentator calling the commitment "fiscal jiggery-pokery") — that is the thing asked for. She then spends the rest attacking Verrall, but the question's core was reached before the pivot. Marked down slightly because only one reaction is given before the answer turns into rebuttal; the rudeness itself is not penalised.
question: What reaction has the Minister seen to this announcement?
statement: Well, I have seen one commentator—who should know better—describe this $1.77 billion commitment to continue funding much-needed medicines as “fiscal jiggery-pokery”. Personally, I would reserve the term “fiscal jiggery-pokery” to describe the practice of funding medicines for one year only and then taking it away again. I think that is being highly misleading to New Zealand, and I would expect much better from the Labour health spokesperson, Ayesha Verrall.

explanation: A yes/no question — will the Budget establish any fiscal cliffs? She never says yes or no. She does engage the substance sideways by conceding there will be cases funded pending review rather than committed to baseline, which is the mechanism the question is about, so this is more than a pure pivot. But the core (any or none?) is left for the listener to infer.
question: Will Budget 2024 establish any fiscal cliffs?
statement: Well, I thank the member for her question. It seems that her and Ayesha Verrall are great minds thinking alike today. As I said, we are going to be upfront and transparent in our Budget. There will be important cases where we will ensure that a review is undertaken before we commit to baseline funding—for the very good reason that, as I’ve said to this House many times, we are a Government that is committed to fiscal discipline on value for money and ensuring that where we commit New Zealand taxpayer money permanently into the future, we can first assure New Zealanders that we know that dollar is going to its best purpose.

explanation: Two-part question. The first part is answered explicitly ("yes"). The second — will she guarantee every New Zealander is better off — gets no guarantee and no refusal to guarantee; instead a deflection to "many factors affect wellbeing" followed by spending talking points. Half the question squarely answered, half circled.
question: Does she stand by her commitment to deliver meaningful tax cuts for New Zealanders; if so, will she guarantee that every New Zealander will be better off under her Budget?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the second part, many factors affect New Zealanders’ wellbeing, not just a Government Budget, which the member seems to imply is the only way New Zealanders can be better off. I can tell the member, however, that we will be putting in more money to improve health services in this Budget. We will be putting in more money to improve education and we will be putting in more money to strengthen law and order. Better public services and tax relief for hard-working Kiwis will help improve people’s wellbeing and help them get ahead. But there is a catch. New Zealanders who commit violent crime—they’ll be worse off under our Budget.

explanation: Asked specifically how the 12,000 newly unemployed benefit from tax cuts. The answer offers one generic line ("all New Zealanders benefit from a strong economy") and then recites inflation, interest rates and recession history. The named group is never addressed. The long recital is not what drops the score — the failure to reach the question is.
question: How will the additional 12,000 New Zealanders who are now unemployed, according to today’s unemployment figures, benefit from the tax cuts and be better off in Budget 2024?
statement: All New Zealanders benefit from a strong economy, and we as a Government are embarking on a significant project to rebuild an economy that has been drastically weakened by a period of prolonged, very high inflation that has eroded people’s real incomes and purchasing power, that has led to a significant increase in interest rates, that is in turn leading to four of the past five quarters having been in recession and very challenging economic conditions. That is the reality we are faced with. It is difficult for many New Zealanders. Our job is to get on with delivering the plan to rebuild our economy and that is what our Budget will do.

explanation: Asked whether people facing insurance and rates increases will be better off. The response addresses no part of it, instead mocking an imputed Labour policy of subsidising insurance. A pivot to attacking the questioner's party in place of any answer.
question: Will the increasing number of New Zealanders who are struggling with increases in insurance premiums and higher rates that are significantly outstripping inflation be better off in Budget 2024?
statement: This is a novel new policy from the Labour Party today. They’re going to be subsidising everyone’s insurance bill, I see.

explanation: The literal question is whether she understands she is responsible for her choices, and she answers it head-on in the first sentence: she fully understands the responsibility for the choices this Government makes. The remainder is a counter-attack on Labour's record, and she declines the question's embedded premise about causing the deterioration — but the question as put was engaged and answered before the pivot.
question: Does she understand that a Minister of Finance—she is responsible for the choices she makes that are causing these deteriorating economic conditions?
statement: I fully and solemnly understand the responsibility we in this Government have for the choices we make. And I would point that member to the colleagues either side of her on that front bench, who actively chose not to adjust tax thresholds, even while inflation ate away at people’s incomes, who actively chose to pour fuel on the inflation fire while a cost of living crisis surged, who actively chose to spend money on a TVNZ and RNZ merger when New Zealanders couldn’t pay for their groceries. Take responsibility for your own choices as a party and I’ll take responsibility for mine every day of the week. [Interruption]

explanation: First part answered directly ("yes"). Second part — will he commit to public scrutiny of selected projects — is engaged but not settled: he points to the existing select committee and parliamentary stages rather than committing or declining to commit, then diverts to what the previous Government did under COVID fast-track. The question's core is approached and left just short.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that “No projects have been selected yet for the fast-track process”; if so, will he commit to providing an opportunity for public scrutiny of the projects when they are selected for Part A of Schedule 2 of the Fast-track Approvals Bill?
statement: In response to the first part of the question, yes. As we’ve said a number of times, both publicly and in the House, no projects have been selected for the fast-track process. Cabinet has made a decision to set up a thorough and independent panel process for the selection of projects to be included in the schedule of the bill. In regard to the second part of the question, the public currently has the ability to submit to the select committee considering the bill. Parliament will have the opportunity to consider the projects in the schedule of the bill. The member might be interested to know we have based the process on the COVID-19 fast-track legislation introduced by the previous Government, in which Cabinet delegated to David Parker decision making for what projects were to be listed in the bill upon introduction. These decisions were made without any public consultation prior to the select committee.

explanation: "Not currently." A complete answer to whether he has received such advice; the second conditional limb falls away because the answer is no. Its brevity and unhelpfulness are not forthrightness failures.
question: Has he received any advice about options for providing public scrutiny of projects to be listed in the legislation, and, if so, what was that advice?
statement: Not currently.

explanation: "Yes. And, in relation to the second part of the question, no." Both limbs answered explicitly and completely. The refusal on the second part is a direct answer, not a dodge.
question: Does he stand by his statement “We’re open to constructive changes on the fast-track regime to ameliorate some of the concerns that people have”, and, if so, will he support sending the bill back to the select committee to allow for scrutiny of projects?
statement: Yes. And, in relation to the second part of the question, no.

explanation: A narrow factual question — did he check with Cabinet colleagues before sending the 3 April letter? He never says whether he checked. Instead he characterises the letter as a courtesy form letter that raises no conflict concerns, i.e. answers a different question (was there anything to check?) than the one asked. A specific question squarely avoided.
question: Did he check with any of his Cabinet colleagues about potential or perceived conflicts of interest before deciding to send the letter on the fast-track bill on 3 April?
statement: Mr Speaker, the member, like others in her party, has made much of a courtesy form letter that went to 200 organisations, some of whom are interested in fast-track, some of whom are not interested in fast-track. So writing a letter to someone which is, essentially, a press release letting them know that the fast-track process is open does not raise any concerns like the member is raising.

explanation: Asked what announcements he had made on RMA reform; he states the announcement and enumerates the changes and the bill being introduced. Directly and completely responsive. The detail is not what earns the score — the fact that the question asked for announcements and announcements are what he gives is.
question: What announcements has he made regarding reforms to the Resource Management Act 1991?
statement: Last week, the coalition Government announced we’re delivering on our commitment to improve resource management laws and give certainty to consent applications, with a bill being introduced to Parliament next month, the bill we’re calling the Resource Management Amendment Bill (No 1). A number of changes will be included, which include making it clear that while the National Policy Statement on Freshwater Management is being reviewed and replaced, resource consent applicants no longer need to demonstrate their proposed activities follow Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations. We’re amending stock exclusion regulations in relation to slope land, repealing intensive winter grazing regulations, and suspending the National Policy Statement for Indigenous Biodiversity (NPSIB) requirement for councils to identify new significant natural areas (SNAs) for three years.

explanation: Asked for the average weekly cost to families. He engages the question's shape ("it depends on their circumstances") and openly defers it to a written question rather than pivoting or attacking — but the figure asked for is never given, and a procedural deferral is not an answer the way a flat refusal would be. Partial engagement of a narrow factual question.
question: What will the average weekly cost be to families, due to the Government’s decision to no longer fund half-price public transport for people under the age of 25?
statement: It depends on their circumstances, but if the member would like to put the question in writing, we’ll get him a proper answer.

explanation: Asked why he isn't aware of a specific $70-a-fortnight figure from his own party's calculator. He never engages the figure, the calculator, or his awareness of it; he pivots to forthcoming tax relief and then to what Labour used to care about. Talking points plus a swipe at the questioner, on a narrowly specified question.
question: Why isn’t he aware that, using the National Party’s own tax cut calculator, someone in their early 20s that takes the bus each day and earns the average wage could be worse off by more than $70 a fortnight as a result of that change?
statement: Well, look, I thank the member for their concern about that constituent, but what I’d say is that help is on the way, because we are going to deliver low and middle income tax relief to hard-working Kiwis. These are the people that the Labour Party used to care about but have long forgotten.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of two specific cost impacts (under-13 fares, school lunches at $33/week/child). The reply is a single line of "help is on the way" messaging plus blame for the previous Government. Neither impact is acknowledged, and the yes/no on awareness is never reached.
question: Is he aware that parents will now need to pay more to get their under-13s to school as a result of that change, while his Government is also threatening to cut the school lunch programme that could see those same parents $33 a week, per child, worse off?
statement: I’d just say to that member, again, help is on the way to low and middle income New Zealanders doing it tough in a cost of living crisis created by that member’s previous Government.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: will the landlord tax changes result in lower rents. He stays on the topic of rents and names the mechanisms he says bear on them, which is real engagement, but he substitutes "downward pressure" for the yes/no that was asked and closes on a comparison with the last Government. Gestures at the question without reaching its core.
question: Will the $2.9 billion of tax cuts for landlords result in lower rents, given Trade Me reporting that rents have surged 8.3 percent since last year?
statement: This Government is committed to putting downward pressure on rents, and we are bringing the brightline test back from 10 to two years; we’re making sure we restore interest deductibility and we get the balance of laws right between tenants and landlords. But what I’d say to that member is we are not going to see a $170 per week increase in rents, as we saw under his administration.

explanation: The narrowed re-ask — will rents decrease — is about as squarely put as a question gets, and the answer again substitutes "downward pressure on rents" for decrease/not-decrease. On topic, but the one word asked for is deliberately withheld; a dodge is clearer when the questioner has already stripped the question to its core.
question: So will rents decrease as a result of this Government’s tax cuts for landlords?
statement: The series of actions we’re taking in the rental market will put downward pressure on rents.

explanation: Asked which of eight named cost-of-living outcomes best reflects his "laser-like" commitment. Not one of the eight is touched; he lists Government initiatives and an inflation figure instead. The question was loaded and sprawling, which softens it slightly, but he answers a different question — what are you doing — rather than the one asked.
question: What does he think best reflects his promised laser-like commitment to tackling the cost of living: higher public transport costs, his Government’s new drivers tax, higher costs for prescriptions, higher rents, higher fuel prices, higher rates, lower pay increases, or higher unemployment?
statement: Well, I can tell you there is a series of things that this Government is doing to focus on lowering the cost of living and lowering inflation. We’ve got the Reserve Bank focused on a single target of fighting inflation, we’ve actually made sure we’ve introduced our Family Boost policy to give families that are struggling with childcare costs some support and subsidy, and we’re making sure that we’re going to give tax relief in this Budget for low and middle income working New Zealanders. We’re serious about lowering inflation, and isn’t it good that inflation hit 4 percent—the lowest it’s been for three years—we’re on our way.

explanation: Asked what evidence she has that three strikes reduces crime. She names the evidence directly: a Ministry of Justice evidence brief and US studies on similar laws. Whether that evidence is sound or fairly characterised is a Veracity/Rigor matter; on the question asked, the response is direct and complete.
question: What evidence, if any, does she have that reintroducing three-strikes legislation will reduce crime in Aotearoa?
statement: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence brief suggesting that reintroducing the three-strikes legislation in New Zealand has the potential to reduce crime. US studies on similar laws have shown reductions in both minor and serious violent crimes, along with decreased arrest rates among offenders with previous strikes. The tougher sentences for offending that this regime will introduce for second- and third-strike offenders will ultimately keep serious repeat violent and sexual offenders off the street and prevent them from victimising more New Zealanders, including Māori.

explanation: Asked for her response to the 2018 English report's charge that three strikes is dogma rather than evidence. She does frame an explicit response ("my response to that report is..."), which is engagement, but its content answers a different question — what changes were made to the regime — and the dogma-versus-evidence charge is never met. Partial.
question: What is the response to the 2018 report by then Prime Minister Bill English which called out Aotearoa’s high rates of incarceration for being based on dogma, not evidence, and criticised policies such as three strikes for being a retributive rather than restorative approach to crime based on unsupported claims that prisons can solve the problem of crime?
statement: My response to that report is that we have made constructive changes to the regime that will be implemented to ensure that those serious repeat violent sexual offenders are off our streets and our communities are safe. The reason for that is because this Government is committed to restoring law and order to our communities.

explanation: Asked whether she accepts specific 2022 US findings. She never says accept or not, but she meets the substance by putting contrary US evidence against it, which is an implicit rejection with reasons. Half-answered: the question's core (do you accept these findings) is engaged obliquely rather than avoided.
question: Does she accept the findings from research from the United States in 2022, where this law was modelled from, that showed three strikes has no measurable deterrent effect, that it disproportionately locked up African Americans, and that it had no impact on lowering crime rates at all?
statement: The Ministry of Justice has previously produced an evidence brief which cited US studies showing similar three-strike laws have reduced serious violent crimes and reduced arrest rates for offenders who had received a first or second strike. I think what is really important here is that we have taken learnings from the previous regime and we will be introducing a new regime which goes about making sure that our communities are kept safe. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked for her response to the 99 percent of submitters opposing the bill. She gives one — bring it back through select committee once the bill is produced — which is a real, if minimal, answer to "what is your response". She sidesteps the substance of the objection, but the question asked for her response and she gave one.
question: Tēnā koe e te Pīka. What is your response to the unequivocal majority, the 99 percent of submitters at select committee who represented most of the law associations of this country, that this bill is not fit to be passed into the House, should be done away with, and something new put in place?
statement: I invite those people, when they actually see the bill once it’s produced, to use the select committee process to give us their new version of what they think about it.

explanation: Asked what challenges she faced building the Budget; the answer opens directly on a challenge (the state of the economy inherited) but the record cuts off mid-sentence. The fragment is on-point rather than evasive, so it cannot be scored low, but nothing complete was delivered. Score is provisional on a truncated response.
question: What challenges has she faced in putting together this year’s Budget?
statement: Well, aside from the state of the economy that was left to us—

explanation: Asked to name the biggest fiscal cliff. She names it in the first clause — time-limited Pharmac funding — and then quantifies it. A friendly question, but the scoring axis here is engagement only, and the question is answered squarely and completely.
question: What is the biggest fiscal cliff the Government has faced?
statement: The biggest fiscal cliff in Budget 2024 was time-limited funding for Pharmac. The previous Government gave Pharmac additional funding of $350 million for the 2023-24 fiscal year to purchase new medicines and widen access to some that were already funded, but this expires on 30 June and there was no funding set aside for future years. My colleague David Seymour announced on Monday that Budget 2024 will extend this additional funding and, critically, make it permanent. That will be welcome news to people who rely on these medicines, but we have had to find the $1.77 billion cost of this from within our operating allowance because the previous Government did not put one cent towards it.

explanation: Asked what changes the bill makes to help farmers. Opens with a slogan and a swipe at the last Government, but does turn to the question and begins naming an actual change ("removing the need for resource applicants to demonstrate—") before the excerpt cuts off. Engages the question, incompletely.
question: What changes is the Government making in this bill to help farmers?
statement: Well, I’m proud to say this coalition Government is ending the war on farmers. The last Government loaded on the regulations, putting unnecessary costs on farmers and growers. We’re removing the need for resource applicants to demonstrate—

explanation: Asked what else the bill does for farmers. Names a specific measure — suspending the NPSIB requirement for councils to identify new SNAs for three years — and explains it. Direct and complete.
question: What else does this bill do to help farmers?
statement: More good news: we’re suspending the NPSIB requirement for councils to identify new significant natural areas for three years, enabling farmers and growers to find the right solutions for their farm and catchment, rather than a dictatorial, centralised approach. The criteria for identifying new SNAs were an attempt to provide a standard approach to identifying the most important areas of biodiversity.
