We think of ourselves as the leading-edge agricultural and horticultural nation in the world, and it was a great shock to me to realise that often New Zealand farmers and horticulturalists find themselves without products that their competitors overseas are accessing, simply because the Ministry for Primary Industries and the Environmental Protection Authority can take years to approve products that would be helpful for them raising their productivity.

explanation: Asked what initiatives the Minister has announced to improve ECE regulation. He recounts sector frustration and says the Ministry has been consulting and "will soon be reporting a set of initiatives" — no announced initiative is ever named. It circles the topic without reaching the question; if the honest answer is "none yet", he never says so plainly.
question: What initiatives has the Minister announced to improve the quality of regulation in early childhood education (ECE)?
statement: I recall, prior to becoming a Minister, attending a meeting of over 500 ECE operators completely beside themselves with the level of red tape and regulation that often subjects them to absurdities, takes up their time, and prevents them from doing the real work of helping the youngest New Zealanders learn and grow into confident and competent citizens. As a result, the Ministry for Regulation has been out and about, talking to people in the sector, hearing about the regulatory roadblocks and red tape they face as they try to rear the next generation of confident and inquisitive New Zealanders. They will soon be reporting a set of initiatives to slash that red tape so people can get on to the very important job of running early childhood education centres that young people are happy to go to, who learn, and where their parents can be confident that they’re safe and well looked after.

explanation: Asked how the regulatory standards bill will improve the quality of new regulations. After a preamble about the Public Finance Act and Reserve Bank Act, he answers the mechanism directly: the bill will require governments to identify the problem, the costs versus benefits, who wins and loses, and whether property rights are impaired. The core "how" is squarely engaged.
question: How will the regulatory standards bill improve the quality of new regulations?
statement: Well, in days gone by in this Parliament, you would see spending and money printing completely out of control in a sort of politicised wild west of fiscal and monetary policy. Since then, the Public Finance Act and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act have led to some certainty and some consistency in the way that the Government spends and the Reserve Bank operates. We have no such statutory base for the way that the Government regulates people’s private property and its use and exchange. The regulatory standards bill will ensure that when Governments regulate, they identify what problem we’re trying to solve, what the costs of a solution are, if they are they less than the benefits, who wins and who loses, and if private property rights are impaired. That kind of standard will be a major improvement not just to laws made today but for New Zealand’s long-term future as a regulator.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. "Yes, I do" — a complete answer to a yes/no question. The long follow-on about maths results is padding, not evasion; the question itself was answered in the first three words.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I do, and especially our action to teach the basics brilliantly to our Kiwi kids. The maths results released on the weekend are absolutely appalling, when four out of five of our children at year 8 are below where they need to be, and three out of five are more than a year behind where they need to be. It is safe to say that the system has failed. We have to fix it, and now we have a plan to do exactly that—a world-leading curriculum based on the science of learning, top quality resources to support our teachers, regular assessments, and clearer reporting for parents. We have an outstanding Minister of Education, Erica Stanford, who has achieved more, I think, in six days than the last member did and the last Government did in six years, and it is more evidence for what Kiwis already know: that this is a Government that is for the parents and also for education.

explanation: Asked whether the new maths requirements will apply in charter schools, and if not, why not. He never says yes or no and never gives a reason. "Held ruthlessly accountable ... then left to get on with the job" hints at no but leaves both halves of a narrow, two-part question unanswered.
question: Will the new requirements around maths that he announced over the weekend also apply in charter schools; if not, why not?
statement: Again, we think charter schools are an important feature of innovation to bring into the education system. They will be held ruthlessly accountable for delivering improved academic achievement, attendance, a number of key metrics, and then left to get on with the job that they need to get on with.

explanation: Asked why the public should have confidence that boot camps won't repeat the abuse in the royal commission report. He gives direct grounds for that confidence: vetted and qualified staff versus unvetted, psychologists and social workers, family involvement, oversight and monitoring where there was none. The "why" is answered; only the sub-clause about the Minister's refusal to guarantee is left aside.
question: Why should the New Zealand public have confidence in his Government’s reintroduction of boot camps and that they won’t result in a repeat of the shocking abuse highlighted in last week’s royal commission report when his Minister for Children said last week that she cannot guarantee that abuse won’t take place?
statement: Well, again, what I’d say to you is that the royal commission of inquiry report into the boot camps at Aotea Great Barrier are incredibly different from what we are proposing here—completely different. What we’ve got is unvetted and unqualified staff, as that member would have read in that report. Here we have senior psychologists and two social workers working with 10 kids. We had very isolated conditions, appalling conditions. We have a three-month residential programme that involves the family, whānau, siblings, and community organisations from the get-go. On the other hand, it was focused on punishment and also abuse. This is focused on powerful interventions in these young people’s lives to turn them around. And there was no oversight or monitoring, as the member would understand from that reporting, and there is deep monitoring and protection in place under our military-style academies.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that no child in a boot camp will be abused. He answers with effort language — "doing everything we can", "going to try new things" — and never gives or refuses the guarantee. A plain "no, I won't guarantee that" would have scored high; talking past the yes/no is the dodge.
question: Will he do what his Minister for Children refused to do last week and guarantee that no children attending boot camps established by his Government will be subjected to abuse?
statement: We are doing everything we can to make powerful, targeted, and safe interventions in those young people’s lives, and we will not give up on them. We’re going to do everything we can. We’re going to try new things. We have a good pilot, with good oversight and good monitoring, but we are going to do things differently to get things done in this country.

explanation: Asked why he won't give the assurance if he is confident abuse won't happen. The answer opens with "Because" and then lists programme features rather than any reason for withholding the assurance. The question asked for a reason for a refusal and no reason is supplied.
question: If he is confident that abuse will not happen in boot camps, why won’t he give that assurance now?
statement: Because I am doing everything we can in this Government to make sure that we are going to make powerful, targeted interventions on these young people’s lives. We are making sure we’ve got qualified and vetted staff. We are making sure we’ve got monitoring and protection in place. We are making sure that we actually have family and whānau and community organisations in place. This is a trial. This is a pilot. We will learn from it. But I can tell you, we’re doing everything we can to make powerful interventions to change the trajectory of where these lives are going.

explanation: Asked again why he won't guarantee no child will be abused. He substitutes a different guarantee — "I am guaranteeing that we are doing everything we can" — which answers a question that was not asked. The "why not" is never touched.
question: If all of those things are going to be effective, why won’t he guarantee that no child will be abused in boot camps?
statement: Well, I am guaranteeing that we are doing everything we can to turn those lives around.

explanation: Asked for an assurance he will not intervene in future fast-track consent applications, with a specific prior case cited. He calls the questioner petty and pivots to generic fast-track advocacy; neither the assurance nor the Cockle Bay intervention is addressed at all.
question: Will he assure the public that he will not intervene in any future fast-track resource consent applications, as he did in the case of the redevelopment of a disused petrol station in Cockle Bay, which was being redeveloped into 54 apartments, where his objection was cited as one of the reasons it isn’t going ahead?
statement: Look, the member has gotten very petty in Opposition. I have to say, look, we are interested in solving problems. One of the big observations of the previous Government was that there were lots of words, lots of post-it notes, lots of strategies, and nothing getting done. We believe in fast-track, one-stop provisions. We think that’s the way that we get things done. We strengthen our regional communities. We strengthen our national economy. We’re going to get it done. Come and join us. Support and vote for fast-track legislation, support and vote for the oil and gas repeal, and get on board.

explanation: Asked for the Budget 2025 operating allowance. Answered with the figure — $2.4 billion, clarified as per year of additional net spending across the forecast period. Direct and complete.
question: What is the operating allowance for Budget 2025?
statement: No sooner has one Budget been delivered than the next is under way. The operating allowance for the next Budget, Budget 2025, is $2.4 billion. To be clear, that is $2.4 billion per year of additional net spending or revenue reduction, on average, across the forecast period. That is a very tight allowance indeed. In fact, it is the lowest operating allowance since Steven Joyce’s Budget in 2017. The Government is committed to controlling spending and getting the books back to surplus.

explanation: Asked how much has been pre-committed against the Budget 2025 allowance. Answered with the figure — $1.37 billion per annum for Health New Zealand pressures, plus pre-committed medicines funding. The number asked for is given.
question: How much has been pre-committed against the Budget 2025 allowance?
statement: The Government has pre-committed $1.37 billion per annum against the Budget 2025 allowance to meet forecast demographic, volume, and price pressures for front-line health services delivered by Health New Zealand. We have done this to give the health sector confidence to plan for the future so that New Zealanders can get the healthcare they need. The Government has also pre-committed funding for additional medicines, including up to 26 new cancer treatments.

explanation: Asked how much the allowance leaves for new decisions. Answered directly: less than a billion dollars remaining. Slightly less precise than the two prior answers and followed by caveats about allowances being a net concept, but the question is squarely answered.
question: How much does that leave in the allowance for new decisions?
statement: After pre-commitments and some non-discretionary forecast items, there is currently less than a billion dollars remaining in the operating allowance for Budget 2025. Clearly, managing within that remaining allowance will require tight controls on new spending. It is also important to remember that allowances are a net concept. They include savings initiatives as well as new spending, and revenue increases as well as tax relief. So any savings or new revenue initiatives will boost that billion-dollar figure. As I said in the Budget speech, savings and reprioritisation will be a feature of future Budgets, just as they were in Budget 2024. Finding better ways to use public money will be a business-as-usual activity for this Government.

explanation: Asked how confident she is in finding savings; she says "I am very confident" and stays on that question throughout. The partisan padding and detail don't bear on whether the question was engaged — it was, directly.
question: How confident is she in finding savings?
statement: I am very confident, and I say that because, as I said to the member earlier, we found an average saving of $5.9 billion per year across the forecast period in the Budget just gone. Despite some members predicting that the sky would fall in if the Government made any savings whatsoever, we found that $5.9 billion per year so that we could direct it to higher-value uses—things like 500 additional police, things like Gumboot Friday, things like new classrooms and maintaining our existing classrooms—and I am confident that across the public sector there are many more savings and re-prioritisation opportunities.

explanation: A yes/no standing-by question answered "Yes" in the first word. The subsequent pivot to maths achievement is off-topic padding, but the question itself was squarely answered before it.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially this Government’s action to turn around the miserable track record of achievement in maths for children from low-decile schools. Our Government believes in giving every child a shot, no matter what school they go to or wherever they grow up. The latest maths data shows that just 8 percent—8 percent—of children in our lowest-decile schools are at curriculum in maths in year 8, and we can and will do so much better than that. I’m proud that we have a Minister who has a plan to turn that track record of underachievement around and to deliver opportunity for every child across New Zealand, in every town. I’d say to that member, if she cares about equality of opportunity, get on board and back these changes.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts poverty/parental income is the major determinant of educational achievement. He never says whether he accepts it — he substitutes "what I accept is that there has been system failure" and answers a different question about system performance.
question: Does the Prime Minister accept that the major determinant of educational achievement in this country is in fact poverty or parental income?
statement: What I accept is that there has been system failure over many, many years in this country on education. What I accept is that four out of five of our kids not being where they need to be at year 8 and three out of five being more than a year behind is utterly unacceptable, and we make no apologies for focusing the education system around academic achievement. We need to teach our kids to read and we need to teach our kids to do maths.

explanation: Asked to reconcile his quoted statement with lowered child poverty targets allowing 23,000 more children in poverty. He stays on the topic of child poverty and offers a counter-figure (17,000 lifted), but never addresses the lowered targets or the quote — it circles the question without reaching its core.
question: How can the Prime Minister say to the children of this country, “I cannot change the … home that you were born into” when his Government’s decision to lower child poverty reduction targets will intentionally allow for up to 23,000 more children to live in poverty under his Government’s economic and social policies?
statement: Well, I’d just say to that member that we are committed to reducing child poverty with this Government’s actions. We are doing that by rebuilding the economy, restoring law and order, and delivering better health and education. I’d just also say the Treasury advised us, in the changes in the last Budget, that we will lift 17,000 children out of poverty. I think that’s a good move.

explanation: A narrow factual question — what section 7AA currently does — answered with what the Government wants the legislation to do. The current effect of the section is never stated; this is a different question answered in its place.
question: What does section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act currently do?
statement: What we’re doing with section 7AA, just so we’re—[Interruption] We want the legislation to make sure it protects the wellbeing and the interests of our children above and beyond anything else and is unambiguous doing so.

explanation: Two legs: does he know what 7AA does, and can he outline it. The first is answered directly and completely ("yes"); the second — the substantive one — is simply ignored, with no refusal stated. Half the question engaged.
question: Does the Prime Minister know what section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act actually currently does, and can he please outline that specifically for the House?
statement: In answer to the first leg of your question, yes.

explanation: Asked whether he sees a problem between the data-and-evidence commitment and the absence of evidence for removing 7AA. The response pivots entirely to talking points about protecting vulnerable children; the tension put to him is never acknowledged.
question: Does the Prime Minister see any problem at all with his coalition agreement promise to make decisions based on data and evidence, and his complete inability to produce any data and evidence about why he wants to remove the section of the Oranga Tamariki Act which does the bare minimum on upholding Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: What we are focused on is actually making sure the wellbeing and the best interests of the most vulnerable children in this country are protected. We want that to come first, above and beyond anything else—above and beyond their cultural needs or anything else. It’s important that children are protected and are safe. We’ll continue to do that.

explanation: A two-part question answered part by part: "yes" to the first, "no" to the second. Maximally terse and unhelpful, but nothing was dodged — both legs got a direct answer.
question: Meitaki maata, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by her statement, “Our Budget was very deliberate in the funding of core priorities because our priorities are the same priorities as New Zealanders”; if so, is she concerned that her choices are disconnected from everyday New Zealanders?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes; in answer to the second part of the question, no.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet approved funding to break the contract, and whether she thinks the payment is a priority. She declines to comment — a stated refusal, which is not a dodge — but the refusal is grounded on it being a commercial matter between KiwiRail and Hyundai, which does not cover what Cabinet itself decided. Partial: an explicit refusal that sidesteps the leg actually asked about, with the second leg unaddressed.
question: Has Cabinet approved funding for KiwiRail to break its contract with Hyundai Mipo for two new rail-enabled interisland ferries; and does she believe paying Hyundai hundreds of millions of dollars not to build ferries is a priority for New Zealanders?
statement: The negotiations between KiwiRail and Hyundai are a commercial matter between those two parties and not something that I view that is in the public interest to comment on in this House. I have previously made clear the Government’s view that we can have safe, reliable ferry services and that we will take the action needed to ensure that is the case.

explanation: Asked (a) is she aware of the 50 percent price rise and (b) can she guarantee costs under $2 billion. Neither is answered: awareness is not confirmed, and the guarantee is replaced with a relative claim (cheaper than iReX) plus a CentrePort anecdote. It engages the cost subject but substitutes a different, easier question for the one asked.
question: Is she aware that since KiwiRail contracted for the ferries, the price of new ships has risen by 50 percent in US dollars; and can she guarantee the new ferries and sunk costs from cancelling the ferries will be less than $2 billion?
statement: On the advice I have received to date, I can be very confident that the cost of delivering new ferries will be less than the projected cost of the failed and flawed project iReX, even when sunk costs are taken into account. And I had the experience yesterday of visiting CentrePort, where they showed me where hundreds of millions of dollars would have had to be poured in to allow for enormous ships with enormous berths and rail enablement, and I asked them, “How much would it cost to ensure that wharf could take a normal-sized ferry?” And they said, “Zero.”

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on fuel security; he names the announcement — a study including reopening Marsden Point. Direct hit, with a partisan tail that doesn't detract from the answer given.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding fuel security?
statement: Ensuring New Zealand is a resilient and self-sufficient economy is a priority for our Government in so far that productivity and a flourishing economy needs reliable access to fuel. I recently announced that a study of New Zealand’s fuel security, including investigating the reopening of the Marsden Point refinery, is getting under way, as per the coalition agreement. Since Marsden Point was permitted to be mothballed by the previous Government, we have seen resilience undermined. It is important that we explore all options. Now, this study, it may come to pass, does not find favour with those who do not support the business community—they sit on the other side of the House, not with me.

explanation: Asked why the study is needed and he gives reasons: continued reliance on internal combustion engines, other countries strengthening fuel security, its link to economic security. Wrapped in partisan rhetoric, but the "why" is actually answered.
question: Why is the fuel security study needed?
statement: The internal combustion engine is not going anywhere in a hurry. No doubt, we will see a slow growth in electrical vehicles, the growth of which will be determined by investment in the electricity system, and work is under way to ensure that our electricity system does not contain any deficiencies that might impede competitiveness. In recent years, countries around the world have been scrambling to strengthen fuel security. We’ve, sadly, headed off in the opposite direction. We’ve followed a path of flakiness and green ruination, and fuel security is critical to our economic security and the boost of our economy of jobs and exports—something that defines this side of the House; sadly, absent from a distant corner.

explanation: Asked what reports he had received on energy security. He names the report (the Gas Industry Co. quarterly report) and states its finding (gas production down 20 percent). The question is squarely answered; the subsequent blame-laying is padding that belongs to Focus/Civility, not here.
question: What reports has he received regarding energy security in New Zealand?
statement: I have received the report today otherwise known as the quarterly report of the Gas Industry Co., and this is the home of New Zealand’s gas governance advice and data—advice and data demonstrably superior to any loose, random international report that may be doing the rounds in other parts of the world. What it actually says—what it actually says—is that gas production is 20 percent down, and the result and the blame for that degradation of gas resilience can be laid at the feet of that Prime Minister and that Minister, who, in thinking that they were going to enjoy the political upside of the term “a nuclear moment”, cancelled the gas industry in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked why energy security is critical for the economy. He does reach reasons — loss of resilience, loss of investor confidence and certainty, competitiveness of the electricity sector — but arrives there via a digression about coal imports and closes on an attack line. Partially answered; the core is touched but not squarely developed.
question: Why is energy security critical for New Zealand’s economy?
statement: Not only is the ongoing availability of gas and, sadly, Indonesian coal—how perverse that those people who thought that they would improve energy resilience in New Zealand are now reduced to requiring ongoing imports of Indonesian coal. That never featured seven, eight years ago, or six years ago, in the analysis, but that is what is happening in this very day. We cannot afford to have a situation where we are losing our resilience. We’re losing confidence, and there is no certainty for investors. For those reasons, the study is taking place in terms of fuel resilience. Additional work will take place to ensure that the energy settings, the electrical industry settings, are such that it gives a greater level of competitiveness, and we will stand with industry and ensure that industry is not monstered by green termites nibbling away at our economic capital.

explanation: Asked what announcements she had made about maths education. She enumerates them: curriculum acceleration, professional development, twice-yearly assessments, small-group support, plus the ERO reporting change. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has she made about transforming maths education?
statement: This Government has announced four immediate interventions as part of our Make It Count maths action plan to turn around our poor results. We’re accelerating the shift to a new maths curriculum next year. To support teachers, we are delivering targeted professional development focused on structured maths for primary and intermediate teachers, alongside providing quality resources aligned to the curriculum. Thirdly, there will be twice-yearly assessments for maths in primary school, for years 3 to 8, starting from next year so that we can provide the support where needed. In line with this, we are going to provide targeted support in small groups, using structured maths, to give our kids who need extra help the best chance to succeed. Yesterday, I announced faster and overhauled Education Review Office reporting in numeracy and literacy assessment, and the Ministry of Education are going to intervening earlier and more often to provide support to schools who need to raise achievement, because, if we’re going to close the equity gap and raise achievement, we need to have a knowledge-rich curriculum year by year that’s explicitly taught and consistently measured against.

explanation: Asked what evidence supports the announcements. She cites the Curriculum Insights and Progress Study with figures and explains why the results differ from prior assessments. Directly on the question asked.
question: What evidence has she seen to support these announcements?
statement: Data from the Curriculum Insights and Progress Study show that just 22 percent of year 8 students in New Zealand are at the expected curriculum benchmark in year 8 for mathematics, and it showed that just 12 percent of Māori students were where they should be and that 63 percent of the overall year 8 cohort are more than a year behind. It’s the first time we’ve seen results like this. These results, while shocking, are not any worse than before. Previous assessments just neglected to ask the right questions. This is the first time that we have assessed our kids in comparison to the curriculum benchmark for their year. Until now, New Zealand has assessed students in broad multi-year bands, where a child could be years behind where they should be but they’re still considered to be at curriculum. Essentially, this means many parents were being told that their children were at curriculum or doing just fine when the reality is that they could have been years behind. Parents deserve to know exactly where their kids are at, what they will be learning, and what we can do to help them—and from next year, they will.

explanation: Asked what the announcements mean for teachers. She answers in teacher terms: $20m of PLD funding, workbooks, teacher guides, aligned resources. Direct, with a short mission-statement close that does not displace the answer.
question: What will her recent announcements mean for teachers?
statement: As part of this announcement, $20 million is being made available within the professional learning and development budget to build confidence and capability in our teaching workforce. We know from a range of studies that too many teachers don’t feel they have the confidence to teach maths to young people. Teachers deserve our support, and we are going to deliver. As part of this announcement, we will be rolling out student workbooks, detailed teacher guides, and other top-quality resources aligned to the new curriculum to support every teacher and child in every classroom in New Zealand. As Minister, it’s my responsibility to ensure the system is working for our teachers to improve these results as quickly as we can, and we’ll continue to work with the sector to make sure that we are achieving what we need to be.

explanation: Asked what feedback she had heard from school principals. She relays two school responses, including a named principal at Kerikeri Primary. The question is engaged directly; the closing pitch is surplus but does not replace the answer.
question: What feedback has she heard from school principals since the announcement?
statement: One school, Gore Main School, who have embedded structured literacy with outstanding results say, “This year, we started a structured maths approach, and we are seeing similar results. Already we are seeing improvements within our student achievement. We are happy to hear that structured maths is going to be brought into schools, and we know it is long overdue.” Also, I heard from Dr Sarah Brown from Kerikeri Primary School, who has brought in structured maths with teacher guides and student workbooks. She has closed the equity gap. Her Māori students are now achieving at the same rate and, in some cases, above the average students in her school for the first time. This announcement is just one step towards closing the equity gap across New Zealand, giving our children every opportunity to succeed and setting New Zealand up for future prosperity.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statement and, if so, why. She answers both limbs: yes, with a stated scope, and because the status quo is not an option. Complete on its own terms.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “stakeholder groups, Opposition parties, Governments, and Māori have all called for Oranga Tamariki to change. This is what change looks like”; if so, why?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes, in the context in which I said it, which was in relation to the proposed Oranga Tamariki organisational restructure. In answer to the second part of the question, because it’s not an option to keep the status quo. To do so would say we’re happy with how the organisation is running now and delivering for children—and we know it’s not.

explanation: Asked whether repealing section 7AA is the change Māori called for — a yes/no on a specific claim. The reply pivots entirely to a talking point about children's best interests and never engages the question. A clear dodge.
question: Is the repeal of section 7AA, which requires partnerships with Māori and reducing disparities for Māori, the change that Māori have called for?
statement: I have made it very clear since becoming Minister for Children that the best interests and safety of children are at the forefront of every decision that Oranga Tamariki makes.

explanation: Asked whether boot camps are the change abuse-in-care survivors called for. She neither answers nor refuses; she rules the question outside the scope of her statement. Rejecting the premise is more engagement than a talking-point pivot, but the substance is left untouched.
question: Is the reintroduction of military-style boot camps the change that survivors of abuse in care have called for?
statement: My statement is in relation to the proposed restructure of Oranga Tamariki.

explanation: Asked whether $120m of cuts to prevention services is the change providers called for, with a named provider quoted against her. She repeats the scope objection verbatim. The question was narrower and better evidenced than the last, and the same deflection covers less of it.
question: Is cutting $120 million in community prevention services, like Family Start, the change that community organisations have called for when Social Service Providers Aotearoa chief executive Belinda Himiona is saying that providers are very worried that child safety and that whānau wellbeing is going to be impacted by these reductions?
statement: I’ll say it again: my statement was in relation to the proposed restructure of Oranga Tamariki.

explanation: Asked whether Toni Jarvis was correct that she told him she was unhappy with decisions. She answers no — she never made that statement. A flat denial is a complete answer to a yes/no question.
question: Was survivor of abuse in care Toni Jarvis correct when he said about a conversation he had with the Minister that “She told me she was not happy in some of the decisions she was having to make.”?
statement: I don’t know what that is about, but I have never made that statement.

explanation: Asked, given the previous denial, whether she is therefore happy to make those decisions and why. She returns to the scope formula for a third time, which does not fit this question at all — it asks about her position, not about her original statement. Effectively unanswered.
question: Is the Minister, therefore, saying that she is happy to make the decision she is making about the reintroduction of boot camps, the repeal of section 7AA, the significant funding cuts to community service providers on the front line, and, if so, why?
statement: I’ll repeat again: my statement was in relation to the proposed restructure of Oranga Tamariki.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. He opens with a flat "Yes" — the question is a yes/no and it is answered outright. The maths-achievement material that follows is self-promotional padding, but padding after a direct answer is a Specificity/Focus matter, not a dodge.
question: Kia orana kotou katoatoa i roto i te ʻepetoma o te reo Kūki ʻĀirani. Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our actions to turn maths achievement around for young Māori. The maths achievement data released on the weekend was deeply concerning, especially for the just 12 percent of young Māori who are not at curriculum in maths at year 8, according to the data from last year. Shockingly, 76 percent were more than a year behind. All Kiwis, Māori or non-Māori, deserve a shot at a better life, and that starts with an outstanding education. That’s why our Government is taking action to deliver a world-leading curriculum and to turn those results around for Māori and non-Māori children.

explanation: Asked whether he has confidence in the Minister for Children. Answer: "Yes." One word, complete, no evasion.
question: Does he have confidence in the Minister for Children?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how he can have confidence given the Minister cannot guarantee children will not be abused in boot camps. He engages the premise head-on — concedes no Government can guarantee it, then states the basis for his confidence (protections, safeguards, wrap-around services). The basis is thin and unevidenced, but thinness is Specificity; the question itself was met.
question: How can he have confidence in the Minister for Children given that she cannot guarantee that tamariki and rangatahi will not be abused in her boot camps?
statement: Well, no Government can guarantee that, but they can do everything they possibly can to make sure there is protection and safeguards in place for our children. These are our most vulnerable children. We want powerful, targeted interventions, and we’re putting huge amounts of service around them to make sure that they are safe. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he stands by repealing section 7AA in light of Tracey Martin's submission. He never says yes or no and never touches the submission. "We do not want any ambiguity" hints at a rationale for repeal, which is why this is not a zero, but the yes/no core is left unstated and the cited evidence is ignored.
question: Does he stand by his decision to repeal section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act given that the former children’s Minister Tracey Martin said in her oral submission yesterday, “We do not have a child protection service in this country. We have a child crisis service. As a nation, we wait until there is damage done to a child, either emotionally, physically, or spiritually, before we [can] take any action. 7AA is the key to making this change to become a country that supports child protection.”?
statement: We do not want any ambiguity. We want the wellbeing and the best interests of the most vulnerable children in our country to be at the heart of what is happening here.

explanation: Asked why he would not strengthen section 4A instead of repealing 7AA — a pointed, specific alternative put to him. The reply restates a general commitment to children's safety and wellbeing and never addresses section 4A, the comparison, or the word "why". A narrow question wholly avoided.
question: If his primary concern is prioritising “health and wellbeing of the individual child”, why doesn’t he strengthen section 4A of the Oranga Tamariki Act, which makes it clear that “well-being and best interests of the child or young person are the first and paramount consideration”, instead of repealing section 7AA?
statement: We want the immediate safety, stability, and wellbeing of a child to be at the heart of what the Government does, caring for our most vulnerable children—period.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen about community beat patrols. He reports the feedback directly — overwhelmingly positive, from communities and from officers he met in the Auckland CBD. A patsy question, but it is squarely answered.
question: What feedback has he seen about Police’s community beat patrols?
statement: The feedback has been overwhelmingly positive. Communities across the country have responded positively to the Government’s approach of getting police back to basics and focused on getting out in their communities. It was great for the Prime Minister and me to get out with one of the beat teams in the Auckland CBD recently. The team told me how much they’re enjoying the public contact. Often, they attend jobs that are very negative, and they highlighted how much they’re enjoying the positive interaction they’re having with the public whilst on the beat. They’re enjoying getting to know their beat and identifying and dealing with the problems and issues that exist. They feel like they have real ownership of it and are proud of the difference they’re making. I am proud of them also.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen from shopkeepers. He gives a specific instance: a Wellington retailer, the police response, and a store manager's complimentary feedback on the beat initiative. One anecdote where a body of feedback was asked for, but it does answer the question asked.
question: What feedback has he seen from shopkeepers?
statement: Well, following a central Wellington retailer reporting a woman putting clothing in her bag, early last month, the beat team responded swiftly. They apprehended the woman, who turned out to be a prolific shoplifter with over $1,000 worth of products on her person from several of the other shops in the area. A store manager contacted police and provided highly complimentary feedback on the beat initiative, the visibility of police staff, and the timely response she received.

explanation: Asked whether members of the public have had anything to say. "Yes" plus what they said, including a quote. Direct and complete.
question: Have members of the public had anything to say?
statement: Yes, my inbox has been inundated with correspondence from the public, who are relieved and happy to see police out and about and providing reassurance. One quote that stood out to me was: “I know it’s only day one, but great to see the first of the new community beat officers out on the streets. A big thumbs up. I feel that will help make me and others safer on our streets.”

explanation: Asked whether other communities have benefited from visible policing. He says yes and cites Rangitīkei retailers' feedback. He answers with reported feedback rather than evidence of benefit, which is a Veracity/Rigor gap, not evasion — the yes/no was given and supported.
question: Have any other communities benefited from police being highly visible?
statement: Yes, the hard-working member for Rangitīkei has passed on to me that as she meets with retailers in her communities, the feedback has been extraordinary. Everyone is delighted to see police back on the beat and keeping our community safe.

explanation: A two-part question: does she stand by the statement, and when will the process be completed. She explicitly answers both — "yes" to the first, and the second action plan expected in the last quarter of 2024 for the second. A date was asked for and a date was given; the Te Aorerekura and violent-crime-target material that follows is padding, not a pivot.
question: Does she stand by her statement regarding the availability of services that support victims of family violence, “sometimes it’s not about just throwing extra money at stuff. It’s about making sure that the money is going to the right places. And we’re working through where those gaps are and where the money we have currently got isn’t being spent well and focusing it to where it is being spent … So that is a process … that takes time”; if so, when will that process be completed?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, the Government is currently working on the second action plan to implement Te Aorerekura, the 25-year strategy to address family and sexual violence in this country. This action plan is expected to be published in the last quarter of 2024, and this will help drive collective efforts and investment decisions across Government in the family violence and sexual violence space. Family violence and sexual violence are an important component of the Government target to reduce violent crime by having 20 percent fewer people be the victims of assaults, robberies, and sexual assaults by 2029. The Government targets will also help focus attention and resources on achieving better results that New Zealanders expect and deserve.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Mark Mitchell's claim that family violence calls are being triaged, and if not why not. She never says agree or disagree; she redirects to the scope of her own role and says individual Ministers own their statements. This is close to a portfolio-based refusal, which would score higher if stated plainly as one, but she never actually says she will not comment — the agree/disagree core is simply left unaddressed.
question: Does she agree with Mark Mitchell regarding the 3,000 fewer family violence investigations since December 2023, “Those calls are being triaged and the number has come down”; if not, why not?
statement: I just want to make it very clear that my role is to be responsible for leading the whole-of-Government approach, where we work together to identify shared priorities and make trade-offs around funding. Once decisions are taken, individual Ministers and agencies remain responsible for their statements and for what they’re doing.

explanation: Asked why victimisations by known offenders fell 24 percent since December. She gives no reason, so the substance is not delivered — but the form is candid rather than evasive: no pivot, no talking point, no attack on the questioner, just a plain statement that she will answer it in writing. A frank deferral sits between a dodge and an answer, so it lands mid-scale rather than near zero.
question: Why, then, has there been a reduction in victimisations where the offender is known to the victim, by 24 percent since December last year?
statement: That specific issue—if you would like to ask that in writing, I shall get you an answer.

explanation: Asked which of two causes explains the drop in family violence investigations (triage change vs. police not attending with no service to fill the gap). The answer offers a generality about police always having a role, then pivots to the previous Government having started the trial. Neither alternative is engaged and the causal question is never reached.
question: If the reduction in family violence investigations is due to a new triaging process—or is it because police are not attending family violence as they were previously and there is no additional family violence support services in place to take up the gap left?
statement: I’d just like to say, police will always play a role when it comes to responding to violence, including family violence or where there has been a crime where someone is in immediate danger. But I would also like to remind them that it’s important to note that the six-month proof of concept trial for this was trialled by the previous Government before we even began this. So this is something that the previous Government was on board with and I would expect they still will be.

explanation: Asked what happens to a 111 caller below the attendance threshold with no resourced agency. The response declines outright and refers the question to another Minister — plainly stated and not a talking-point pivot, so not a full evasion, but the substance of the question goes entirely unanswered rather than being answered in the negative.
question: If a family violence call to 111 does not meet the new police threshold to attend and there is no support agency resourced in that area to attend, what happens?
statement: I would suggest that you direct those questions to the Minister of Police.

explanation: The question bundles 'who is stepping into the space police have left' with an assertion that this is her responsibility. She squarely rebuts the responsibility half (her role is facilitation; delivery sits with individual Ministers) but never addresses who is covering the gap. Half the question engaged directly, half untouched.
question: As the Minister responsible for the prevention of family violence, who is currently undertaking a review of what adequate services are in place, to be able to respond to who is stepping into the space that police have left—I believe that falls within her responsibility as the Minister responsible for preventing family violence.
statement: My role is just to facilitate all the Government agencies. What happens after that is the responsibility of the individual Ministers.

explanation: A loaded yes/no question; 'I just reject the premise of that question' is in substance a direct denial. It is curt and gives no elaboration, but elaboration is Specificity — the question was engaged and answered in the negative rather than dodged.
question: Is it her plan to achieve the Prime Minister’s target of 20,000 fewer victims of crime simply by making it harder for victims to report family violence and even harder for them to get the help they need?
statement: I just reject the premise of that question. [Interruption]

explanation: 'Does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions?' is answered 'Yes' in the first word, complete for the question asked. The energy-policy material that follows is unsolicited but does not detract from a direct answer.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially the steps that we are taking to restore confidence in New Zealand’s energy industry. New Zealand needs a rational energy policy, but, instead, previous Governments spent years undermining private sector investment, creating the conditions for future shortages and pricing spikes. Now Kiwis are experiencing the consequences. This morning, Simeon Brown called in the gentailers to make it clear that they must be competitive in the energy market. We’re taking action to restore confidence in the energy sector and to enable investment. That means ending the ban on oil and gas; it means cancelling Lake Onslow; it means bringing in fast track to enable more investment, including renewables; and, of course, it’s all part of our plan to rebuild the economy and to make sure we have energy security.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister's remark reflects the standard he expects. The reply engages the specific incident and, by welcoming the withdrawal and apology, implies disapproval — but it never states whether the conduct met his expected standard. Partial engagement that stops short of the core.
question: Does his Minister for Trade’s statement “You’re not in Mexico now. We don’t do things like that here.” and subsequent dismissal of concern, calling it “friendly banter”, reflect the standard of behaviour he expects from his Ministers?
statement: It was good to see the Minister withdraw and apologise for that statement.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware 'friendly banter' is a standard excuse for harassment and whether that is the culture he wants. The entire response is a counter-attack on the questioner's own record and a Labour MP's video. Neither limb is touched.
question: Is he aware that the number one excuse invoked by the perpetrators of harassment in the workplace, be it racism, sexism, or otherwise, is to excuse that behaviour as friendly banter, and, if so, is that the type of workplace culture he is trying to create?
statement: Well, I’d just say it’s a bit rich coming from that member, who this morning, just a few hours ago, was on Radio New Zealand exhorting the fact that everybody needs to watch their rhetoric—a message that I have played back over a number of months—and yet he has a former Minister and a senior MP condoning putting up a video saying that I’m killing children. I don’t think that’s appropriate.

explanation: The supplementary narrows the question explicitly to a Minister in his Government, not other MPs. The answer repeats the same generic line about all political leaders watching their rhetoric, which is the framing the question was raised to exclude — the narrowed question is answered with the answer to a different one.
question: The Prime Minister doesn’t have any responsibility for other members of Parliament. He does have responsibility for Ministers in his Government, and that was what my question was about. It was about a comment made by a Minister in his Government.
statement: As I’ve been saying, I am asking all political leaders to watch their rhetoric.

explanation: A direct yes/no question answered 'No.' One word, but it is the complete answer to what was asked; brevity is not a dodge.
question: In that case, is his Minister of Foreign Affairs providing a running commentary on the gender of international athletes consistent with the standard of behaviour that he expects of his Ministers?
statement: No.

explanation: Never says yes or no to whether the decision meets his expected standard, but does engage the substance by defending the decision on its merits (overseas recipient, clarity in English), which functions as an implicit endorsement. Partial: the core question is circled and answered only by implication.
question: Does his Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage’s decision to remove te reo Māori from formal letters inviting an Australian Minister, who is a champion of indigenous languages, to New Zealand for Matariki celebrations reflect the standard of behaviour that he expects from his Ministers?
statement: Well, I would just say to that member we value te reo in this Government. What I’d also say to that member is the correspondence was being directed to an Australian Minister overseas, and what I’d say to you is, in my dealings with Australians, it always pays to be incredibly simple and clear and use English.

explanation: 'I fully support our Minister... she's doing a fantastic job' is a thin implicit answer to whether the conduct meets his standard, but the specific conduct asked about (refusing to answer questions, the party badge) is never addressed, and the reply then turns to attacking the line of questioning as petty.
question: Thank you. Does his Minister for Children’s refusal to answer questions in the House last week in preference to wearing an ACT Party badge reflect the standard of behaviour he expects of his Ministers?
statement: Again, I fully support our Minister for Children and Oranga Tamariki—she’s doing a fantastic job. What I’d say to the member is what a petty line of questions that we’re seeing today. This is a country where our economy is in real trouble, this is a country where we cannot deliver health and education services as well as we need to—

explanation: Asked whether the Minister's conduct reflected the standard he expects of Ministers. He opens with a flat "No" — a direct answer to the yes/no put to him — then adds that the Speaker has dealt with it. The core was engaged; the follow-on is padding, not evasion.
question: Did his Minister for Children’s refusal to answer questions in the House last week, in preference to wearing an ACT Party badge, reflect the standard of behaviour that he expects of his Ministers?
statement: No, the Speaker has addressed that question, I think, very well. There were challenges last week, he has reset the tone of this House, and we deal with that going forward.

explanation: Asked why his Ministers are behaving in a list of specified ways. He answers a different question entirely — what he observes about his Cabinet's work rate and portfolio achievements — and never touches any of the five conduct items raised. Pure talking-point pivot.
question: If that is indeed the priorities of this Government, why are his Ministers refusing to answer questions in the House, and prioritising wearing party badges instead; making racial taunts to members on the opposite side of the House; refusing to use te reo Māori in their correspondence promoting things like Matariki; providing a commentary on the gender of international athletes; and, of course, attacking the courts—which is something we haven’t got to yet?
statement: What I observe is I see a hard-working Cabinet and a set of Ministers that are actually doing the business for New Zealand. I look at our economic Ministers who are actually reducing inflation, lowering the cost of living, and making sure we’ve got a growth plan, going forward. I look at our law and order Ministers and I see them focused on lowering crime. I look at our education Minister, who did more in six hours and six days than that member did as education Minister for six years. I look at what our health Minister is doing to make sure that we improve our health outcomes for Māori, non-Māori, and all New Zealanders. That’s what I see.

explanation: Asked what approach the Government is taking to spending and reprioritisation in Budget 2025. She sets out three enumerated elements of the fiscal approach. Squarely and completely responsive.
question: What approach is the Government taking to managing spending and reprioritisation in Budget 2025?
statement: The Government’s fiscal approach to Budget 2025 has three elements: first, there will be a very high bar for new initiatives in the Budget, and these will be limited to the most important Government priorities; second, significant savings will need to be found beyond those already identified in this year’s Budget; and, third, with a small number of exceptions, Government departments should expect to receive no additional funding in the Budget. They must manage cost pressures within their baseline, and if they want to do new things, they will need to reprioritise from existing activities. This Government is serious about responsible management of public finances.

explanation: Asked how she will ensure departments deliver within baselines. She names the mechanism — performance plans — and explains what they require departments to do. Directly answers the "how".
question: How will she ensure departments are delivering within their baselines?
statement: The Government has introduced a new tool called “performance plans”, which departments must now prepare. Departments must set out how they are planning to deliver within set baselines over the medium term. That will almost certainly involve trade-offs. Performance plans must be clear about those trade-offs so Ministers can make the necessary decisions. Performance plans will also set out any risks to financial sustainability, department performance, or delivery, and explain how those risks will be managed. Performance plans are an important part of our Government’s approach to Budget 2025 and to future Budgets, as well.

explanation: Asked what information performance plans will contain. She lists the contents: purpose and resources, impact, and cost-pressure drivers. Direct and on point.
question: What sort of information will performance plans contain?
statement: Among other things, a performance plan must provide information about a department’s purpose and resources, its impact—for example, how the department is currently delivering value—and the drivers of its cost pressures and how these will be managed. This will help change people’s focus to medium-term fiscal sustainability and away from the idea of an annual Budget lolly scramble.

explanation: Asked where the requirements for performance plans are set out. She names the source precisely — a Cabinet Office circular on the DPMC website — before drifting into general spending rhetoric. The narrow factual question was answered first.
question: Where are the requirements for performance plans set out?
statement: Last week, the Cabinet Office released a circular setting out in detail the requirements for developing and maintaining performance plans. This can be found on the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet website. Over the past six years, Government spending has been taken from $80 billion a year to $140 billion a year, and, in response, this Government is embedding a culture of responsible spending, restoring fiscal discipline, rightsizing the Government’s footprint, and improving the efficiency and productivity of spending. Performance plans will help achieve that.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. He says "Yes" and then elaborates. The unqualified affirmative fully answers what was asked; the elaboration is added material, not a substitute.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially this Government’s action to enable more energy investment and to fight climate change. We need more gas and more renewable energy if we want to fight climate change and grow our economy, and now our Government is taking action to achieve exactly that. We are ending the broken ban on offshore gas exploration, we are bringing in fast track to enable more investment in renewables, and we won’t beat climate change by importing more coal from offshore while making it so hard to build a new wind farm or a solar farm. So I’d say to that member, if she’s sick of the bumper stickers and slogans and actually wants to fight climate change, get on board.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the statement, and if so, define article 1. He explicitly answers only "the first part" with "yes" and leaves the substantive definition untouched, without declining it either. Half the question — the half with any content — goes unengaged.
question: Does he stand by his statement “we know that … the promise and the obligations of the Treaty were not upheld by the Crown.”, and, if so, can he outline what those promises and obligations are by defining article 1 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: Again, in answer to the first part of the question, yes.

explanation: Asked how he would define article 2. He declines outright — he won't define it here. That is an explicit refusal rather than a wander into talking points, which the rubric treats as forthright, but the "I'm well aware of the articles" framing sidesteps rather than plainly states a refusal, so it falls short of a clean "no, I won't".
question: How would the Prime Minister define article 2 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: I’m well aware of the articles; I don’t think I need to define them for you here in this House.

explanation: Asked how he would define article 3. He gives a definition — "Equal citizenship for all." Short and contestable on the merits, but it is an answer to exactly what was asked; accuracy is Veracity's problem, not this one.
question: How would the Prime Minister define article 3 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: Equal citizenship for all.

explanation: Asked what He Whakaputanga is and does — a narrow, factual question. He never approaches it, pivoting to Māori maths achievement and what the Opposition should be talking about instead. A specific question comprehensively dodged.
question: Can the Prime Minister tell the House what He Whakaputanga is and does?
statement: Again, the member may want to get into this conversation—I’d just say to her that on this side, in our Government, what we’re focused on is improving outcomes for Māori. I think it’s incredibly sad that only 12 percent of our Māori students are actually at where they need to be at maths at year 8, and that’s the thing that we should be talking about in this House and that I haven’t heard from the Opposition.

explanation: Asked whether New Zealanders should be concerned about the PM's grasp of the founding documents while legislating at pace. He substitutes his own version of what viewers will see — cost of living, law and order, health and education — and never addresses the concern raised. The question was sprawling and rhetorical in tone, which is the only reason this is not lower.
question: Should New Zealanders watching be concerned that their Prime Minister is demonstrating such a clear lack of understanding about this nation’s founding documents while progressing legislation—i.e., this Government’s actions—at pace to undermine that very constitution?
statement: What New Zealanders watching will actually see is a Government that is focused on the things that they care about. They want us to fix the cost of living, they want us to restore law and order, and they want us to deliver better health and education, and if they’re watching, that’s what they’ll be seeing through this House.

explanation: Two-part question (stand by statement; are you concerned). Answers both explicitly: "yes" to the first, "no" to the second. Terse and dismissive, but that is Civility, not Forthrightness — the question is squarely engaged and completely answered.
question: Kia orana katoatoa, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by her statement, “Our Budget was very deliberate in the funding of core priorities because our priorities are the same priorities as New Zealanders”; if so, is she concerned that her priorities are disconnected from everyday New Zealanders?
statement: This is exactly the same primary question as the member asked yesterday, so you won’t be surprised that the answer is also exactly the same. In answer to the first part of the question, yes; in answer to the second part of the question, no.

explanation: The core question is "is it a priority to support Kiwis into work" and it opens with a direct "Yes, it is a priority". The subsequent blame of the previous government is talking points, but they come after the question has been answered, and the answer also engages the sanctions premise by defending incentives. Slight deduction because the embedded challenge (that sanctions are her only solution) is only glanced at.
question: Is it a priority to support Kiwis into work when unemployment is up to 4.6 percent and her only solution is to sanction beneficiaries?
statement: Yes, it is a priority to support New Zealanders into work, and today’s unemployment statistic is yet another reminder of how letting inflation get a grip on the economy was so damaging. That is the legacy that we have inherited, and this Government is not only rebuilding our economy; we are also taking sensible, prudent steps to ensure that New Zealanders in receipt of a benefit are properly incentivised to find work.

explanation: Asked how 21,000 additional beneficiaries can find jobs given flat employment and a 32% slump in job ads. The answer states a desire for businesses to create more jobs — a bare gesture at the "how" — then pivots entirely to inherited inflation and the previous government's spending. The specific conditions in the question are never addressed.
question: How can the 21,000 additional people on the benefit find jobs when the employment rate is unchanged and job ads have slumped by 32 percent, leaving Kiwis no other choice than to look overseas?
statement: On this side of the House, we want to rebuild this economy so that we can see businesses creating more jobs so New Zealanders have better options. The sad fact of the matter is this: we inherited a grossly damaged economy which had sustained out-of-control inflation for three years, causing interest rates to rise very, very high. That previous Government perpetuated that with its own wasteful spending, and now we are cleaning up the mess.

explanation: Asked whether supporting front-line social workers who lost jobs is her priority. She declines to answer, redirects to "the relevant Minister", and then supplies a generic statement about beneficiary supports that is not about social workers at all. Redirection to another Minister is a partial engagement, not a refusal she owns ("no, that is not my priority" would have scored high), so it reads as a dodge.
question: Is it her priority to support front-line social workers who have lost their jobs because of funding cuts to services and programmes like Tākai that have had to shut after 20 years of serving the community?
statement: Well, if the member has a specific question, specific to contracts provided by a particular agency, I suggest she put those questions to the relevant Minister, and I know that if the Minister for social development were to be answering this question, she would say that she expects her agency to provide sufficient supports to all New Zealanders in receipt of a benefit to ensure they have the maximum opportunity to find work and get work.

explanation: Two parts: what do you say to Ana, and can you assure her of a job. The first part is answered directly with a message to Ana. The second — the assurance, which is the harder half — is never given; it turns into a warning about "politicians who claim they're on your side". Half the question engaged, the pointed half avoided.
question: What does she say to nursing students like Ana, who have asked, “What is the point of me completing this degree when I’m so uncertain whether I will get a job?”, and can she assure Ana that she will have a job in the public healthcare system when she graduates this year?
statement: My message to Ana is this: thank you for taking on the incredibly important job of nursing New Zealanders. Taking the chance to learn those skills and learn that capability is a great one because your skills will be needed in the future for New Zealand, and my encouragement to you is not only work hard and make sure you complete that qualification but also be wary of those politicians who like to claim they’re on your side and then ruin the economy so that, actually, there are fewer opportunities in it.

explanation: Asked what evidence supports the announcement; the answer names the Curriculum Insights and Progress Study finding and cites the science of learning and cognitive research on explicit teaching. That is evidence, offered in response to a request for evidence. Small deduction for the closing政 policy advocacy, which is padding rather than evasion.
question: What evidence has she seen to support her recent announcement on Make it Count, an action plan to transform maths education in New Zealand?
statement: As we heard in the House yesterday, the Curriculum Insights and Progress Study showed that only 22 percent of learners at year 8 were at curriculum for mathematics. We took immediate action to accelerate our Make it Count action plan to introduce structured mathematics. A structured maths approach is underpinned by the science of learning and decades of cognitive research which show that explicit teaching, when supported by a knowledge-rich, year-by-year curriculum that develops mastery, supported by high-quality instructional resources, lifts student achievement. This action plan is just another step towards closing the equity gap, giving our children every opportunity to succeed in turning round these dismal results.

explanation: Asked for further evidence and supplies two more sources: NCETM research on coherent learning progression and a 2023 ERO survey of new primary teachers. Interleaved with policy announcements ($20m PLD, ITE entry standards) that were not asked for, but the evidence requested is actually delivered.
question: What other evidence has she seen to support this announcement?
statement: Research from the National Centre for Excellence in the Teaching of Mathematics in the UK highlights the importance of enabling a coherent learning progression though the curriculum. That is why our Government is rolling out a knowledge-rich, year-by-year curriculum grounded in the science of learning, and bringing it forward by a year. The Education Review Office surveyed new primary teachers in 2023, finding that nearly a quarter felt unprepared in their maths content knowledge when they first started in their role. That’s why, as part of this action plan, we’re prioritising maths when it comes to professional learning and development, with $20 million of funding being made available, alongside raising the level of maths for entry into initial teacher education to level 2 NCEA mathematics and working with the Teaching Council to boost the amount of mathematics training happening at initial teacher education. Teachers deserve our support and we’re going to deliver it.

explanation: Asked what feedback she received from principals; she quotes two principals verbatim and characterises the feedback as positive. This is a soft patsy question, but forthrightness measures engagement, not question quality — the answer lands exactly on what was asked.
question: What feedback has she received from principals on her announcement?
statement: I have received really positive feedback. One principal wrote to me saying, “Thank you, I am excited at the idea of a structured maths programme. After 13 years of principalship and several years with primary teachers, this is fabulous news. Thank you. I am excited as a principal and look forward to supporting and embedding the structured maths programme at our school.”, and another wrote: “Excellent news, Erica, and well done. We have been aware of this decline for years, so it’s great we’re putting in place clear expectations for achievement and resources to support, as well as addressing standards for teacher entry.” I am hugely grateful to all of those who have shared their thoughts.

explanation: The standard "does he stand by all statements and actions" opener is answered "Yes" in the first word — complete for a question of that form. The extended attack on Te Pāti Māori that follows is a Focus and Civility problem, not a dodge; the question was already answered before it began.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to lift maths achievement among young people—Māori and non-Māori. It’s absolutely appalling that just 12 percent of Māori heading off to high school are at curriculum for mathematics, and if we’re serious about achievement and opportunity, then we actually have to turn that around. So we have a plan and that means more resources for every child—Māori and non-Māori—in every classroom in New Zealand, and since we’ve released that plan, I have to say to that member we haven’t heard anything from Te Pāti Māori on student achievement—no, nothing to say about Māori achievement, nothing to say about our plan, and nothing to say about turning the lives around of our young people.

explanation: Asked whether he believes his Government is treating Māori with respect. He says Key is entitled to his views and that he agrees with him — i.e. he endorses the principle that Māori should be treated with respect, which is not what was asked. Whether his own Government is doing so is never stated. The form of the reply looks responsive, which is what makes it a hedge around the core rather than a flat non-answer.
question: In light of comments made by John Key at the National Party conference that “Māori are the indigenous population of New Zealand and Treaty partners, so you have to treat them with respect.”, does he believe that his Government is treating Māori with respect?
statement: John Key is a private citizen and a former Prime Minister and he’s entitled to his own views, but in this case I agree with him.

explanation: A narrow question about what actions he will take to uphold NZ's obligations following the ICJ ruling. The answer restates a longstanding position (the occupations are illegal) and says NZ supports the ruling. No action is named. A specific "what will you do" question answered only with a statement of view is a near-total avoidance of the core.
question: What actions will he take to uphold New Zealand’s legal obligations as ruled by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) to hold Israel accountable for their illegal occupation of Palestinian lands and their war crimes against Palestinian people?
statement: Well, as that member will well know, we have said for many years that those occupations are illegal. The ICJ has actually confirmed New Zealand’s longstanding position, so we support that.

explanation: Asked whether it is appropriate for te reo Māori to be used in a Matariki invitation. Answers "Yes" immediately and substantiates it by producing the invitation and its te reo title. The jab at the questioner and Hipkins comes after the question is fully answered and does not displace it.
question: Does the Minister think it’s appropriate that te reo Māori be used in an invitation for Matariki, a distinct holiday to celebrate the Māori New Year; if not, why not?
statement: Yes, which is why the official invitation to Matariki contained te reo Māori—as I have here—entitled “Mānawa maiea te Mātahi o te Tau” [“Arise the New Year”], and he would know this if he’d checked with his leader, the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins, who received one of the invitations and declined to come.

explanation: Asked what the problem was with using "tēnā koe" in the invitation. He gives an actual reason — he was encouraged to sign off "Nāku noa, nā" and judged "Yours sincerely" would be better understood by an Australian. He engages the question and supplies his rationale, but shifts the object from the greeting asked about to the sign-off, so the core is reached obliquely rather than squarely.
question: The Minister knows what I’m referring to is his letter to his counterpart yesterday, and I want to ask the question: what is the big problem with saying “tēnā koe”, which means “hello”, in his official invitation?
statement: Well, I was writing to a Minister from Australia and I was encouraged to sign it off with “Nāku noa, nā” [“Humbly yours, from”], and I thought “Yours sincerely” would be more easily understood by the Australian.

explanation: Two-part question: awareness of Burke's statement, and, if so, why he said what he said. He answers the first part flatly — "No, I wasn't aware of that quote" — which makes the conditional second part moot. He then turns on the questioner, but only after answering; the jab is a Civility matter and does not replace an answer that was already given.
question: Is the Minister aware of a recent statement from the Hon Tony Burke, his Australian counterpart and the person the invitation was for, stating that support for First Nations’ culture, stories, and languages is crucial, and, if so, why did he jump to the conclusion yesterday, saying, “I didn’t think he needed a lot of … reo in his invitation, because he’s an Australian.”?
statement: No, I wasn’t aware of that quote, and I must say I’m amazed that that member thinks that this is a matter that deserves an urgent debate in the House and that my writing to an Australian Minister is a matter of such interest.

explanation: "Will the Minister advise the King...; if not, why not?" — "No, I wouldn't be making any such instructions to the King of New Zealand." A blunt, unambiguous no to the question actually asked, which is forthright by design. Marked slightly below the top only because the trailing "why not" is left unaddressed.
question: Will the Minister now do the consistent thing and advise the King of England and the King of New Zealand, His Majesty King Charles, to remove te reo Māori greetings from his Matariki message; if not, why not?
statement: No, I wouldn’t be making any such instructions to the King of New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he will advise the Sport Minister to act, and if not why not. "I'm sure that Minister can handle his arrangements perfectly well" never says yes or no and never gives a reason; it gestures at a rationale (another Minister's business) without stating a position. It brushes past the question rather than attacking it, so not a zero, but the core is avoided.
question: Will the Minister be advising the Minister for Sport and Recreation to write to the New Zealand Olympic team and to our Olympic medallist Eliza McCartney to stop referring to New Zealand as Aotearoa, and, if not, why not?
statement: I’m sure that Minister can handle his arrangements perfectly well.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government is taking on gang harm; he names the action — progressing the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill, which reached a further reading last night. Directly responsive. The talking-point padding around it is a Focus/Specificity concern, not a dodge.
